### BRS3(KC1) - Glutathione Precursor Sufficiency (Cysteine- and glycine-linked precursor availability for glutathione synthesis) ### 1. Ambition Maintain cysteine and glycine availability for glutathione synthesis so endogenous GSH-centred redox buffering can remain available under oxidative demand. ### 2. Core Nutritional Requirements
- Cysteine - Glycine
### 3. Evidence Base #### Summary This constraint concerns cysteine and glycine availability for glutathione synthesis. Both amino acids are substrates of glutathione, and a human study in older adults with deficient synthesis found that glycine plus N-acetylcysteine (a cysteine source) restored red-cell synthesis and glutathione concentrations. Their availability can therefore form a coherent precursor bottleneck under relevant deficiency states. The evidence is conditional, however, and does not establish ordinary dietary limitation, a universal intake threshold or isolated effects of either amino acid in the general population ([Sekhar et al., 2011](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#sekhar_glutathione_2011)). - **Constraint and membership boundary:** Glutamate is required for glutathione structure but is not shown to be nutritionally limiting; polyphenols and vitamin C belong to wider redox biology rather than this precursor-availability constraint ([Packer et al., 1997](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#packer_vitamin_1997)). - **Evidence and measurement boundary:** Eight older adults were restudied after 14 days of glycine plus N-acetylcysteine, alongside eight younger controls. Isotope tracing measured red-cell glutathione synthesis; there was no placebo-controlled treatment arm, no isolated constituent comparison and no brain measurement ([Sekhar et al., 2011](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#sekhar_glutathione_2011)). - **Biological relevance and provision limitation:** Adequate precursor availability can prevent glutathione-synthesis constraint under the studied conditions, but this does not show that extra intake improves redox function or clinical outcomes in glutathione-replete people ([Sekhar et al., 2011](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#sekhar_glutathione_2011)).
#### Biological Importance Cysteine is the sulfur-amino-acid substrate in glutathione. In older adults with deficient glutathione synthesis, combined glycine and N-acetylcysteine provision restored red-cell synthesis, supporting conditional cysteine availability as one part of the precursor constraint.

Supporting Evidence

  • Sekhar et al., 2011 — In eight older adults, 14 days of glycine plus N-acetylcysteine restored red-cell glutathione synthesis measured by isotope tracing. This supports a conditional shared precursor limitation, not an isolated cysteine effect, an ordinary-food equivalent or a brain outcome.

#### Biological Importance Glycine contributes the terminal amino-acid residue of glutathione. In the same older-adult study, glycine given with N-acetylcysteine corrected deficient red-cell synthesis, supporting glycine as a conditional co-limiting precursor rather than a universally limiting dietary input.

Supporting Evidence

  • Sekhar et al., 2011 — Glycine plus N-acetylcysteine restored deficient red-cell glutathione synthesis and concentrations in eight older adults after 14 days. The before/after study does not isolate glycine or establish ordinary dietary glycine shortage, brain synthesis or long-term clinical benefit.

### 4. Emerging Biological Supports No Emerging Biological Supports are currently prioritised for this KC. ### 5. Connected Mechanisms These links identify related biology for separate relationship assessment. They do not establish that this precursor pool constrains every listed mechanism. #### Functional Mechanisms - [BRS3(FM1) - Anti-Inflammatory Signalling Tone](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-anti-inflammatory-signalling-tone) - [BRS3(FM2) - Antioxidant Defense Capacity](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity) #### Primary Mechanisms - [BRS3-FM1-PM1 - NF-kB Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm1-nf-kb-signalling-regulation) - [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation) - [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance) - [BRS3-FM2-PM5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) - [BRS3-FM1-PM2 - Gut-Derived Inflammatory Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm2-gut-derived-inflammatory-signalling) - [BRS3-FM2-PM6 - Antioxidant Network Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm6-antioxidant-network-recycling) ### 6. scientific_findings_intro: 'IKK experiments establish an activation gate, while redox studies demonstrate glutathione-dependent regulation of kinase activity and DNA binding. Human precursor tracing supports glutathione provision, but does not measure NF-κB. Together these findings support a bounded upstream supply relationship, not a proven dietary anti-inflammatory effect.'
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM1-F1
    finding_label: IKK phosphorylation is required for NF-κB activation
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: 'A purified complex from HeLa cells contains two related kinases, IKK-1 and IKK-2. They phosphorylate the inhibitor proteins that hold NF-κB. Mutant IKK-2 changes NF-κB movement into the nucleus and NF-κB-dependent reporter activity.'

(Turning Down Overactive Inflammatory Switches)

## 1. Mission & Overview

### Mission

Regulate NF-κB transcriptional tone so pro-inflammatory gene programmes do not fire excessively.


**Intervention Dominance:** Not established — No principal intervention route established

### Overview

NF-κB helps cells translate immune signals into inflammatory gene programmes. Its activation and DNA binding are regulated at several steps, including inhibitor phosphorylation and glutathione-dependent redox control. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[11]](#pm-ref-11) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) Keeping this response appropriate is the biological aim; suppressing every response is not an established health benefit.

- **Benefits:** This mechanism governs inflammatory signalling rather than a proven nutrient treatment or clinical outcome. The reviewed experiments establish regulation of activation and DNA binding. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[11]](#pm-ref-11)
- **Implementation Notes:** Cysteine and glycine have supported upstream roles through glutathione. Combined supplementation increased red-cell glutathione synthesis in older adults, but did not measure NF-κB or establish a food dose. [[13]](#pm-ref-13)
- **Biological Relevance:** Glutathione provision connects this PM to redox biology; NF-κB regulation remains distinct from glutathione synthesis and downstream cytokine-network outputs. [[11]](#pm-ref-11) [[12]](#pm-ref-12)

## 2. Primary Biological Effects
NF-κB activation, DNA binding and redox-sensitive inflammatory gene regulation

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

When inflammatory transcriptional programmes remain engaged, downstream cytokine and immune-signalling tone escalates. NF-κB is a principal upstream node through which those programmes are expressed within [BRS3(FM1) - Anti-Inflammatory Signalling Tone](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-anti-inflammatory-signalling-tone).

<strong>NF-κB signalling and inflammatory transcription</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (NF-κB as an inflammatory transcriptional node)

Mercurio et al. (1997) identified IKK-1 and IKK-2 as the kinases that phosphorylate the inhibitor proteins holding NF-κB, and showed that IKK-2 is required for NF-κB activation in the cell systems tested. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) That kinase step permits activation; it is not transcription itself. The cytokine messengers that follow it are a later step — see PM7.

#### (Signalling pressure and pattern context)

Glutathione-dependent redox regulation acts on IKK activity and NF-κB DNA binding. [[11]](#pm-ref-11) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) Redox state can inhibit as well as permit activation, so more precursor supply cannot be assumed to suppress inflammation. The attached dietary-pattern studies do not independently establish a PM-specific intervention. Adams (2001) reviews ATP-dependent protein-kinase chemistry, including the usual metal partner of that reaction. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) That chemistry is not a dietary magnesium result.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

Downstream cytokine-network expression is handled by [BRS3-FM3-PM7 - Cytokine Network Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm7-cytokine-network-modulation). Gut-derived endotoxin load is represented by [BRS3-FM1-PM2 - Gut-Derived Inflammatory Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm2-gut-derived-inflammatory-signalling). EPA/DHA as specialised pro-resolving mediator substrates, and review claims that SPMs downregulate NF-κB, belong to [BRS3-FM3-PM8 - Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance). This PM does not currently carry an evidence-qualified EPA/DHA dietary requirement or System Optimisation Practice for NF-κB transcriptional tone. Endogenous antioxidant induction and net redox balance belong to [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation) and [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance).

#### (Integration within BRS3)

This PM anchors transcriptional inflammatory tone within [BRS3(FM1)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-anti-inflammatory-signalling-tone). Gut-barrier context imported through [BRS5-FM1-PM1 - Gut Barrier / Tight Junction Integrity](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-pm1-gut-barrier-tight-junction-integrity) conditions endotoxin-linked pressure on this pathway.

</div>
</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

IKK experiments establish an activation gate, while redox studies demonstrate glutathione-dependent regulation of kinase activity and DNA binding. Human precursor tracing supports glutathione provision, but does not measure NF-κB. Together these findings support a bounded upstream supply relationship, not a proven dietary anti-inflammatory effect.

## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections

### 5.1 BRS Pathways

- None listed

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS5-FM1-PM1 — Gut Barrier / Tight Junction Integrity](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-pm1-gut-barrier-tight-junction-integrity) — A compromised tight junction lets lipopolysaccharide cross. That is inflammatory pressure on this transcription factor, not the IKK phosphorylation step.
- [BRS5(FM1) — Gut Barrier Integrity and Immune Interface](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-gut-barrier-integrity-and-immune-interface) — The gut–immune interface sets how much microbial product reaches systemic signalling. That is upstream context for this transcription step.
- [BRS6-FM1-PM2 — Glycaemic Variability Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs6/fm1/brs6-fm1-pm2-glycaemic-variability-regulation) — Postprandial glycaemic swings are cited as inflammatory context around this pathway. They are not the IKK phosphorylation reaction.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS3-FM1-PM2 - Gut-Derived Inflammatory Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm2-gut-derived-inflammatory-signalling) — Gut-derived signalling is the barrier-entry step that can raise the inflammatory load this transcription factor responds to.
- [BRS3-FM3-PM8 - Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance) — Eicosanoid and resolving-mediator balance is a later lipid-signal step. It is not the IKK release of NF-κB.

## 7. Phenome Connections

These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

Mission & Overview ### Mission Keep inflammatory signalling intensity in check so pro-inflammatory transcription, cytokines, and gut-derived immune load do not chronically dominate. ### Overview A diet-actionable control point that helps regulate how intensely inflammatory signals fire across cytokine networks, NF-κB transcription (a master switch for pro-inflammatory gene expression), gut-derived inputs, and lipid-mediator pathways. * Helps keep pro-inflammatory transcriptional tone in check through NF-κB regulation. * Limits gut-derived endotoxin spillover into systemic inflammatory signalling — Supporting BRS5. * Connects dietary antioxidant and fatty-acid context to inflammatory intensity. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↓ NF-kB tone; ↓ pro-inflammatory cytokines; ↑ immune signalling balance ## 4. Mechanistic Basis (Integrated FM Narrative) ### 4.1 Functional Rationale Inflammatory transcriptional regulation and containment of gut-derived endotoxin contribute to managing inflammatory signalling pressure. They act at distinct stages, so a change in one readout does not establish control of the entire system. ### 4.2 Evidence Summary Kinase studies establish the NF-κB activation step, while metabolic-endotoxaemia reviews connect barrier translocation with systemic inflammatory exposure. Fermentation and SCFA sources supply relevant gut–host context, but do not directly measure reduced endotoxin translocation following fibre intake. [[5](#fm-ref-5), [8](#fm-ref-8), [9](#fm-ref-9), [10](#fm-ref-10), [11](#fm-ref-11)] Effective containment and regulated transcription would be expected to limit excessive inflammatory signalling. The aggregated evidence does not demonstrate dietary control of both steps or show that a circulating inflammatory marker identifies which step changed. ### 4.3 Suboptimal Function & Its Effects Anti-inflammatory signalling tone may weaken when antioxidant substrate availability becomes chronically inadequate or when habitual EPA/DHA intake fails to support resolution-competent lipid-mediator context. Low fruit and vegetable intake may reduce [BRS3(KC1) — Antioxidant Substrate Availability](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/kc/brs3-kc1-antioxidant-substrate-availability). Low polyphenol density, poor sulfur-amino-acid and glutathione-building substrate availability, chronic oxidative burden, and ultra-processed patterns displacing antioxidant-rich foods may further amplify inflammatory signalling pressure. Low omega-3 intake may limit EPA/DHA substrate availability for lipid-mediator pathways. Excessive omega-6 dominance, low oily-fish consumption, poor fatty-acid diversity, and chronic inflammatory load may skew lipid-mediator context away from resolution-competent signalling. Gut barrier compromise and metabolic endotoxemia may amplify gut-derived inflammatory inputs—see [BRS5(FM1) — Gut Barrier Integrity and Immune Interface](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-gut-barrier-integrity-and-immune-interface). These pressures may impair [BRS3-FM1-PM1 — NF-kB Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm1-nf-kb-signalling-regulation) and weaken [BRS3-FM1-PM2 — Gut-Derived Inflammatory Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm2-gut-derived-inflammatory-signalling). At the FM level, this may shift BRS3(FM1) toward chronically elevated pro-inflammatory tone. ## 5. Connected Mechanisms - [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation) — Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation - [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance) — rOS Generation vs Clearance Balance - [BRS3-FM3-PM7 - Cytokine Network Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm7-cytokine-network-modulation) — cytokine Network Modulation - [BRS5-FM1-PM1 — Gut Barrier / Tight Junction Integrity](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-pm1-gut-barrier-tight-junction-integrity) — gut Barrier / Tight Junction Integrity - [BRS5(FM1) — Gut Barrier Integrity and Immune Interface](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-gut-barrier-integrity-and-immune-interface) — Upstream NF-κB transcriptional control - [BRS6-FM1-PM2 — Glycaemic Variability Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs6/fm1/brs6-fm1-pm2-glycaemic-variability-regulation) — Insulin Sensitivity & Glucose Disposal ## 7. ## BRS3-1-2 - Gut-Derived Inflammatory Signalling

(Endotoxin Spillover and Gut Interface Management)

## 1. Mission & Overview

### Mission

Limit gut-derived endotoxin spillover so barrier dysfunction does not drive systemic inflammatory load.


**Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Supported in an obese-mouse experiment; no principal intervention route established

A defined oligofructose exposure changed permeability and circulating LPS in obese mice. Human implementation and comparative route prominence remain unestablished. [[14]](#pm-ref-14)

### Overview

The gut barrier helps contain microbial products within the intestine. When that containment changes, endotoxin can contribute to systemic inflammatory signalling. This PM concerns the gut-derived load reaching the circulation, connecting intestinal barrier function with inflammatory regulation elsewhere. Experimental evidence identifies epithelial redox protection and a prebiotic-sensitive barrier route, while their context determines what can be inferred about dietary action. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) [[14]](#pm-ref-14)

- **Benefits:** Limiting inappropriate microbial-product entry helps contain inflammatory pressure; the reviewed experiments do not establish a clinical treatment benefit. [[1]](#pm-ref-1)
- **Implementation Notes:** Cysteine and glycine provide upstream glutathione resources. Oligofructose altered barrier readouts in obese mice, but a human intake protocol is not established. [[11]](#pm-ref-11) [[14]](#pm-ref-14)
- **Biological Relevance:** Gut-barrier processes connect BRS5 to this gut-derived load; [PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm1-nf-kb-signalling-regulation) concerns the downstream NF-κB response.

## 2. Primary Biological Effects
Gut-to-blood microbial-product handling; barrier-related systemic inflammatory signalling.

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Systemic inflammatory tone can be driven partly by gut-derived signals. When barrier integrity weakens, endotoxin and related microbial inputs enter circulation more readily, increasing low-grade inflammatory signalling within [BRS3(FM1) - Anti-Inflammatory Signalling Tone](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-anti-inflammatory-signalling-tone).

<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Endotoxin-linked inflammatory load)

Mohammad and Thiemermann (2021) review lipopolysaccharide reaching the blood after a change in the gut lining, with inflammatory signalling through Toll-like receptor 4. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) That is the spillover this mechanism governs.

#### (Microbial and barrier modulation logic)

Koh et al. (2016) describe fermentation of dietary fibre to short-chain fatty acids. [[10]](#pm-ref-10) Cavaliere et al. (2022) gave butyrate to obese mice and saw a partial fall in cortical neuroinflammation. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Neither result measures lipopolysaccharide crossing the barrier, so neither is a dietary requirement of this spillover.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

Downstream NF-κB transcriptional control is handled by [BRS3-FM1-PM1 - NF-kB Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm1-nf-kb-signalling-regulation). Downstream cytokine-network expression belongs to [BRS3-FM3-PM7 - Cytokine Network Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm7-cytokine-network-modulation). Native gut-barrier biology is represented within [BRS5](/docs/biological-targets/gut-brain-axis-enteric-nervous-system); this PM captures the BRS3 inflammatory-tone output of gut-derived signals.

#### (Integration within BRS3)

This PM links gut-derived inputs to inflammatory tone within [BRS3(FM1)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-anti-inflammatory-signalling-tone). Barrier and endotoxin-containment context imported through section 4.3 connected mechanisms conditions translocation load.

</div>
</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

The evidence supports gut-derived inflammatory load as a barrier-related process. Glutathione participates in oxidant-sensitive epithelial protection, but is not a universal barrier constraint. A defined prebiotic intervention changed permeability and circulating LPS in obese mice; this does not establish a generic fibre requirement or a human intake target.

## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections

### 5.1 BRS Pathways

- None listed

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS5-FM1-PM1 — Gut Barrier / Tight Junction Integrity](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-pm1-gut-barrier-tight-junction-integrity) — Tight-junction integrity limits lipopolysaccharide crossing into the circulation that this page treats as the inflammatory exposure.
- [BRS5(FM1) — Gut Barrier Integrity and Immune Interface](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-gut-barrier-integrity-and-immune-interface) — The gut–immune interface is the setting in which barrier failure lets microbial products raise systemic inflammatory signalling.
- [BRS6-FM1-PM2 — Glycaemic Variability Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs6/fm1/brs6-fm1-pm2-glycaemic-variability-regulation) — Glycaemic variability is neighbouring metabolic context. It is not the measurement of endotoxin crossing the gut barrier.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS3-FM1-PM1 - NF-kB Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm1-nf-kb-signalling-regulation) — NF-κB transcriptional control is the neighbouring response once inflammatory load is already raised. It is not this gut-entry step.

## 7. Phenome Connections

These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

## BRS3-2-3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation (Regulating cellular defence gene expression) ## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers ### Mission Regulate the expression of cellular defence genes in response to oxidative and electrophilic stress. **Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Supported
- Sulforaphane
No evidence-supported cofactors or substrates are currently established for this mechanism.
No mapping established.
### Overview Nrf2 is held by Keap1 until oxidative or electrophilic stress lets it reach defence genes. Itoh et al. (1999) showed that Keap1 represses Nrf2 and that electrophiles release that repression. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Zhang et al. (2004) showed that Keap1 marks Nrf2 for disposal until stress or sulforaphane slows that disposal. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) A three-day broccoli sprout homogenate raised phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) That is airway gene expression, not brain Nrf2, and sulforaphane is not a nutrient this regulation requires. - **Benefits:** This regulation lets cells raise defence-gene transcription when oxidative or electrophilic stress rises. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) - **Implementation Notes:** The tested practice is a myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate once a day for three days. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) Capsules of extracted sulforaphane did not raise the same class of genes in COPD lung cells. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) - **Biological Relevance:** The enzymes this regulation induces are used by later clearance, membrane, and recycling steps — see PM4, PM5 and PM6. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects Defence-gene transcription rises when stress releases Nrf2 from Keap1 ## 3. Intervention Levers

Only the category with a reviewed practice is shown.

A three-day broccoli sprout homogenate, prepared with added myrosinase, raised phase II enzyme gene expression in nasal cells. This is not an ordinary broccoli serving or a sulforaphane capsule.

- Myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate
No lifestyle lever is established. Sleep, stress, and activity were not shown to change this regulation.
## 4. Mechanistic Basis ### Summary Cellular defence-gene expression is regulated when oxidative or electrophilic stress releases Nrf2 from Keap1. That regulation sits within [BRS3(FM2) - Antioxidant Defense Capacity](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity).
#### (Nrf2-ARE signalling) Itoh et al. (1999) showed that Keap1 represses Nrf2 until electrophiles release that hold. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Zhang et al. (2004) showed that Keap1 marks Nrf2 for disposal, and that oxidative stress or sulforaphane slows that disposal. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) Raising the response is not, by itself, the aim of this regulation. #### (Isothiocyanate signalling and induction kinetics) Riedl, Saxon and Diaz-Sanchez (2009) found that a three-day broccoli sprout homogenate, finished with daikon myrosinase, raised phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) Wise et al. (2016) found that four weeks of extracted sulforaphane capsules did not raise Nrf2 target genes in COPD lung cells. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Sulforaphane is an inducer in this preparation, not a nutrient the regulation requires. #### (Boundaries of the mechanism) Net ROS generation versus clearance dynamics are handled by [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance). Membrane lipid protection belongs to [BRS3-FM2-PM5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control). Antioxidant-network recycling and regeneration are represented by [BRS3-FM2-PM6 - Antioxidant Network Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm6-antioxidant-network-recycling). #### (Integration within BRS3) This PM supports endogenous defence capacity within [BRS3(FM2)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity). Vitamin C, zinc and selenium are not established here as requirements of the activation step.
### 4.1 Scientific Findings #### Summary Keap1 holds Nrf2 until oxidative or electrophilic stress lets defence genes be transcribed. A three-day myrosinase-completed broccoli sprout homogenate raised phase II enzyme RNA in nasal cells. Extracted sulforaphane capsules did not raise that class of genes in COPD lung cells. Sulforaphane is not a nutrient this regulation requires. ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections ### 5.1 BRS Pathways - None listed ### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism. - [BRS4-FM1-PM1 — Electron Transport Chain Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function) — Mitochondrial electron transport is a source of reactive oxygen that this regulation responds to. It is not Nrf2 transcription itself. - [BRS4-FM2-PM4 — ROS Production and Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm4-ros-production-and-control) — Mitochondrial reactive-oxygen control is an upstream source of oxidative load. This page regulates defence-gene expression rather than generating that load. ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance) — Clearance enzymes set net oxidative pressure. This page regulates expression of those defence genes. It is not the clearance balance. - [BRS3-FM2-PM5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) — Lipid peroxidation is membrane damage downstream of oxidative load. This regulation does not itself stop that chain reaction. - [BRS3-FM2-PM6 - Antioxidant Network Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm6-antioxidant-network-recycling) — Recycling regenerates vitamin and thiol antioxidants after use. This page regulates defence-gene expression and does not restore the spent vitamins. ## 7. Phenome Connections These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. ## BRS3-2-5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control (Protecting Membrane Fats from Oxidative Damage) ## 1. Mission & Overview ### Mission Protect membrane fats from oxidative damage so vulnerable polyunsaturated fatty acids remain intact. **Intervention Dominance:** Not established — No principal intervention route established Vitamin E is required for the chain-breaking reaction. No cited study shows that raising vitamin E intake lowers membrane peroxidation. ### Overview Peroxyl radicals can keep oxidising polyunsaturated fats in membranes. Niki (2014) shows that vitamin E is the main lipophilic antioxidant that breaks that chain, and that it does so for peroxyl radicals rather than for every oxidant. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) Traber and Atkinson (2007) place that job in protecting those fats in membranes. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Extra vitamin E was not shown to lower peroxidation. - **Benefits:** Breaking this chain helps keep polyunsaturated fats intact in membranes. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) - **Implementation Notes:** Vitamin E is the nutrient in that reaction. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) No intake was shown to lower peroxidation. A prevention trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU a day. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) - **Biological Relevance:** Generation versus clearance of reactive oxygen is the upstream pressure — see PM4. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↓ lipid peroxidation; ↑ membrane stability ## 3. Intervention Levers
- Vitamin E
Vitamin E is already the dietary requirement above. It is not repeated here.
No mapping established.
No evidence-qualified System Optimisation Practice is established.
No lifestyle lever is established. Sleep, activity, and meal timing were not shown to change membrane peroxidation.
## 4. Mechanistic Basis ### Summary Polyunsaturated fatty acids in membranes are especially vulnerable to oxidative attack. When peroxidation outpaces lipid-phase antioxidant protection, structural and signalling lipid pools destabilise within [BRS3(FM2) - Antioxidant Defense Capacity](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity).
#### (Lipid peroxidation burden) Niki (2014) shows that peroxyl radicals propagate through polyunsaturated fats and that vitamin E breaks that chain. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) Malondialdehyde comparisons in clinical cohorts are not this reaction. #### (Lipid-phase antioxidant protection) Traber and Atkinson (2007) place the vitamin function of vitamin E in protecting polyunsaturated fats in membranes. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Lutein and lycopene absorption are not this chain-breaking job. Vitamin E's later regeneration by vitamin C is a different job — see PM6. #### (Boundaries of the mechanism) Net ROS generation versus clearance is handled by [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance). Transcriptional Nrf2 induction belongs to [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation). Eicosanoid and SPM substrate quality downstream is represented by [BRS3-FM3-PM8 - Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance). #### (Integration within BRS3) This PM protects membrane lipid integrity within [BRS3(FM2)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity). No shared-pool mapping is established. Mitochondrial reactive-oxygen generation is a neighbouring pressure — see BRS4.
### 4.1 Scientific Findings #### Summary Vitamin E breaks peroxyl-radical chains in membranes and is placed there to protect polyunsaturated fats. Extra vitamin E was not shown to lower peroxidation. A long trial found more prostate cancers with 400 IU a day. ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections ### 5.1 BRS Pathways - None listed ### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism. - [BRS4-FM1-PM1 — Electron Transport Chain Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function) — Electron transport can supply the oxidative load that propagates into membrane polyunsaturated fats. It is not the lipid-phase interruption step. - [BRS4-FM2-PM4 — ROS Production and Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm4-ros-production-and-control) — Mitochondrial reactive-oxygen control is upstream pressure. This page is the membrane-fat chain reaction that follows when that pressure is high. ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation) — Nrf2 regulates defence-gene expression. It does not interrupt peroxidation of membrane polyunsaturated fats. - [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance) — Generation versus clearance is the oxidative pressure upstream of this membrane-fat damage. - [BRS3-FM2-PM6 - Antioxidant Network Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm6-antioxidant-network-recycling) — Vitamin C and vitamin E recycling keeps the lipid-phase antioxidant working. summary: 'Cells generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) during ordinary immune and metabolic activity, and enzymatic clearance uses selenium, zinc, copper, and manganese. ### Overview

Cells generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) during ordinary immune and metabolic activity, and enzymatic clearance uses selenium, zinc, copper, and manganese. [[21]](#pm-ref-21) Net oxidative pressure is the balance of generation and clearance, not the level of one marker. [[21]](#pm-ref-21) When generation outruns clearance, oxidative damage accumulates across membranes, proteins, and mitochondria. [[21]](#pm-ref-21) High-heat cooking can add advanced glycation end products that raise this pressure. [[5]](#pm-ref-5)

- **Benefits:** Balancing production against clearance helps keep net oxidative pressure within what cells can tolerate. [[21]](#pm-ref-21) When production outruns clearance, the excess reaches membranes, proteins, and mitochondria. [[21]](#pm-ref-21)
- **Implementation Notes:** Selenium and copper are the provision routes. [[22]](#pm-ref-22) [[23]](#pm-ref-23) Glutathione is the thiol used in peroxidase clearance, not a dietary target. [[21]](#pm-ref-21) Extra intake when status is already adequate is not established. [[22]](#pm-ref-22)
- **Biological Relevance:** [Membrane lipid damage](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) is a later result of that pressure, not this balance. [[11]](#pm-ref-11)

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Net oxidative pressure is whether superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase keep up with reactive oxygen made in ordinary metabolism. [[21]](#pm-ref-21) Selenium and copper are the intake routes that restore glutathione peroxidase and copper-zinc superoxide dismutase when status is low. [[22]](#pm-ref-22) [[23]](#pm-ref-23) Zinc, manganese and glutathione belong to those enzymes and are not separate dietary targets. [[21]](#pm-ref-21)

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">

<strong>ROS generation, clearance capacity, and net redox pressure</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Generation and clearance)

Cells make superoxide and hydrogen peroxide during ordinary aerobic metabolism. Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. Catalase and glutathione peroxidase convert hydrogen peroxide to water. [[21]](#pm-ref-21) Copper-zinc superoxide dismutase is cytosolic. Manganese superoxide dismutase is mitochondrial. Glutathione peroxidase is a selenoprotein and uses glutathione. [[21]](#pm-ref-21)

#### (What intake has been shown to change)

In adults whose diet supplied about 14 micrograms of selenium a day, plasma glutathione peroxidase activity levelled off at a total intake of about 35 micrograms a day. More selenium did not raise that enzyme further. [[22]](#pm-ref-22) In infants recovering from malnutrition with marginal copper, copper supplementation raised red-cell superoxide dismutase. [[23]](#pm-ref-23) Neither result is a reason to add more when status is already adequate.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

Catalase uses haem iron. No human study retrieved for this page shows that iron intake sets catalase activity, so iron is not a dietary requirement here. Mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen is [BRS4-FM2-PM4 — ROS Production and Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm4-ros-production-and-control). Transcriptional induction of the enzymes is [BRS3-FM2-PM3 — Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation). Membrane lipid damage is [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control). Recycling among network antioxidants is [BRS3-FM2-PM6 — Antioxidant Network Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm6-antioxidant-network-recycling).

#### (Integration within BRS3)

This page is the generation-versus-clearance balance inside [BRS3(FM2)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity). A shared precursor-pool constraint is not established for this balance.

</div>
</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Net oxidative pressure is the balance of reactive-oxygen generation and enzymatic clearance. Superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase do that clearance. Selenium and copper are the dietary provision routes. Zinc, manganese and glutathione stay with the enzymes and are not separate dietary targets. Extra intake when status is adequate is not established.

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS4-FM1-PM1 — Electron Transport Chain Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function) — Electron transport is a source of reactive oxygen that this balance has to clear. It is not the clearance-enzyme cofactor step.
- [BRS4-FM2-PM4 — ROS Production and Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm4-ros-production-and-control) — Mitochondrial reactive-oxygen control is the production side that this page balances against enzymatic clearance.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS3-FM2-PM3 — Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation) — Nrf2 regulates defence-gene expression. It does not clear superoxide or hydrogen peroxide itself.
- [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) — membrane-specific lipid damage downstream of net redox imbalance
- [BRS3-FM2-PM6 — Antioxidant Network Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm6-antioxidant-network-recycling) — regeneration among network antioxidants that sustain clearance

## BRS3-2-6 - Antioxidant Network Recycling (Recycling the Body's Antioxidant Defences) ## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers ### Mission Regenerate vitamin and thiol antioxidants across networked systems so endogenous defence capacity is sustained. **Intervention Dominance:** Not established — No principal intervention route established Ascorbate reduces the vitamin E radical in a chemical observation. No cited study shows that raising vitamin C or vitamin E intake speeds that recycling.
- Vitamin C - Vitamin E
Vitamin C and vitamin E are already the dietary requirements above. They are not repeated here.
No mapping established.
### Overview Vitamin C can reduce the vitamin E radical and return vitamin E toward its working form. Packer, Slater and Willson (1979) observed that reaction directly. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Niki (2014) describes the same partnership as extending vitamin E capacity. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) This is regeneration, not the chain-breaking job vitamin E does in membranes, and it is not a high-dose rule. - **Benefits:** Regenerating vitamin E after it has acted lets that antioxidant keep working longer than one reaction. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) - **Implementation Notes:** Vitamin C and vitamin E are the nutrients in this reaction. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) No intake was shown to speed it. Extra vitamin E is not a benefit. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) - **Biological Relevance:** Defence-gene regulation is a different step — see PM3. Vitamin E breaking peroxyl-radical chains in membranes is a different job — see PM5. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↑ antioxidant regeneration; ↑ persistence of antioxidant protection ## 3. Intervention Levers
No evidence-qualified System Optimisation Practice is established.
No lifestyle lever is established. Sleep, stress, and activity were not shown to change this recycling step.
## 4. Mechanistic Basis ### Summary Antioxidant protection persists only when depleted antioxidants are regenerated across interacting systems. Network recycling—not isolated nutrient presence—determines whether redox defence remains effective within [BRS3(FM2) - Antioxidant Defense Capacity](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity).
#### (Network rather than single-nutrient protection) Packer, Slater and Willson (1979) observed ascorbate reducing the vitamin E radical. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Niki (2014) describes that partnership as extending vitamin E capacity. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) Glutathione and other thiols are sometimes placed in a wider network. They are not a dietary glutathione target here — see PM4. #### (Regeneration cycles and cofactor dependence) The recycling job is vitamin C reducing the vitamin E radical. [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Vitamin E stopping peroxyl radicals in the membrane is a different job — see PM5. Klein et al. (2011) found more prostate cancers with 400 IU of vitamin E a day, so this chemistry is not a high-dose rule. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) #### (Boundaries of the mechanism) Transcriptional Nrf2 induction belongs to [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation). Net ROS generation versus clearance is handled by [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance). Membrane lipid peroxidation control is represented by [BRS3-FM2-PM5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control). #### (Integration within BRS3) This PM encodes regeneration of vitamin E by vitamin C within [BRS3(FM2)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-antioxidant-defense-capacity). No shared-pool mapping is established. Mitochondrial electron transport can change how fast radicals are formed, which is a neighbouring pressure on this recycling step, not the recycling reaction itself — see [BRS4-FM1-PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function).
### 4.1 Scientific Findings #### Summary Vitamin C can reduce the vitamin E radical and return vitamin E to its working form. That regeneration is distinct from vitamin E breaking peroxyl-radical chains. It is not a high-dose rule. ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections ### 5.1 BRS Pathways - None listed ### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism. - [BRS4-FM1-PM1 — Electron Transport Chain Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function) — Electron transport is a source of the oxidative load this network regenerates against. It is not the vitamin-to-vitamin recycling step. - [BRS4-FM2-PM4 — ROS Production and Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm4-ros-production-and-control) — Mitochondrial reactive-oxygen control is upstream oxidative pressure. This page regenerates spent antioxidants and does not set that production rate. ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS3-FM2-PM3 - Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation) — Nrf2 regulates defence-gene expression. It does not return oxidised vitamin E to its working form. - [BRS3-FM2-PM4 - ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance) — Clearance balance is the net oxidative pressure. Recycling keeps the antioxidant network available for that clearance. - [BRS3-FM2-PM5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) — Lipid peroxidation is the membrane-fat damage that vitamin E interrupts. Recycling restores that vitamin after it has been used. ## 7. Phenome Connections These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. ## BRS3(FM2) - Antioxidant Defense Capacity (Antioxidant Defence & Redox Protection) ### Primary Mechanisms - [BRS3-FM2-PM3 — Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation) - [BRS3-FM2-PM4 — ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance) - [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) - [BRS3-FM2-PM6 — Antioxidant Network Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm6-antioxidant-network-recycling) ### Key Constraints - [BRS3(KC1) — Antioxidant Substrate Availability](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/kc/brs3-kc1-antioxidant-substrate-availability) ## 1. Mission & Overview ### Mission Maintain endogenous and dietary antioxidant protection so oxidative damage and lipid peroxidation stay controlled under everyday metabolic and immune load. ### Overview A functional control point regulating endogenous and dietary antioxidant protection against redox overload, oxidative damage, and lipid peroxidation (oxidative breakdown of membrane fats). * Raises endogenous antioxidant defence through Nrf2-dependent gene programmes. * Balances reactive oxygen species production against clearance capacity. * Protects membrane lipids and polyunsaturated fatty acids from oxidative degradation. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↑ antioxidant enzyme induction; ↑ ROS buffering; ↓ oxidative damage ## 4. Mechanistic Basis (Integrated FM Narrative) ### 4.1 Functional Rationale Defence-gene activation, reactive-oxygen clearance, lipid protection and antioxidant recycling provide complementary contributions to antioxidant capacity; adequate function means maintaining protection, not maximising every antioxidant measure. ### 4.2 Evidence Summary Human sprout exposures produced different gene-expression results in nasal cells and COPD lung cells. Selenium and copper repletion studies support status-dependent enzyme activity in specific low-status populations. Reviews establish lipid-phase protection and antioxidant regeneration, while the attached lipid-peroxidation evidence does not establish a vitamin E intake response. [[1](#fm-ref-1), [17](#fm-ref-17), [18](#fm-ref-18), [19](#fm-ref-19), [20](#fm-ref-20), [21](#fm-ref-21)] Functioning induction, clearance, protection and recycling capacities would collectively support redox defence. This evidence spans different tissues, populations and endpoints; it does not demonstrate a combined reduction in brain oxidative pressure or justify higher intake when status is adequate. ### 4.3 Suboptimal Function & Its Effects Suboptimal function describes common ways this functional capacity becomes overloaded or inefficient. They are not separate PMs and should not duplicate PM definitions. **A. High-temperature food preparation burden** Repeated frying, charring, grilling, and high-temperature cooking can increase AGE/ALE formation, oxidised lipid exposure, and redox pressure [Uribarri et al., 2010]. **B. Oxidised fat and reheated oil exposure** Repeatedly heated oils, rancid fats, and oxidised PUFA-rich foods can increase lipid oxidation products and antioxidant demand. **C. Low antioxidant network support** Low intake of polyphenol-rich foods, colourful plants, selenium, zinc, copper, manganese, and glutathione-supportive substrates may reduce clearance capacity [Packer et al., 1997; Mocchegiani & Malavolta, 2019; Vertuani et al., 2004]. **D. Environmental and contaminant oxidative load** Smoking, air pollution, heavy metals, and micro/nanoplastics may increase oxidative burden and interact with dietary antioxidant capacity [Zhai et al., 2015; Berglund et al., 1994; Dufault et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025]. **E. Hyperglycaemic and ultra-processed food burden** High refined-sugar, low-fibre, ultra-processed patterns may increase glycaemic variability, oxidative stress, and inflammatory–redox coupling [Jiang et al., 2021]. #### Summary Antioxidant defense capacity becomes overloaded when exogenous oxidant exposure rises while endogenous clearance support falls. High-heat cooking and oxidised or repeatedly heated fats increase lipid oxidation products and AGE/ALE burden [Uribarri et al., 2010]; low polyphenol density, trace-mineral gaps, and weak glutathione-building substrate availability reduce network recycling and enzyme sufficiency [Packer et al., 1997; Mocchegiani & Malavolta, 2019; Vertuani et al., 2004]. Environmental contaminants and ultra-processed, hyperglycaemic dietary patterns add further oxidative and inflammatory–redox load [Jiang et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2015; Berglund et al., 1994; Dufault et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025]. Together, these pressures strain the coordinated Nrf2 induction, ROS clearance, membrane protection, and antioxidant recycling that define BRS3(FM2). These FM2 failure modes may secondarily amplify [BRS3(FM1) — Anti-Inflammatory Signalling Tone](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-anti-inflammatory-signalling-tone) inflammatory signalling, but their primary home is FM2 because they increase redox burden or reduce antioxidant defense capacity. When failure modes persist, they may impair [BRS3-FM2-PM3 — Nrf2-Mediated Cellular Defence Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm3-nrf2-are-antioxidant-activation), weaken [BRS3-FM2-PM4 — ROS Generation vs Clearance Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm4-ros-generation-vs-clearance-balance), reduce the effectiveness of [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control), and compromise [BRS3-FM2-PM6 — Antioxidant Network Recycling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm6-antioxidant-network-recycling). At the FM level, this may shift BRS3(FM2) toward reduced antioxidant defense capacity performance. ## 5. Connected Mechanisms - [BRS3-FM3-PM8 - Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance) — eicosanoid / SPM Balance - [BRS3(FM1) — Anti-Inflammatory Signalling Tone](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-anti-inflammatory-signalling-tone) — anti-Inflammatory Signalling Tone - [BRS4-FM1-PM1 — Electron Transport Chain Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function) — electron Transport Chain Function - [BRS4-FM2-PM4 — ROS Production and Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm4-ros-production-and-control) — biological connection relevant to this mechanism ## 7. Phenome Connections These outcomes describe translational contexts for the FM as an integrated biological capacity. They are not single-mechanism treatment claims. FM confidence uplift: FM confidence may exceed that of any individual child PM only where multiple PMs converge on the same phenome and the integrated FM biology provides additional biological rationale (biological uplift) beyond the individual mechanisms.

## BRS3-3-8 - Eicosanoid / SPM Balance (Shifting from Pro-Inflammatory to Calming Pro-Resolving Lipid Signals) ## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers ### Mission Shift lipid mediator balance from pro-inflammatory eicosanoids toward pro-resolving signals that terminate inflammation. **Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Dominant Short-term n-3 fatty acid supplementation raised some circulating pro-resolving mediators in healthy adults. Not every mediator rose, and this is not a disease-resolution outcome.
- EPA - DHA
EPA and DHA are already the dietary requirements above. They are not repeated here.
No mapping established.
### Overview Resolvins and protectins are made from EPA and DHA, and they help inflammation finish rather than only blocking it. Serhan and Petasis (2011) describe that pathway. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) Barden et al. (2014) found that 2.4 g a day of n-3 fatty acids for five days raised RvE1 and several pathway markers in healthy adults. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) Not every mediator rose. - **Benefits:** These mediators support the finishing of inflammation, which is a different job from blocking the signal at the start. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) - **Implementation Notes:** EPA and DHA are the substrates. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) The intake that raised some mediators was 2.4 g a day for five days in healthy adults, not a disease-resolution dose. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) - **Biological Relevance:** Cytokine intensity is a later messenger readout — see PM7. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↑ pro-resolving mediator bias; ↓ pro-inflammatory eicosanoid dominance ## 3. Intervention Levers
No evidence-qualified System Optimisation Practice is established.
No lifestyle lever is established. Sleep, stress, and activity were not shown to change these mediators.
## 4. Mechanistic Basis ### Summary Inflammation termination depends on lipid mediators that actively resolve rather than merely suppress immune activity. EPA and DHA substrate availability shapes whether signalling bias moves toward specialized pro-resolving mediators within [BRS3(FM3) - Inflammation Resolution Capacity](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-inflammation-resolution-capacity).
#### (Lipid mediator balance) Serhan and Petasis (2011) describe resolvins and protectins as mediators made from EPA and DHA, distinct from blockade of inflammation. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) #### (Fatty-acid substrate competition) Barden et al. (2014) found that five days of n-3 fatty acids raised some of those mediators in healthy adults, and not others. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) An evolutionary omega-6 to omega-3 review is not that measurement. #### (Boundaries of the mechanism) Downstream cytokine-network readouts are handled by [BRS3-FM3-PM7 - Cytokine Network Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm7-cytokine-network-modulation). Membrane PUFA protection upstream belongs to [BRS3-FM2-PM5 - Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control). Transcriptional inflammatory control is represented by [BRS3-FM1-PM1 - NF-kB Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm1-nf-kb-signalling-regulation). #### (Integration within BRS3) This PM anchors resolution-oriented lipid signalling within [BRS3(FM3)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-inflammation-resolution-capacity), supported by habitual EPA/DHA intake through §4.1.1 Direct and/or Derived Dietary Requirements.

## BRS3(FM3) - Inflammation Resolution Capacity (Inflammation Resolution & Lipid Mediator Balance) ### Primary Mechanisms - [BRS3-FM3-PM7 — Cytokine Network Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm7-cytokine-network-modulation) - [BRS3-FM3-PM8 — Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance) ## 1. Mission & Overview ### Mission Enable active termination of inflammation through pro-resolving lipid signals rather than relying on simple immune suppression. ### Overview A functional control point governing active termination of inflammation through pro-resolving lipid mediators (specialised molecules that switch inflammation off) rather than simple suppression of immune activity. * Modulates cytokine signalling tone across IL-6, TNF-α, and CRP-linked pathways. * Balances arachidonic-acid inflammatory mediators against EPA/DHA-derived pro-resolving mediators. * Depends on essential fatty acid balance and antioxidant substrate sufficiency. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↑ resolvins/protectins/maresins; ↑ debris clearance; ↓ unresolved inflammation ## 4. Mechanistic Basis (Integrated FM Narrative) ### 4.1 Functional Rationale Inflammatory messenger regulation and production of specialised resolving mediators contribute to an appropriate inflammatory response and its resolution. Resolution is a distinct biological task from suppressing inflammation. ### 4.2 Evidence Summary Human endotoxin-challenge evidence reads cytokine responses; pathway evidence identifies EPA- and DHA-derived specialised pro-resolving mediators and substrate competition. These sources establish different parts of inflammatory signalling and resolution rather than a single dietary resolution experiment. [[1](#fm-ref-1), [2](#fm-ref-2), [6](#fm-ref-6), [8](#fm-ref-8)] If messenger regulation and resolving-mediator production operate appropriately, they would support progression from inflammatory response toward resolution. Substrate availability and cytokine changes alone do not establish clinical resolution or define an intake that optimises it. ### 4.3 Suboptimal Function & Its Effects Inflammation resolution capacity may weaken when habitual EPA/DHA intake and omega-3/omega-6 dietary balance become chronically unfavourable for specialized pro-resolving mediator formation. Low omega-3 intake may limit EPA/DHA substrate availability for resolvin, protectin, and maresin pathways. Excessive omega-6 dominance, low oily-fish consumption, poor dietary fatty-acid diversity, and chronic inflammatory load may further constrain specialised pro-resolving mediator formation [Serhan & Petasis, 2011]. Oxidative damage to membrane lipids—when [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) is strained—may further compromise the lipid environment required for active resolution rather than prolonged cytokine elevation. These pressures may impair [BRS3-FM3-PM7 — Cytokine Network Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm7-cytokine-network-modulation) and weaken [BRS3-FM3-PM8 — Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance). At the FM level, this may shift BRS3(FM3) toward impaired inflammation resolution capacity. ## 5. ## BRS3-3-7 - Cytokine Network Modulation (Coordinating Immune Signalling Intensity) ## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers ### Mission Tune downstream cytokine signalling intensity so inflammatory tone does not remain chronically elevated. **Intervention Dominance:** Not established — No principal intervention route established No cited study establishes a preparation, supplement protocol, sleep practice, activity practice, or stress-recovery practice that changes this circulating cytokine step. Omega-3 capsules were tested in two attached trials. One did not change plasma IL-6, TNF-α, or CRP. The other lowered stimulated IL-6 production in student blood cells. Neither result is a practice for this circulating cytokine network.
No Direct or Derived Dietary Requirement is currently established for cytokine-network modulation.
No PM-specific cofactor Dietary Requirement is established.
No mapping established.
### Overview IL-6 and TNF-α are inflammatory messengers. Slavich and Irwin (2014) place them on the path from stress-related immune signalling to inflammatory tone. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) Ferguson et al. (2014) used an endotoxin challenge in healthy adults to read that response. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) EPA plus DHA did not significantly change IL-6 or TNF-α in that challenge. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) CRP is a blood marker, not the messenger step. - **Benefits:** Tuning this intensity is about the messengers themselves, including IL-6 and TNF-α, after upstream genes have already been switched on. [[5]](#pm-ref-5) - **Implementation Notes:** No dietary requirement is established. In the endotoxin trial, EPA plus DHA did not significantly change IL-6 or TNF-α. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) - **Biological Relevance:** The transcriptional step that sits ahead of these messengers is separate — see PM1. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↓ IL-6/TNF-a pressure; ↓ inflammatory signalling tone ## 3. Intervention Levers

No preparation, supplement protocol, or fasting practice is established for this cytokine step.

No sleep, activity, or stress-recovery practice is established for this cytokine step.
## 4. Mechanistic Basis ### Summary Inflammatory tone is expressed not only at transcriptional nodes but through circulating cytokine networks. This PM captures whether IL-6, TNF-α, and CRP-linked signalling remains elevated or moves toward resolution within [BRS3(FM3) - Inflammation Resolution Capacity](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-inflammation-resolution-capacity).
#### (Cytokine signalling burden) IL-6, TNF-α, and CRP-linked pathways act as downstream readouts of inflammatory tone, reflecting how unresolved immune signalling is expressed systemically. #### (Network modulation logic) Cytokine pressure integrates upstream inputs from transcriptional, gut-derived, and lipid-mediator pathways. Modulation here reflects whether inflammatory signalling remains escalated or is progressively brought down—not a single receptor or cytokine in isolation. #### (Boundaries of the mechanism) Upstream NF-κB transcriptional control is handled by [BRS3-FM1-PM1 - NF-kB Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm1-nf-kb-signalling-regulation). Gut-derived endotoxin signalling belongs to [BRS3-FM1-PM2 - Gut-Derived Inflammatory Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm1/brs3-fm1-pm2-gut-derived-inflammatory-signalling). Lipid-mediator resolution substrate balance is represented by [BRS3-FM3-PM8 - Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance). #### (Integration within BRS3) This PM supports resolution-oriented inflammatory tone within [BRS3(FM3)](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-inflammation-resolution-capacity). EPA and DHA are substrates on the neighbouring eicosanoid page. They are not a requirement of this cytokine step.
### 4.1 Scientific Findings #### Summary IL-6 and TNF-α are messenger signals of inflammatory tone. CRP is a blood marker linked to that tone, not the messenger step. An endotoxin challenge in healthy adults has been used to read these responses. EPA plus DHA did not significantly change IL-6 or TNF-α in that challenge. ## 5. BRS Pathways and Connections ### 5.1 BRS Pathways - None listed ### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism. - [BRS1-FM3-PM7 — Neuronal Membrane DHA Incorporation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm3/brs1-fm3-pm7-neuronal-membrane-dha-incorporation) — membrane long-chain PUFA substrate pools feeding specialized pro-resolving mediator formation - [BRS5-FM1-PM2 — LPS / Endotoxin Containment](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-pm2-lps-endotoxin-containment) — gut endotoxin containment upstream of systemic cytokine network tone - [BRS5(FM1) — Gut Barrier Integrity and Immune Interface](/docs/biological-targets/brs5/fm1/brs5-fm1-gut-barrier-integrity-and-immune-interface) — gut–immune interface context influencing inflammatory resolution substrate availability - [BRS6(FM1) — Glycaemic–Insulin Stability & Cognitive Energy Availability](/docs/biological-targets/brs6/fm1/brs6-fm1-glycaemic-insulin-stability-and-cognitive-energy-availability) — post-prandial glycaemic context conditioning inflammatory cytokine expression ### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function. - [BRS3-FM3-PM8 - Eicosanoid / SPM Balance](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm3/brs3-fm3-pm8-eicosanoid-spm-balance) — Eicosanoid and resolving-mediator balance is a lipid-signal step. Cytokine intensity is a later messenger readout, not that substrate shift. ## 7. Phenome Connections These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. ### BRS4(KC1) - Macronutrient Substrate Availability (Glucose and fatty-acid fuels for mitochondrial energy metabolism) ### 1. Ambition Maintain adequate glucose and fatty-acid availability so mitochondrial ATP generation and fuel selection can track physiological demand. ### 2. Core Nutritional Requirements
- Glucose - Fatty acids
### 3. Evidence Base #### Summary Cellular energy metabolism draws on a flexible resource of oxidizable carbon supplied by glucose and fatty acids. Dietary pattern, fasting and substrate availability can shift mitochondrial fuel use, oxidative function and adaptation ([Kyriazis et al., 2022](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#kyriazis_impact_2022)). These fuels therefore form a coherent availability constraint: inadequate access can restrict oxidative ATP production or fuel switching, while the evidence does not justify treating every macronutrient or metabolite that enters mitochondrial metabolism as part of the same constrained resource. - **Constraint and membership boundary:** Glucose and fatty acids are the supported fuel classes; the attached corpus does not establish dietary amino-acid availability as part of this shared limiting pool, and butyrate cell exposure is modulatory evidence rather than fuel-pool membership ([Kyriazis et al., 2022](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#kyriazis_impact_2022); [Rose et al., 2018](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#rose_butyrate_2018)). - **Evidence and measurement boundary:** The review compares dietary patterns and mitochondrial responses; it does not define intake thresholds, directly measure substrate limitation across every connected mechanism or establish one optimal fuel mix ([Kyriazis et al., 2022](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#kyriazis_impact_2022)). - **Biological relevance and provision limitation:** Adequate oxidizable-substrate availability is necessary for energy production and adaptation, but preventing fuel constraint is not evidence that increasing carbohydrate or fat intake improves mitochondrial function or clinical outcomes in fuel-replete people ([Kyriazis et al., 2022](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#kyriazis_impact_2022)).
#### Biological Importance Glucose supplies oxidizable carbon for mitochondrial ATP generation after glycolytic conversion to pyruvate. Its availability is one arm of the shared fuel resource, while switching away from glucose during fasting or carbohydrate restriction illustrates that this is a flexible substrate constraint rather than a requirement for continuous high intake.

Supporting Evidence

  • Kyriazis et al., 2022 — Reviewed how fasting, ketogenic, high-fat and other dietary patterns alter energy-substrate availability and mitochondrial physiology, supporting glucose availability as one arm of a flexible fuel constraint without defining a universal intake threshold.

#### Biological Importance Fatty acids provide oxidizable carbon through mitochondrial β-oxidation and form the complementary lipid arm of the shared fuel resource. Their contribution varies with fasting, dietary pattern and metabolic state; this supports availability and switching claims, not one optimal dietary fat composition.

Supporting Evidence

  • Kyriazis et al., 2022 — Reviewed mitochondrial responses to high-fat, ketogenic, fasting and other dietary contexts, supporting fatty-acid availability as an adaptable mitochondrial fuel while leaving intake thresholds and mechanism-specific limitation unresolved.

### 4. Emerging Biological Supports No Emerging Biological Supports are currently prioritised for this KC. ### 5. ### BRS4(KC2) - Mitochondrial Cofactor Sufficiency (Vitamins & Minerals for Mitochondrial Energy Production) ### 1. Ambition Maintain mitochondrial cofactor sufficiency so enzyme systems can sustain electron transfer, redox stability, and ATP-generating efficiency. ### 2. Core Nutritional Requirements
- B vitamins - Iron - Magnesium
### 3. Evidence Base #### Summary Mitochondrial energy metabolism depends on a distributed micronutrient resource: B-vitamin-derived coenzymes support substrate conversion and redox transfer, iron supports oxygen handling and electron-transfer proteins, and magnesium supports ATP-associated reactions ([Tardy et al., 2020](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#tardy_vitamins_2020)). Inadequate status can therefore constrain several bioenergetic processes at once. Human niacin-responsive mitochondrial myopathy provides condition-specific evidence that correcting a defined cofactor deficiency can restore NAD⁺ availability, but it does not generalise to universal supplementation benefit ([Pirinen et al., 2020](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#pirinen_niacin_2020)). - **Constraint and membership boundary:** B vitamins, iron and magnesium belong to the shared micronutrient-sufficiency domain; endogenous CoQ10 and creatine/phosphocreatine biology are distinct carrier or buffering systems, not members of this dietary cofactor resource ([Tardy et al., 2020](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#tardy_vitamins_2020); [Crane, 2001](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#crane_coq10_2001)). - **Evidence and measurement boundary:** The main source is a narrative synthesis of biochemical and clinical evidence, while the niacin study addresses a defined mitochondrial disease and high-dose intervention; neither measures simultaneous limitation across every listed mechanism ([Tardy et al., 2020](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#tardy_vitamins_2020); [Pirinen et al., 2020](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#pirinen_niacin_2020)). - **Biological relevance and provision limitation:** Adequate status prevents cofactor-dependent energy metabolism from being constrained, but biochemical necessity and deficiency correction do not show that extra intake improves mitochondrial performance or clinical outcomes in nutrient-replete people ([Tardy et al., 2020](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#tardy_vitamins_2020)).
#### Biological Importance B vitamins are dietary precursors for coenzymes used across energy-yielding metabolism, including substrate conversion and redox-transfer reactions. Their grouped role is coenzyme availability across several processes, not a claim that all B vitamins share one reaction, one deficiency threshold or one supplementation response.

Supporting Evidence

  • Tardy et al., 2020 — Reviewed B-vitamin roles in energy-yielding metabolism and manifestations associated with inadequate status, supporting a class-level coenzyme-sufficiency constraint while not establishing one response for every vitamin.

  • Pirinen et al., 2020 — Found that high-dose niacin restored systemic and muscle NAD⁺ deficiency in adults with mitochondrial myopathy and improved muscle performance; this is condition-specific deficiency correction, not general-population supplementation evidence.

#### Biological Importance Iron is required for oxygen transport and iron-containing proteins involved in electron transfer. Inadequate iron status can therefore constrain energy metabolism even when fuel is present, but this requirement does not imply that more iron is beneficial when status is adequate.

Supporting Evidence

  • Tardy et al., 2020 — Reviewed iron's roles in oxygen transport and energy-yielding metabolism and the functional manifestations of inadequate supply, supporting deficiency-prevention rather than supplementation-benefit claims.

#### Biological Importance Magnesium participates in ATP-associated chemistry and numerous enzymes involved in energy-yielding metabolism. Its role supports a mineral-sufficiency constraint, while the attached evidence does not establish a mitochondrial-specific dietary threshold or a benefit from increasing intake when status is adequate.

Supporting Evidence

  • Tardy et al., 2020 — Reviewed magnesium as an essential participant in energy metabolism and linked inadequate status with functional consequences, supporting sufficiency while leaving mitochondrial-specific limitation and dose response unresolved.

### 4. Emerging Biological Supports No Emerging Biological Supports are currently prioritised for this KC. ### 5. Connected Mechanisms #### Functional Mechanisms - [BRS4(FM1) - Cellular Bioenergetics](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-cellular-bioenergetics) - [BRS4(FM2) - Mitochondrial Resilience & Redox Stability](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-mitochondrial-resilience-and-redox-stability) - [BRS4(FM3) - Substrate Utilisation Flexibility](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm3/brs4-fm3-substrate-utilisation-flexibility) - [BRS4(FM4) - Mitochondrial Capacity Expansion & Adaptation](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm4/brs4-fm4-mitochondrial-capacity-expansion-and-adaptation) #### Primary Mechanisms - [BRS4-FM1-PM1 - Electron Transport Chain Function](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm1-electron-transport-chain-function) - [BRS4-FM4-PM9 - Mitochondrial Biogenesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm4/brs4-fm4-pm9-mitochondrial-biogenesis) - [BRS4-FM2-PM4 - ROS Production and Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm4-ros-production-and-control) - [BRS4-FM1-PM2 - NAD⁺ Metabolism](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm2-nad-metabolism) - [BRS4-FM1-PM3 - Creatine–Phosphocreatine Energy Buffering](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm1/brs4-fm1-pm3-creatine-phosphocreatine-buffer) - [BRS4-FM2-PM5 - Mitochondrial Protection (Redox Integrity)](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm2/brs4-fm2-pm5-mitochondrial-protection-redox-integrity) - [BRS4-FM3-PM6 - Carnitine-Mediated Fat Transport](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm3/brs4-fm3-pm6-carnitine-mediated-fat-transport) - [BRS4-FM3-PM7 - Ketone Utilisation Capacity](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm3/brs4-fm3-pm7-ketone-utilisation-capacity) - [BRS4-FM3-PM8 - Metabolic Fuel Switching](/docs/biological-targets/brs4/fm3/brs4-fm3-pm8-metabolic-fuel-switching) ### 6. parent_brs: BRS4

summary: >-

  in maintenance and repair. Cells must continually recycle and replenish this
  molecule to keep those functions available. This PM focuses on maintaining
  that cellular resource. Dietary vitamin B3 forms and tryptophan provide
  building material, while exercise can influence part of the recycling
  machinery. Supporting normal availability is different from assuming that
  raising NAD⁺ improves cognition or wellbeing.
