### BRS2(KC1) - Methyl Donor Pool (Folate- and betaine-linked input to the methionine/SAM pool) ### 1. Ambition Maintain adequate folate- and betaine-linked methyl-group input to sustain homocysteine remethylation and the methionine/SAM resource used across connected mechanisms. ### 2. Core Nutritional Requirements
- Vitamin B9 (folate) - Choline - Betaine
### Membership and applicability boundary The registered constituents are **Vitamin B9 (folate), betaine and choline**. Folate supplies the carrier/substrate forms used by the folate remethylation route; betaine supplies the alternative methyl donor, and choline can supply betaine. This is a named shared donor-resource network, not an exhaustive inventory of all one-carbon sources or a claim that every constituent supplies every connected reaction ([Froese et al., 2019](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#froese_vitamin_2019); [Obeid, 2013](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#obeid_metabolic_2013)). Canonical membership establishes identity within this pool. Each PM separately adjudicates **Supported upstream supply**, **Conditional constraint**, or an unresolved/not-established relationship. A limiting effect, tissue-wide response or benefit from extra intake cannot be inherited from membership. Vitamin B12 supports the folate reaction as a cofactor and remains outside KC1 membership. SAMe supplementation, creatine and genotype-specific riboflavin remain separately labelled emerging support, not additional registered members. ### 3. Evidence Base #### Summary This constraint concerns methyl-group supply from folate and betaine for homocysteine remethylation. Folate provides **5-methyltetrahydrofolate**, while betaine supplies an alternative donor route and choline can be converted to betaine ([Ducker and Rabinowitz, 2017](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ducker_one-carbon_2017); [Zeisel, 2006](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#zeisel_choline_2006)). Together, these inputs replenish methionine used to produce **S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)**, the body's principal methyl donor, so they form one coherent donor-resource network rather than a list of nearby nutrients ([Obeid, 2013](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#obeid_metabolic_2013)). - **Constraint and membership boundary:** Vitamin B12 is necessary for methionine synthase but acts as a catalytic cofactor rather than a net methyl-group input; choline's membrane and acetylcholine roles also sit outside this constraint ([Froese et al., 2019](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#froese_vitamin_2019); [Zeisel, 2006](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#zeisel_choline_2006)). - **Evidence and measurement boundary:** Deficiency evidence and plasma-homocysteine responses support remethylation-linked donor constraint, but they do not establish uniform effects on SAM balance, tissue methylation or every connected mechanism ([Obeid, 2013](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#obeid_metabolic_2013); [Olthof et al., 2003](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#olthof_low_2003)). - **Biological relevance and provision limitation:** Adequate donor availability helps prevent constraint under relevant deficiency or demand states; evidence that provision alters remethylation-related biology does not by itself show that extra intake improves methylation or downstream outcomes in nutrient-replete people ([Obeid, 2013](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#obeid_metabolic_2013); [Olthof et al., 2003](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#olthof_low_2003)).
#### Biological Importance Folate carries activated one-carbon units. In its 5-methyltetrahydrofolate form it donates the methyl group used to remethylate homocysteine, replenishing methionine for SAM synthesis. Folate insufficiency can therefore constrain the shared donor network, although tissue responses and downstream methylation effects are not uniform.

Supporting Evidence

  • Ducker and Rabinowitz, 2017 — Reviewed folate-mediated one-carbon transfer, homocysteine remethylation and methionine/SAM biology, establishing the shared resource pathway while distinguishing it from downstream outcomes.

  • Obeid, 2013 — Reviewed folate deficiency as a cause of hyperhomocysteinaemia, lower SAM and impaired methyl balance, supporting constraint-level membership with tissue and state limitations.

#### Biological Importance Choline can be irreversibly oxidised to betaine in liver and kidney. This makes dietary choline an upstream source of methyl groups for BHMT-mediated remethylation, while its separate membrane and acetylcholine roles remain outside this constraint.

Supporting Evidence

  • Zeisel, 2006 — Reviewed choline as an essential nutrient and major dietary methyl-group source, including its oxidation to betaine and variation in human dietary requirement.

  • Obeid, 2013 — Synthesised evidence that choline deficiency perturbs methionine formation and hepatic SAM/SAH balance; much of the pool-specific evidence is hepatic and does not establish a universal intake response.

#### Biological Importance Betaine is the methyl-donor substrate for BHMT-mediated homocysteine remethylation. This folate-independent route contributes to methionine/SAM availability, especially in liver and kidney and under states in which methyl-donor demand or folate limitation increases reliance on BHMT.

Supporting Evidence

  • Olthof et al., 2003 — Demonstrated plasma-homocysteine lowering after betaine supplementation in healthy adults, showing that betaine availability can alter remethylation-linked physiology without establishing a universal dietary requirement.

  • Obeid, 2013 — Reviewed betaine as the BHMT methyl donor and bounded its contribution by organ distribution, metabolic state and interaction with folate and choline.

### 4. Emerging Biological Supports This section considers whether an intervention can support methyl-resource availability or reduce a major methyl demand under defined conditions. Candidates do not need to be indispensable nutrients, and they remain separate from the Core Nutritional Requirements above.
**Why it is interesting:** Supplemental S-adenosylmethionine (SAMe) delivers the downstream methyl donor directly and can raise circulating SAM exposure. This is pharmacological support of methyl-resource availability; it does not restore dietary folate, choline or betaine input or show that those donor routes were deficient ([Loehrer et al., 1997](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#loehrer_same_1997); [Mischoulon et al., 2012](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#mischoulon_same_2012)). **Why it remains emerging:** Human studies show higher plasma SAM, but often also higher SAH, and do not establish improved intracellular SAM:SAH balance, tissue-specific methylation flux or broad functional benefit. Oral exposure is formulation- and food-dependent, long-term safety is incompletely characterised, and mood activation is a material practical limitation ([Yang et al., 2009](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#yang_same_2009); [Gören et al., 2004](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#goren_same_2004)). **Evidence interpretation:** Increased circulating resource availability is demonstrated. Altered downstream biomarkers are demonstrated, but improved tissue methylation capacity is not. A condition-specific antidepressant response has been reported, but metabolite changes did not predict that response; this does not establish a general methyl-resource functional benefit.

Supporting Evidence

  • Loehrer et al., 1997 — Exposure: one 400 mg oral dose. Population: 14 healthy adults. Measured endpoints: plasma SAM, SAH, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, homocysteine and methionine over 24 hours. Results: SAM rose from 38.0 to 361.8 nmol/L and returned toward baseline with a 1.7-hour half-life; SAH and 5-methyltetrahydrofolate also rose transiently, while homocysteine and methionine did not change. Limitations: small, acute and uncontrolled; circulating metabolites do not demonstrate tissue methylation or function.

  • Yang et al., 2009 — Exposure: 1,000 mg/day enteric-coated oral or intravenous SAMe for five days. Population: 20 healthy Chinese adults, ten per route. Measured endpoints: plasma pharmacokinetics and adverse events. Results: oral exposure was only about 2.1–2.6% of intravenous exposure, with no accumulation or reported adverse events. Limitations: open-label, very short and formulation-specific; no SAM:SAH, methylation-flux or functional endpoint.

  • Mischoulon et al., 2012 — Exposure: 800–1,600 mg/day oral SAMe or placebo for six weeks alongside a stable serotonin-reuptake inhibitor. Population: a 35-person biomarker subset of adults with major depressive disorder. Measured endpoints: plasma SAM, SAH, homocysteine, methionine, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate and depression response. Results: SAM and SAH increased in the SAMe arm, but metabolite changes were not associated with clinical improvement. Limitations: small disease-specific subset, baseline homocysteine imbalance and plasma rather than tissue measurements.

  • Gören et al., 2004 — Exposure: oral SAMe titrated to 1,600 mg/day for four weeks. Population: 15 healthy adults. Measured endpoints: serum SAM, homocysteine, selected methylated toxicants and mood ratings. Results: SAM increased without a sustained homocysteine or toxic-metabolite rise; one participant developed a mixed manic state with suicidal ideation that resolved after withdrawal. Limitations: small and unblinded; too short to establish long-term safety.

**Decision:** Prioritise as a condition-specific, clinically supervised emerging support. SAMe should not be presented as restoration of dietary donor intake. Avoid unsupervised use in bipolar disorder or a history of mania; use with serotonergic medicines or supplements, levodopa/Parkinson's disease, pregnancy, lactation, childhood or immunocompromising conditions requires clinical review. Common tolerability concerns include gastrointestinal upset, headache, anxiety, agitation and insomnia; long-term safety remains uncertain ([Sharma et al., 2017](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#sharma_same_2017)).
**Why it is interesting:** Endogenous creatine synthesis methylates guanidinoacetate using SAM. Supplemental creatine feeds back on this pathway and lowers guanidinoacetate, so it can reduce the precursor supply for a substantial SAM-consuming reaction ([Peters et al., 2015](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#peters_creatine_2015)). **Why it remains emerging:** The demand-reduction action is supported, but whether it improves methyl-resource availability for other pathways or produces a functional benefit through methyl sparing remains unresolved. The best powered human trial did not increase whole-blood SAM, reduce SAH or lower homocysteine on average. Animal homocysteine effects support the biochemical premise but do not establish human methyl redistribution or downstream function ([Peters et al., 2015](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#peters_creatine_2015); [Stead et al., 2001](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#stead_creatine_2001)). **Evidence interpretation:** Reduced demand at the creatine-synthesis precursor step is demonstrated in humans. Improved methyl-resource availability, redistribution into other SAM-dependent pathways and a methyl-sparing functional benefit are not demonstrated.

Supporting Evidence

  • Peters et al., 2015 — Exposure: 3 g/day creatine, placebo, 400 µg/day folic acid or creatine plus folic acid for 12 weeks. Population: Bangladeshi adults; 458 participants in the four relevant groups. Measured endpoints: plasma guanidinoacetate and homocysteine plus whole-blood SAM and SAH. Results: creatine reduced guanidinoacetate by 10.6% while placebo increased it by 3.7%, but creatine did not significantly change homocysteine, SAM or SAH; adding creatine did not improve the folic-acid homocysteine response. Limitations: arsenic-exposed population with frequent folate insufficiency, blood measures are imperfect proxies for hepatic flux, and no direct methyl-redistribution or functional endpoint was measured.

  • Stead et al., 2001 — Exposure: 0.4% dietary creatine for two weeks. Population: rats. Measured endpoints: renal AGAT activity, plasma homocysteine and related metabolites. Results: AGAT activity fell to 18% of control and plasma homocysteine fell by 27%. Limitations: animal dosing and creatine-synthesis regulation do not establish the same homocysteine or methyl-resource response in humans.

**Decision:** Retain as an emerging demand-reduction support. Human evidence supports suppression of endogenous creatine synthesis. Whether this improves methyl-resource availability for other pathways or produces a functional benefit through methyl sparing remains unresolved.
**Why it is interesting:** MTHFR requires flavin adenine dinucleotide derived from riboflavin. In adults homozygous for MTHFR 677TT, a small randomised intervention increased plasma SAM, making riboflavin a specific genotype-conditioned capacity support rather than a generic methyl donor ([Rooney et al., 2020](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#rooney_riboflavin_2020)). **Why it remains emerging:** The evidence is restricted to a small 677TT subgroup and a circulating biomarker. It did not show a clear improvement in SAM:SAH ratio, other one-carbon metabolites or a functional outcome attributable to the SAM change ([Rooney et al., 2020](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#rooney_riboflavin_2020)). **Evidence interpretation:** Increased plasma SAM is demonstrated for the MTHFR 677TT context. Broad resource restoration, improved methylation flux and functional benefit are not demonstrated.

Supporting Evidence

  • Rooney et al., 2020 — Exposure: 1.6 mg/day riboflavin or placebo for 16 weeks. Population: adults with the MTHFR 677TT genotype, 24 receiving riboflavin and 23 placebo, drawn from earlier blood-pressure trials. Measured endpoints: plasma methionine, SAM, SAH, betaine, choline, cystathionine and homocysteine. Results: SAM increased by 19.5 ± 20.6 nmol/L and cystathionine increased; no other measured one-carbon metabolite showed a significant response. Limitations: small genotype-selected secondary analysis, no tissue methylation measurement and no functional outcome linked to the SAM increase.

**Decision:** Prioritise narrowly for genotype-conditioned assessment, not as a general KC1 supplement recommendation.
Phosphatidylcholine was not carried forward as a separate candidate because its relevant effect is provision of choline already represented in the core pool. Guanidinoacetate was excluded because conversion to creatine consumes SAM rather than sparing it. Methionine belongs to the separate sulfur-amino-acid constraint, while vitamin B12 is a methionine-synthase cofactor rather than a donor-pool adjunct. Serine, glycine and cysteine were not retained because available evidence concerns pathway participation or transsulfuration/glutathione biology rather than demonstrated support of this named methyl-resource capacity. ### 5. membership is not inherited. - [BRS1-FM1-PM3 — Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation) — folate, betaine and choline supply the connected methionine/SAM resource route used by COMT; ### BRS2(KC2) - Methionine–Cysteine Sulfur Amino Acid Pool (Shared methionine–cysteine availability across sulfur-amino-acid biology) ### 1. Ambition Maintain adequate methionine and cysteine availability across the shared sulfur-amino-acid requirement that supplies methionine-cycle and transsulfuration-linked biology. ### 2. Core Nutritional Requirements
- Methionine - Cysteine
### 3. Evidence Base #### Summary Methionine and cysteine form a shared nutritional sulfur-amino-acid resource. Methionine is dietarily indispensable, enters the methionine cycle and supplies sulfur to the irreversible transsulfuration route. Dietary cysteine can spare part of the methionine requirement and contribute directly to downstream sulfur-amino-acid availability. Together they constitute a coherent requirement spanning methionine conservation and transsulfuration-linked substrate capacity, rather than an inventory of every compound used by those pathways ([Ball et al., 2006](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ball_methionine_cysteine_2006); [Kumar and Yadav, 2017](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#kumar_transsulfuration_2017)). - **Constraint and membership boundary:** Serine is a transsulfuration cosubstrate, while glycine can co-limit glutathione synthesis under some conditions; neither is established as part of the shared methionine–cysteine nutritional requirement ([Kumar and Yadav, 2017](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#kumar_transsulfuration_2017); [Sekhar et al., 2011](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#sekhar_glutathione_2011)). - **Evidence and measurement boundary:** Human requirement studies establish methionine indispensability and partial cysteine sparing, but the size of that sparing is method-dependent and does not define one threshold for every population ([Ball et al., 2006](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ball_methionine_cysteine_2006)). - **Biological relevance and provision limitation:** Adequate sulfur-amino-acid availability prevents substrate constraint; the evidence does not show that higher methionine or cysteine intake improves function in protein-sufficient people or that every connected mechanism is intake-responsive ([Ball et al., 2006](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ball_methionine_cysteine_2006)).
#### Biological Importance Methionine is the dietarily indispensable member of the shared sulfur-amino-acid requirement. It enters the methionine cycle and supplies sulfur to the irreversible transsulfuration route, so inadequate availability can constrain both methionine-cycle and downstream sulfur-amino-acid capacity.

Supporting Evidence

  • Ball et al., 2006 — Reviewed adult-human sulfur-amino-acid requirement studies: methionine is dietarily indispensable, while cysteine can substitute for part of its requirement. The magnitude of sparing remains method-dependent.

  • Kumar and Yadav, 2017 — Reviewed the irreversible route from methionine-cycle homocysteine through transsulfuration to cysteine, establishing the biochemical bridge across the shared sulfur-amino-acid pool.

#### Biological Importance Cysteine is nutritionally linked to methionine because it can spare part of the dietary methionine requirement. Its availability also contributes to downstream sulfur-amino-acid capacity, including glutathione synthesis under conditions in which cysteine and glycine availability are limiting.

Supporting Evidence

  • Ball et al., 2006 — Reviewed evidence that cysteine can substitute for part of the adult-human methionine requirement, while documenting methodological uncertainty in the magnitude of sparing.

  • Sekhar et al., 2011 — Showed conditional cysteine-plus-glycine limitation of glutathione synthesis in older adults. This supports cysteine availability at the downstream edge of the pool but does not establish isolated cysteine effects or universal limitation.

### 4. Emerging Biological Supports No Emerging Biological Supports are currently prioritised for this KC. ### 5. Connected Mechanisms #### Functional Mechanisms - [BRS2(FM1) - Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency) - [BRS2(FM2) - Transsulfuration & Redox Coupling](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-transsulfuration-redox-coupling) - [BRS2(FM3) - Methylation–Membrane Coupling](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-methylation-membrane-coupling) #### Primary Mechanisms - [BRS2-FM1-PM1 - Folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) - [BRS2-FM1-PM3 - SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis) - [BRS2-FM1-PM4 - Methionine Cycle Flux](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux) - [BRS2-FM2-PM5 - Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) - [BRS2-FM2-PM6 - Glutathione Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm6-glutathione-synthesis) - [BRS2-FM3-PM7 - Phosphatidylcholine Formation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-pm7-phosphatidylcholine-formation) ### 6. title: Methionine Cycle Flux
pm_id: BRS2-FM1-PM4
mission: 'Maintain balanced methionine-cycle flux so methionine availability, SAM-dependent methylation, homocysteine recycling and transsulfuration remain coordinated across changing physiological demand.'
parent_fm: BRS2(FM1)
parent_brs: BRS2
summary: 'The methionine cycle forms S-adenosylmethionine from methionine, transfers its methyl group, and hydrolyses S-adenosylhomocysteine to adenosine and homocysteine. Homocysteine is then remethylated to methionine or sent into transsulfuration toward cysteine. SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate influence that split. Every tissue can remethylate homocysteine, while transsulfuration is limited to liver, kidney, small intestine and pancreas. Metabolite concentrations describe pool state, not the branch rates.'

timing_specific: 'No'

scientific_findings_intro: 'A controlled human tracer study found unchanged mean postprandial remethylation, transmethylation and transsulfuration rates during moderate vitamin B6 restriction, despite sharply reduced plasma PLP and increased cystathionine concentration. scientific_findings:
  - id: PM4-F1
    finding_label: Homocysteine is split between remethylation and transsulfuration
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: 'Methionine becomes SAM, SAM donates a methyl group, and SAH is hydrolysed to homocysteine. Homocysteine is then either remethylated to methionine or sent into transsulfuration toward cysteine.'
    finding_interpretation: 'This is the integrated route and the branch. It does not assign the MAT, remethylation or transsulfuration reactions to this mechanism, and it does not show that ordinary diet changes the rates.'
    finding_statement: 'Methionine-cycle throughput runs from methionine to SAM, methyl transfer and SAH hydrolysis to homocysteine, after which homocysteine is distributed between remethylation and transsulfuration under the influence of SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A methylation review establishes SAM as the methyl donor and SAH hydrolysis to adenosine and homocysteine, and it shows that blocking that hydrolysis can affect methylation of phospholipids, proteins, DNA, RNA and small molecules together. A pathway review then places regulation at the distribution of homocysteine between remethylation, which every tissue can perform, and transsulfuration to cystathionine, which is limited to liver, kidney, small intestine and pancreas, with SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate as effectors. A human tracer study uses that same partition, measuring postprandial remethylation, transmethylation and total transsulfuration as rates.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The pathway accounts are reviews. Transsulfuration is not present in every tissue. The human rate study was a 28-day vitamin B6 restriction in nine healthy young adults. It does not show that ordinary changes in methionine, folate, or B-vitamin intake change those rates. Individual enzyme reactions remain neighbouring mechanisms.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Chiang et al. (1996)
        citation_key: chiang_s-adenosylmethionine_1996
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#chiang_s-adenosylmethionine_1996
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: 'SAM donates methyl groups; SAH formed by that transfer is hydrolysed to adenosine and homocysteine; blocking SAH hydrolysis can affect methylation across phospholipids, proteins, DNA, RNA and small molecules.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Narrative review of SAM-dependent methylation, SAH hydrolysis and downstream methyl acceptors.'
          population: Review of biochemical and cellular literature; no new human cohort.
          result: SAM is the methyl donor. SAH is hydrolysed by SAH hydrolase to adenosine and homocysteine. Blocking that hydrolase can affect methylation of several classes of acceptor at once.
          effect_magnitude: No quantitative flux or concentration effect size.
          evidence_summary: Establishes methyl transfer and the SAH-to-homocysteine step as a shared route into many methylation reactions.
          limitations: 'Does not describe remethylation, transsulfuration or a measured SAM:SAH ratio, and does not test diet or cognition.'
      - label: Finkelstein (1998)
        citation_key: finkelstein_homocysteine_1998
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#finkelstein_homocysteine_1998
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Homocysteine is distributed between tissue-wide remethylation and transsulfuration to cystathionine in liver, kidney, small intestine and pancreas; SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate are effectors of that distribution.'
        assessment:
          study: Review of mammalian methionine-cycle and transsulfuration pathways and their regulation.
          population: Mammalian pathway review; no new human experiment.
          result: 'Every tissue can synthesise SAM, use it for transmethylation, hydrolyse SAH and remethylate homocysteine. Transsulfuration catabolises homocysteine in liver, kidney, small intestine and pancreas. Regulation is the distribution of homocysteine between remethylation and conversion to cystathionine.'
          effect_magnitude: No numeric rate or intake-response estimate.
          evidence_summary: 'Establishes the regulated branch between recycling and transsulfuration and names SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate as effectors.'
          limitations: 'Review-level pathway evidence. It does not measure human rates, test ordinary diets, or show a cognitive or attention outcome.'
      - label: Lamers et al. (2011)
        citation_key: lamers_vitamin_b6_methionine_cycle_2011
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#lamers_vitamin_b6_methionine_cycle_2011
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Human postprandial kinetics were quantified as remethylation, transmethylation and total transsulfuration rates, confirming that the branch is measurable as rates rather than as a single metabolite level.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Primed constant infusion of labelled methionine and leucine in the postprandial state, repeated after 28 days of dietary vitamin B6 restriction.'
          population: 'Nine healthy adults (4 men, 5 women), aged 20–35 years.'
          result: 'The protocol quantified remethylation, transmethylation and total transsulfuration. Mean rates were unchanged by the restriction.'
          effect_magnitude: Plasma PLP fell from 49 ± 4 nmol/L to 19 ± 2 nmol/L. Mean cycle rates did not change. No rate delta is reported because the mean change was null.
          evidence_summary: Shows that human cycle throughput can be partitioned into measured rates.
          limitations: 'Small healthy-adult sample, 28-day restriction, postprandial state only, and large individual variation. Not a test of cognitive or attention outcomes.'
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Kumar et al. (2017)
        citation_key: kumar_transsulfuration_2017
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#kumar_transsulfuration_2017
        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: The repository record describes a review of transsulfuration from homocysteine toward cysteine and glutathione.
        why_excluded: That record does not establish remethylation or the regulated split between the two exits.
      - label: Aragão et al. (2024)
        citation_key: aragao_revitalising_2024

        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: Riboflavin was listed beside this mechanism because vitamin B2 is a cofactor of a folate-cycle enzyme.
        why_excluded: The paper is a general riboflavin physiology review and does not test methionine-cycle throughput or the homocysteine split.
      - label: Fanti et al. (2026)
        citation_key: fanti_methionine_longevity_diet_2026

        data_level: Mixed
        why_relevant: Tests how little or how much methionine sits inside a low-amino-acid longevity diet.
        why_excluded: 'The mouse endpoints are frailty and metabolic signalling, and the human component is epidemiology rather than a methionine trial. Neither measures cycle branch rates or an attention or cognitive treatment effect.'
      - label: Parkhitko et al. (2026)
        citation_key: parkhitko_methionine_restriction_mimetics_2026

        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: Reviews methionine restriction as an ageing intervention.
        why_excluded: 'It is an ageing and disease review, not a measurement of human cycle rates and not an ADHD treatment study.'
  - id: PM4-F2
    finding_label: Moderate vitamin B6 restriction left mean cycle rates unchanged
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    finding_summary: 'In healthy young adults, 28 days of dietary vitamin B6 restriction lowered the active B6 coenzyme in blood but did not change mean postprandial remethylation, transmethylation or total transsulfuration rates.'
    finding_interpretation: A lower vitamin B6 supply in this range did not limit the integrated rates. The rise in cystathionine is a separate intermediate signal.
    finding_statement: 'Moderate dietary vitamin B6 restriction that lowered plasma pyridoxal 5''-phosphate did not change mean postprandial remethylation, transmethylation or total transsulfuration rates in healthy young adults.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'One controlled feeding study measured the three cycle rates with methionine tracers before and after restriction. Plasma pyridoxal 5''-phosphate fell sharply. The mean rates did not change, although individuals differed. Cystathionine concentration rose, and its fractional synthesis rate rose in most participants. The integrated rates and that intermediate marker moved differently.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Nine healthy young adults, 28 days, and the postprandial state only. The authors report large individual variation, so a mean null result does not describe every person. The study does not test severe deficiency, folate or vitamin B12 restriction, ordinary mixed diets, or any cognitive or attention outcome.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Lamers et al. (2011)
        citation_key: lamers_vitamin_b6_methionine_cycle_2011
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#lamers_vitamin_b6_methionine_cycle_2011
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Mean postprandial remethylation, transmethylation and total transsulfuration rates did not change after vitamin B6 restriction, while cystathionine concentration and its fractional synthesis rate rose.'
        assessment:
          study: Within-person tracer study of methionine-cycle kinetics at usual B6 status and after 28 days of dietary vitamin B6 restriction.
          population: 'Nine healthy adults (4 men, 5 women), aged 20–35 years.'
          result: 'Mean remethylation, transsulfuration and transmethylation rates were unchanged. Plasma cystathionine rose, and fractional cystathionine synthesis increased in 8 of 9 participants.'
          effect_magnitude: Plasma PLP fell from 49 ± 4 nmol/L to 19 ± 2 nmol/L (P < 0.0001). Cystathionine rose from 142 ± 8 to 236 ± 9 nmol/L (P < 0.001). Fractional cystathionine synthesis rose by a mean of 12% in 8 of 9 participants. Mean cycle-rate changes were null.
          evidence_summary: Direct human evidence that this degree of vitamin B6 restriction did not change the integrated postprandial rates.
          limitations: 'Small sample, short restriction, healthy young adults, postprandial conditions, and wide individual variation. Cystathionine kinetics are not a substitute for the total transsulfuration rate.'
  - id: PM4-IC1
    finding_label: Metabolite concentrations are not cycle branch rates
    presentation: interpretive-constraint
    finding_statement: 'Homocysteine, SAM, SAH and cystathionine concentrations do not measure remethylation, transmethylation or total transsulfuration rates.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'The human studies attached to this mechanism report blood homocysteine, or in one tracer study cystathionine, as concentrations. Folic acid lowered blood homocysteine, with a further fall when vitamin B12 was added, and vitamin B6 added no further concentration change. A separate small trial reported lower plasma homocysteine after vitamin B12, fish oil, or both. In the tracer study, cystathionine concentration rose while mean total transsulfuration rate did not. The pathway review defines the biological quantity as the distribution of homocysteine between two routes, which these concentration changes do not report.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The concentration trials were not designed as flux studies, so their null or positive homocysteine results cannot be reread as rate results. The tracer dissociation is limited to cystathionine versus total transsulfuration in nine young adults. SAM and SAH were not the measured endpoints of the homocysteine trials.'
    evidence_dependency:
      - Finkelstein (1998) is also primary Evidence Considered in PM4-F1. Lamers et al. (2011) is also primary Evidence Considered in PM4-F1 and PM4-F2.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Collaboration (1998)
        citation_key: collaboration_lowering_1998
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#collaboration_lowering_1998
        data_level: Human Study
        exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: 'Folic acid lowered blood homocysteine concentration, vitamin B12 added a further concentration reduction, and vitamin B6 did not.'
        assessment:
          study: Individual-patient meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials of folic acid-based supplements.
          population: 1114 people in the pooled trials.
          result: Blood homocysteine concentration fell with folic acid. Vitamin B12 produced an additional reduction. Vitamin B6 did not add a significant further reduction.
          effect_magnitude: 'After standardisation to pretreatment homocysteine of 12 μmol/L and folate of 12 nmol/L, folic acid reduced homocysteine by 25% (95% CI 23% to 28%). Vitamin B12 (mean 0.5 mg/day) added 7% (3% to 10%). Vitamin B6 (mean 16.5 mg/day) had no significant additional effect.'
          evidence_summary: Establishes a concentration response to folic acid and vitamin B12.
          limitations: The endpoint is blood homocysteine concentration. Remethylation and transsulfuration rates were not measured.
      - label: Huang et al. (2015)
        citation_key: tao_huang_effect_2015
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#tao_huang_effect_2015
        data_level: Human Study
        exposure_context: supplemental-formulation

    finding_label: Homocysteine–cognition evidence does not measure cycle rates
    presentation: phenome-relationship
    primary_phenome: Cognitive Clarity
    finding_summary: 'Reviews link higher homocysteine with cognitive decline and Alzheimer risk. They do not measure cycle branch rates, and they do not show that changing those rates improves Cognitive Clarity.'
    finding_interpretation: Homocysteine can mark strain at the branch point. A dementia risk association is not evidence that this mechanism treats a cognitive disorder.
    finding_statement: Evidence linking homocysteine concentration to cognitive decline or Alzheimer risk does not demonstrate that integrated methionine-cycle rates modulate Cognitive Clarity.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A narrative review treats homocysteine as a risk factor for cerebrovascular disease and degenerative dementias and states that effects on specific cognitive domains are poorly mapped. Neither measures remethylation or transsulfuration rates, and neither tests an intervention on integrated cycle throughput.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'This is a boundary on the attached cognition sources, not a claim that homocysteine is irrelevant to brain disease. Methionine-restriction experiments were assessed separately and address ageing phenotypes rather than Cognitive Clarity.'

          population: Published human studies of homocysteine and dementia or cognitive decline; no new cohort.
          result: 'The review treats homocysteine as a risk factor for cerebrovascular disease and degenerative dementias, and states that domain-specific cognitive effects are poorly investigated.'

    finding_summary: 'Children with ADHD have been reported to have higher homocysteine, lower B vitamins, and less favourable diets. Those associations do not measure cycle branch rates and do not show that changing the rates improves attention.'

### Overview

The methionine cycle forms S-adenosylmethionine from methionine, transfers its methyl group, and hydrolyses S-adenosylhomocysteine to adenosine and homocysteine. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Homocysteine is then remethylated to methionine or sent into transsulfuration toward cysteine. [[12]](#pm-ref-12) SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate influence that split. [[12]](#pm-ref-12) Every tissue can remethylate homocysteine, while transsulfuration is limited to liver, kidney, small intestine and pancreas. [[12]](#pm-ref-12) Metabolite concentrations describe pool state, not the branch rates. [[13]](#pm-ref-13)

- **Benefits:** Maintaining methionine-cycle flux lets cells keep donating methyl groups while directing sulfur toward cysteine. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) That coordination helps keep methylation and sulfur exit together.
- **Implementation Notes:** Methionine, dietary protein, vitamin B9 (folate), vitamin B12 (cobalamin), vitamin B6, and vitamin B2 (riboflavin) are the provision routes. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) [[13]](#pm-ref-13) Folic acid and vitamin B12 can lower blood homocysteine, and moderate vitamin B6 restriction can raise cystathionine, without a shown change in those branch rates. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) [[13]](#pm-ref-13)
- **Biological Relevance:** [SAMe formation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis), each remethylation reaction, and the [transsulfuration enzyme steps](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) are neighbouring mechanisms. [[12]](#pm-ref-12)

## 2. Primary Biological Effects

↑ coordinated throughput from methionine through SAM to homocysteine<br />
↔ distribution of homocysteine between remethylation and transsulfuration<br />
→ methylation continues while SAH is hydrolysed onward

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Methyl-group use and sulfur exit meet at homocysteine. What matters is how that intermediate is divided between return to methionine and transsulfuration, with SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate as effectors of the split.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>Methionine cycle flux — mechanistic detail</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (From methionine to homocysteine)

Methionine is converted to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the principal methyl donor. After the methyl group is transferred, S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) is hydrolysed to adenosine and homocysteine. Blocking that hydrolysis can affect methylation of phospholipids, proteins, DNA, RNA and small molecules together [Chiang et al. (1996) [[2]](#pm-ref-2)].

#### (The regulated split)

Every tissue can remethylate homocysteine back to methionine. Transsulfuration, which converts homocysteine to cystathionine and onward toward cysteine, occurs in liver, kidney, small intestine and pancreas. Regulation is the distribution of homocysteine between those exits. SAM, SAH and methyl-tetrahydrofolate are effectors of that distribution [Finkelstein (1998) [[12]](#pm-ref-12)]. Human postprandial studies can measure the same partition as remethylation, transmethylation and total transsulfuration rates [Lamers et al. (2011) [[13]](#pm-ref-13)].

#### (Concentrations and rates)

Folic acid lowers blood homocysteine concentration, and vitamin B12 adds a further concentration reduction, while added vitamin B6 does not [Collaboration (1998) [[6]](#pm-ref-6)]. A small trial also reported lower plasma homocysteine after vitamin B12, fish oil, or both [Huang et al. (2015) [[11]](#pm-ref-11)]. In the tracer study, cystathionine concentration rose during vitamin B6 restriction while the mean total transsulfuration rate did not [[13]](#pm-ref-13). A concentration change is a different result from a branch rate.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

This mechanism is the integrated throughput and the split at homocysteine. Formation of SAM is [BRS2-FM1-PM3 — SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis). Folate- and vitamin B12-dependent remethylation is [BRS2-FM1-PM1 — Folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation). Betaine-dependent remethylation is [BRS2-FM1-PM2 — Betaine/BHMT Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation). The transsulfuration reactions are [BRS2-FM2-PM5 — Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway). Methionine-restriction experiments in ageing models, and homocysteine associations with dementia or ADHD, do not show that changing these rates treats a cognitive or attention disorder [Fanti et al. (2026) [[3]](#pm-ref-3); Luzzi et al. (2022) [[8]](#pm-ref-8); Lukovac et al. (2024) [[9]](#pm-ref-9)].

#### (Integration within methylation cycle efficiency)

SAM synthesis feeds this throughput. Remethylation returns homocysteine to methionine, and transsulfuration is the catabolic exit. Downstream methyl acceptors include phospholipids, proteins, DNA and RNA [Chiang et al. (1996) [[2]](#pm-ref-2)]. The parent account of methylation cycle efficiency is [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency).

</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

A controlled human tracer study found unchanged mean postprandial remethylation, transmethylation and transsulfuration rates during moderate vitamin B6 restriction, despite sharply reduced plasma PLP and increased cystathionine concentration. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) Pathway reviews provide the regulatory context for these measured branch rates. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) The combined evidence shows why an altered intermediate concentration cannot be treated as an equivalent change in overall cycle flux; individual responses and the restriction conditions limit generalisation.

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- None listed

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS2-FM1-PM1 — Folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) — Remethylates homocysteine to methionine and thereby carries one recycling exit. The split between that exit and transsulfuration is the upstream allocation.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM2 — Betaine/BHMT Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation) — Remethylates homocysteine to methionine by a betaine-dependent route that runs parallel to folate-dependent recycling and stays separate from transsulfuration.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM3 — SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis) — Produces SAM from methionine and ATP. That SAM is the methyl donor consumed as throughput moves from methyl transfer to homocysteine and the branch.
- [BRS2-FM2-PM5 — Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) — Carries homocysteine onward to cystathionine and cysteine after the branch has directed it into transsulfuration, which is the catabolic exit rather than the recycling arm.

## 7. Phenome Connections

These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

scientific_findings_intro: 'Human MAT structural and kinetic studies identify reaction participants, while kinetic models disagree about substrate-binding order. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) These studies directly establish enzyme mechanism and biochemical requirements. They do not test ordinary dietary modulation, human in-vivo synthesis flux or downstream methylation outcomes, so those effects remain beyond the evidence summarised here.'
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM3-F1
    finding_label: 'Biochemical provenance: MAT reaction'
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: MAT-dependent SAMe synthesis directly requires methionine and ATP and uses active-site magnesium and potassium ions to support ATP-dependent catalysis.
    finding_interpretation: 'This establishes the biochemical reaction and its direct requirements. It does not establish that increasing dietary methionine, magnesium or potassium increases SAMe synthesis in adequately nourished humans; ATP is an intracellular biochemical substrate, not a dietary lever.'
    finding_statement: MAT-dependent SAMe synthesis directly requires methionine and ATP and uses active-site magnesium and potassium ions to support ATP-dependent catalysis.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: The MAT reaction and catalytic participants have curated provenance. Human MAT2A studies support conflicting ATP-first and rapid-equilibrium random substrate-binding models; no settled universal order is asserted. MAT2B stability is assessed separately in proposed F5.
    synthesis_limitations: 'The primary evidence uses purified recombinant protein and crystallised human enzyme rather than intact human physiology. Active-site ion requirements do not show that physiological magnesium or potassium availability ordinarily limits MAT activity. The studies do not establish a methionine intake-response relationship, a clinically meaningful reserve-capacity threshold, or a phenome outcome.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Bailey et al. (2021)
        citation_key: bailey_human_mat2a_2021
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#bailey_human_mat2a_2021
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Purified human MAT2A followed an ordered ATP-first, methionine-second kinetic mechanism; MAT2B stabilised the enzyme without materially changing the tested catalytic parameters.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Purified recombinant human MAT2A steady-state kinetics, product/dead-end inhibition and isothermal titration calorimetry, with and without MAT2B.'
          population: 'Purified human MAT2A/MAT2B proteins; no cells, animals or human participants.'
          result: ATP bound before methionine; SAM was released before phosphate and pyrophosphate. MAT2B bound tightly and stabilised low-concentration MAT2A but did not significantly change the tested kinetic parameters.
          effect_magnitude: ATP Kd 80 ± 30 μM and Km 50 ± 10 μM; MAT2B Kd 6 ± 1 nM. No significant catalytic-parameter change under saturating MAT2B conditions.
          evidence_summary: Direct human-enzyme evidence for the ordered MAT2A reaction and distinction between catalytic activity and MAT2B-mediated stability.
          limitations: 'In-vitro purified-enzyme conditions do not establish in-vivo flux limitation, dietary responsiveness, tissue-specific regulation or phenome effects.'
      - label: Murray et al. (2016)
        citation_key: murray_crystallography_2016
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#murray_crystallography_2016
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: High-resolution human MATα2 structures captured substrates/products and active-site ion coordination across ATP-driven SAMe formation.
        assessment:
          study: 'X-ray crystallography of human MATα2 with methionine, ATP analogues, SAMe, adenosine and phosphate-state ligands.'
          population: 'Purified crystallised human MATα2 protein; no cells, animals or human participants.'
          result: 'Structures captured methionine repositioning toward ATP C5′, SAMe/product states and phosphate-group coordination by magnesium and potassium ions.'
          effect_magnitude: Structures ranged from 1.1 Å to 2.34 Å resolution; no physiological effect size applies.
          evidence_summary: Direct structural support for the reaction chemistry and catalytic-ion requirement of human MAT.
          limitations: 'Static ligand-bound structures establish catalytic geometry, not physiological nutrient limitation, in-vivo reaction rate, dietary dose response or clinical outcome.'
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Chiang et al. (1996)
        citation_key: chiang_s-adenosylmethionine_1996
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#chiang_s-adenosylmethionine_1996
        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: Foundational review establishes SAMe as a major methyl donor and places MAT synthesis upstream of transmethylation.
        why_excluded: 'It is a broad methylation review and does not independently quantify human MAT kinetics, active-site ion requirements or dietary control of synthesis flux.'
      - label: Corrillero Bravo et al. (2022)
        citation_key: corrillero_bravo_analysis_2022
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#corrillero_bravo_analysis_2022
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        why_relevant: 'Measured circulating SAM, SAH and SAM:SAH after contrasting four-week dietary patterns in healthy adults.'
        why_excluded: 'The biomarkers do not isolate MAT synthesis flux; group trajectories were similar, so the study does not establish a dietary lever for PM3.'
    sec_assessment_ref:
      id: same-pm3-f1-assessment-v1
      version: 2
      sha256: 2ab92745040cb0d76a604a306ddaf2e56c2d6352500bd3bee6224956b784df8f
  - id: PM3-IC1
    finding_label: 'SAM and SAM:SAH are pool-state markers, not synthesis-flux measures'
    presentation: interpretive-constraint
    finding_statement: 'Measured SAM concentration and the SAM:SAH ratio reflect the balance of synthesis, methyl-group utilisation, SAH formation and clearance and therefore cannot by themselves identify MAT-dependent SAMe synthesis capacity.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'SAM concentration is a metabolite-pool measurement. The SAM:SAH ratio is commonly interpreted as a methylation index because SAM supplies methyl groups while SAH inhibits methyltransferases. Both values integrate production and consumption processes; neither is a direct MAT flux assay. Careful sample handling is also material because SAM is unstable under neutral and alkaline conditions.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The principal source is a methods and profiling study, not a formal validation against isotope-traced MAT flux. The ratio may be useful for methyl-group homeostasis and inherited-metabolism assessment, but its exact meaning varies by biological matrix, compartment and pre-analytical handling.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Corrillero Bravo et al. (2022)
        citation_key: corrillero_bravo_analysis_2022
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#corrillero_bravo_analysis_2022
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Validated SAM/SAH measurement as a pool/homeostasis readout and found no differential change after four-week vegan versus meat-rich dietary assignment in healthy adults.
        assessment:
          study: LC-MS/MS method optimisation plus a randomised four-week vegan-versus-meat-rich dietary intervention.
          population: Method reference cohort of 33 healthy adults and dietary intervention cohort of 53 healthy adult omnivores aged 18–60 years.
          result: 'The method quantified low-nanomolar SAM and SAH across matrices; plasma and urinary SAM, SAH and SAM:SAH showed similar baseline-to-end changes in both diet groups.'
          effect_magnitude: Healthy plasma reference ranges were SAM 120 ± 36 nM and SAH 21.5 ± 6.5 nM (mean ± 2 SD); no between-diet synthesis-flux effect was measured.
          evidence_summary: Direct evidence that SAM/SAH are measurable pool-state biomarkers and that short-term dietary pattern contrast did not establish PM3 modulation.
          limitations: 'Small healthy-adult cohorts, four-week duration, circulating/urinary pools rather than tissue-specific MAT flux, and no cognitive or emotional outcome measurement.'
    finding_summary: 'Measured SAM concentration and the SAM:SAH ratio reflect the balance of synthesis, methyl-group utilisation, SAH formation and clearance and therefore cannot by themselves identify MAT-dependent SAMe synthesis capacity.'

    presentation: phenome-relationship
    primary_phenome: Emotional Regulation
    finding_summary: The repository-attached mood-disorder evidence does not directly demonstrate an effect of endogenous MAT-dependent SAMe synthesis capacity on Emotional Regulation.

    finding_statement: The repository-attached mood-disorder evidence does not directly demonstrate an effect of endogenous MAT-dependent SAMe synthesis capacity on Emotional Regulation.

The PM3-to-Emotional Regulation proposition is therefore an inferred downstream bridge rather than a directly demonstrated relationship.'

## BRS2-1-3 - SAMe Synthesis

(Producing the Cell's Methyl-Donor Pool)

## 1. Mission & Overview

### Mission

Maintain methionine adenosyltransferase capacity to convert methionine and ATP into SAMe, sustaining the methyl-donor pool used by downstream methyltransferases.


**Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Supported

### Overview

Methionine adenosyltransferase forms S-adenosylmethionine from methionine and ATP. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) Magnesium and potassium ions coordinate that ATP-dependent catalysis. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) This reaction supplies the methyl donor used by many later enzymes. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) Upstream methionine regeneration and later methyl-transfer reactions remain separate processes. Circulating SAMe and the SAM:SAH ratio describe pool balance rather than synthesis speed. [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

- **Benefits:** Forming SAMe provides the common methyl donor used by many different enzymes. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) Those later uses include DNA methylation, membrane-phospholipid formation, and neurotransmitter metabolism.
- **Implementation Notes:** Methionine and dietary protein are the provision routes. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) Magnesium and potassium ions take part in the catalysis and are not separate dosing targets. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) These reaction requirements do not set an intake for raising SAMe synthesis. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

## 2. Primary Biological Effects

↑ MAT-dependent SAMe formation<br />
↑ availability of the SAMe methyl-donor pool<br />
→ permissive support for downstream methyl-transfer reactions

## 4. Mechanistic Basis + Scientific Findings

### Summary

SAMe production is the point at which methionine and intracellular ATP become a usable methyl donor. The defining event is MAT catalysis; upstream regeneration of methionine and downstream consumption of SAMe determine context but are not part of the synthesis reaction itself.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">

<strong>SAMe synthesis — mechanistic detail</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

<span id="pm3-mechanism-f1" />
<span id="methionine-adenosyltransferase-reaction" />

#### PM3-F1

MAT catalyses an ATP-dependent reaction in which methionine's sulfur attacks ATP's adenosyl carbon to form SAMe; phosphate products are subsequently released. Human MAT2A studies support conflicting ATP-first and rapid-equilibrium random substrate-binding models; no settled universal order is asserted. See [PM3-F1](#pm3-f1). Human MATα2 structures capture catalytic states and active-site ion coordination [[2](#pm-ref-2)].


Supporting evidence: [PM3-F1](#pm3-f1).

#### (Direct requirements and capacity)

Methionine and ATP are reaction substrates. Magnesium and potassium ions participate in active-site phosphate coordination under biochemical and structural conditions [[1](#pm-ref-1), [2](#pm-ref-2)]. These are biochemical requirements, not evidence that ordinary dietary magnesium, potassium or methionine intake is rate-limiting. MAT isoform abundance, enzyme stability, substrate availability and feedback all contribute to cellular capacity; the reviewed evidence does not establish a simple human basal-versus-reserve dietary threshold.

<span id="pm3-mechanism-f5" />

#### PM3-F5

MAT2B association can preserve MAT2A protein or catalytic stability in purified-human-enzyme and mammalian-cell experiments. This supports a stability contribution to enzyme regulation, not an exclusive explanation of MAT2B action or a demonstrated increase in human SAMe synthesis flux. Bailey et al. (2021) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); 10.1038/s41419-024-07093-8 [[11]](#pm-ref-11); 10.1107/S2052252526005075 [[12]](#pm-ref-12); 10.1021/acs.biochem.0c00998 [[13]](#pm-ref-13)

Supporting evidence: [PM3-F5](#pm3-f5).

#### (Pool state is not synthesis flux)

SAM concentration reflects formation and consumption. The SAM:SAH ratio additionally incorporates SAH production and clearance and is commonly used as a methylation-potential index, not a direct measure of MAT flux. Accurate interpretation also depends on matrix and sample handling because SAM is unstable [[3](#pm-ref-3)].

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

This PM governs methionine → SAMe formation through MAT. Folate/B12-dependent remethylation belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation); betaine/BHMT remethylation to [BRS2-FM1-PM2](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation); integrated methionine-cycle throughput to [BRS2-FM1-PM4](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux); and transsulfuration to [BRS2-FM2-PM5](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway). PEMT, DNA, neurotransmitter and other methyl-transfer reactions are downstream consumers, not SAMe synthesis.

<span id="pm3-mechanism-f4" />
<span id="integration-within-brs2" />

#### PM3-F4

Within [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency), PM1 and PM2 regenerate methionine, PM3 converts it to SAMe, and PM4 represents integrated cycle flux. [BRS2(KC2) — Methionine & Transsulfuration Substrate Pool](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/kc/brs2-kc2-methionine-transsulfuration-substrate-pool) supplies substrate context without proving dietary control of PM3.


Supporting evidence: [PM3-F4](#pm3-f4).

</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Human MAT structural and kinetic studies identify reaction participants, while kinetic models disagree about substrate-binding order. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) These studies directly establish enzyme mechanism and biochemical requirements. They do not test ordinary dietary modulation, human in-vivo synthesis flux or downstream methylation outcomes, so those effects remain beyond the evidence summarised here.
