scientific_findings_intro: >-
  Human structure and mutagenesis studies establish BHMT’s betaine-dependent
  reaction and catalytic zinc requirement. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2)
  Controlled human choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and worsened the
  homocysteine response to a methionine challenge in participants who developed
  hepatic steatosis; repletion restored that response. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Animal
  depletion and enzyme-inhibition studies complement this supported dependency
  chain, but human tissue BHMT flux and cognitive outcomes were not measured.
  [[12]](#pm-ref-12) [[13]](#pm-ref-13)
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM2-F1
    finding_label: BHMT remethylates homocysteine with betaine and catalytic zinc
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Human betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT) transfers one methyl
      group from betaine to homocysteine. The products are methionine and
      dimethylglycine. A zinc ion bound by three cysteines activates
      homocysteine. Folate and vitamin B12 are not part of this reaction.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      This is the reaction boundary. It does not include folate-dependent
      remethylation, the later conversion of methionine to SAMe, whole-cycle
      throughput, phosphatidylethanolamine methyltransferase, or acetylcholine
      formation. It also does not show that dietary zinc intake changes the
      reaction in people.
    finding_statement: >-
      BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, forming
      methionine and dimethylglycine, without folate or vitamin B12 in that
      reaction, and uses an active-site zinc ion to activate homocysteine.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Human crystal structures show that BHMT makes methionine from betaine and
      homocysteine and uses zinc to activate homocysteine. Mutating any of the
      three zinc-binding cysteines to alanine abolishes activity and sharply
      reduces zinc binding, and the same biochemical work states the products as
      methionine and dimethylglycine. A methyl-donor review states that methyl
      flow through this pathway does not depend on folate or vitamin B12.
      Together these sources identify the reaction and its metal. They do not
      test ordinary dietary control or human tissue flux.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The enzyme evidence uses purified or recombinant human protein, not intact
      human metabolism. Loss of activity after removing zinc ligands does not
      show that dietary zinc usually limits the enzyme. The review statement
      that the pathway is independent of folate and vitamin B12 is not a new
      flux experiment. Quantitative claims in that review about choline
      deficiency and liver methionine were not re-checked in the primary animal
      papers.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Evans et al. (2002)
        citation_key: evans_betaine_2002
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#evans_betaine_2002
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Human BHMT structures show methionine formation from betaine and
          homocysteine, with zinc activating homocysteine; oxidation that expels
          zinc rearranges the active site.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            X-ray structures of human BHMT in an oxidised zinc-free form and a
            reduced zinc-bound form with a homocysteine-like bisubstrate analog.
          population: >-
            Purified crystallised human BHMT; no cells, animals or human
            participants.
          result: >-
            The enzyme forms methionine from betaine and homocysteine. Zinc
            activates homocysteine. The zinc-binding sequences sit at the ends
            of barrel strands, and a Cys217–Cys299 disulfide expels zinc.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Structures at 2.15 Å (zinc-free) and 2.05 Å (zinc-bound). No
            physiological effect size applies.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct structural evidence for the human reaction and for catalytic
            zinc.
          limitations: >-
            Static structures establish catalytic geometry, not in-vivo flux,
            dietary zinc responsiveness, or a clinical outcome.
      - label: Breksa and Garrow (1999)
        citation_key: breksa_zinc_1999
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#breksa_zinc_1999
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Replacing any of Cys217, Cys299 or Cys300 with alanine abolished human
          BHMT activity and reduced zinc binding. The reaction produces
          methionine and dimethylglycine from betaine and homocysteine.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Site-directed mutagenesis of recombinant human liver BHMT, with
            activity and zinc-binding measurements.
          population: >-
            Recombinant human BHMT protein expressed in bacteria; no human
            participants.
          result: >-
            Cys217, Cys299 and Cys300 were identified as zinc ligands. Mutation
            of any one to alanine caused complete loss of activity and a
            significant reduction in zinc binding. The catalysed transfer is
            from betaine to homocysteine, yielding dimethylglycine and
            methionine.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Complete loss of activity for each alanine substitution. No human
            effect size applies.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct evidence that catalytic activity of human BHMT depends on
            those zinc ligands, and a clear statement of the reaction products.
          limitations: >-
            Bacterial expression and purified-protein assays do not show that
            dietary zinc limits BHMT in human tissues.
      - label: Obeid (2013)
        citation_key: obeid_metabolic_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#obeid_metabolic_2013
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Methyl-group flow through BHMT does not depend on folate or vitamin
          B12, although the pathway is most active in liver and kidney and talks
          to the folate route.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Narrative review of methyl-donor deficiency with emphasis on the
            BHMT pathway.
          population: >-
            Review of human and animal methyl-donor studies; not a new
            experiment.
          result: >-
            BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine. The
            review states that methyl flow through this pathway is not dependent
            on folate or vitamin B12, while several cross-talk mechanisms exist.
            BHMT is particularly active in liver and kidney.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            No new effect size. The review cites other studies for homocysteine
            and metabolite changes.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Explicit pathway-level statement that folate and vitamin B12 are not
            required for methyl flow through BHMT.
          limitations: >-
            A review cannot replace a flux assay. Some quantitative deficiency
            claims are attributed to other papers and were not re-adjudicated
            here.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        Obeid (2013) is also primary evidence in PM2-F2 for choline oxidation.
        That reuse is one review, not a second experiment.
  - id: PM2-F2
    finding_label: Choline oxidation supplies betaine and is not the BHMT reaction
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Choline can be oxidised to betaine aldehyde and then to betaine. That
      sequence can supply the BHMT substrate. It is not the methyl transfer that
      BHMT carries out, and betaine is not turned back into choline.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Choline is a precursor of the substrate, not a cofactor or substrate of
      BHMT. Acetylcholine formation and phosphatidylethanolamine methylation use
      choline or SAMe in other reactions.
    finding_statement: >-
      Irreversible oxidation of choline to betaine is an upstream supply route
      for the BHMT substrate and is not itself the BHMT reaction.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      A methyl-donor review states that betaine is produced by irreversible
      oxidation of choline through choline dehydrogenase and betaine-aldehyde
      dehydrogenase, and that BHMT then uses betaine. A choline-dehydrogenase
      review places the human enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane, mainly
      in kidney and liver, and separates the first oxidation to betaine aldehyde
      from the second oxidation to betaine. Betaine then donates a methyl group
      in the homocysteine-to-methionine reaction. The two steps are supply, not
      the BHMT reaction.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Purified, stable human choline dehydrogenase has been difficult to obtain,
      so some catalytic detail is inferred from related enzymes and from tissue
      activity rather than from a complete human kinetic characterisation. The
      reviews do not show that raising choline intake increases BHMT flux in
      people.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Obeid (2013)
        citation_key: obeid_metabolic_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#obeid_metabolic_2013
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Betaine can be formed by irreversible oxidation of choline via choline
          dehydrogenase and betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, and BHMT then uses
          that betaine to remethylate homocysteine.
        assessment:
          study: Narrative review of methyl-donor metabolism centred on BHMT.
          population: Review of human and animal evidence; not a new enzyme assay.
          result: >-
            The review states the two-enzyme oxidation of choline to betaine and
            the subsequent BHMT reaction. It treats the oxidation as
            irreversible.
          effect_magnitude: No new effect size for the oxidation steps.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Pathway-level evidence that choline oxidation supplies betaine
            upstream of BHMT.
          limitations: >-
            Review synthesis, not a direct demonstration of human choline
            dehydrogenase kinetics or of dietary choline increasing BHMT flux.
      - label: Salvi and Gadda (2013)
        citation_key: salvi_choline_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#salvi_choline_2013
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Human choline dehydrogenase oxidises choline to betaine aldehyde, and
          betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase completes formation of betaine, which
          can donate a methyl group to homocysteine.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Review of human choline dehydrogenase localisation, physiological
            role and biochemical characterisation.
          population: >-
            Review of human tissue activity and comparative biochemistry; not a
            dietary trial.
          result: >-
            The enzyme sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is found
            mainly in kidney and liver. It oxidises choline to betaine aldehyde.
            A second enzyme, betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase, oxidises that
            aldehyde to betaine. Betaine is described as a methyl donor for
            methionine formation from homocysteine. Purified active human enzyme
            has been difficult to obtain.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Tissue activity was reported mainly in kidney, with about six-fold
            lower activity in liver. No dietary dose-response was measured.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Enzyme-level support for the two-step oxidation that supplies
            betaine.
          limitations: >-
            Incomplete purification of human choline dehydrogenase limits
            kinetic detail. Localisation and pathway role do not show that
            dietary choline changes BHMT flux.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        Obeid (2013) is also primary evidence in PM2-F1 for folate- and vitamin
        B12-independence of BHMT. That reuse is one review, not a second
        experiment.
  - id: PM2-IC1
    finding_label: Plasma homocysteine is not tissue BHMT flux
    presentation: interpretive-constraint
    finding_summary: >-
      Betaine supplements lower plasma homocysteine, and severe choline
      depletion can raise it after a methionine load. The same blood measurement
      also falls after vitamin B12 and fish oil, which are not BHMT substrates.
      The number is not the enzyme's rate in tissue and is not a clinical
      benefit.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      A homocysteine change can be consistent with this route and still fail to
      prove it. Read supplement and depletion studies as blood results unless
      enzyme activity or traced methyl flux was measured.
    finding_statement: >-
      Changes in plasma homocysteine after betaine supplementation, choline
      depletion, or vitamin B12 and fish-oil treatment do not measure tissue
      BHMT flux and do not establish a clinical benefit of this reaction.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      In healthy adults, six weeks of supplemental betaine lowered fasting
      plasma homocysteine relative to placebo, and it also blunted the rise
      after a methionine load. The authors inferred faster betaine-dependent
      remethylation, but they did not measure BHMT activity, tissue methionine
      formation or dimethylglycine flux. In mice, choline deficiency doubled
      post-load plasma homocysteine, and a small male pilot found a higher
      post-load value after clinical choline depletion, yet mouse liver betaine
      did not fall and BHMT was not assayed. A separate trial lowered plasma
      homocysteine with vitamin B12, fish oil or both, without betaine. The
      biomarker is therefore real, shared and non-specific.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The betaine trial selected healthy adults with relatively high
      homocysteine still in a broad reference range. The human choline study was
      a pilot of eight men. None of the three studies measured tissue BHMT flux,
      attention or cognition.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Olthof et al. (2003)
        citation_key: olthof_low_2003
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#olthof_low_2003
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Daily betaine at 1.5, 3 and 6 g lowered fasting plasma homocysteine by
          about 12%, 15% and 20% versus placebo after six weeks, without a
          measurement of tissue BHMT flux.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Randomised, placebo-controlled trial of anhydrous betaine for six
            weeks, with methionine-load tests.
          population: >-
            Four groups of 19 healthy adults selected for higher plasma
            homocysteine within a broad reference range.
          result: >-
            Fasting plasma homocysteine after 1.5, 3 and 6 g/day was about 12%,
            15% and 20% lower than placebo. The post-load rise was also smaller.
            The discussion infers increased betaine-dependent remethylation.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            About 12% (P < 0.01), 15% (P < 0.002) and 20% (P < 0.0001) lower
            fasting homocysteine than placebo at six weeks for 1.5, 3 and 6
            g/day.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct human evidence that supplemental betaine lowers plasma
            homocysteine. The endpoint is a circulating metabolite, not enzyme
            flux.
          limitations: >-
            No BHMT activity, tissue methionine flux, dimethylglycine production
            rate, or clinical symptom outcome was measured.
      - label: da Costa et al. (2005)
        citation_key: da_costa_choline_2005
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#da_costa_choline_2005
        data_level: Mixed
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Choline deficiency raised post-methionine-load plasma homocysteine in
          mice and in a small human pilot, but did not measure BHMT activity,
          and mouse liver betaine did not fall.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Three-week mouse diets with 0, 10 or 35 mmol choline/kg, plus a
            depletion-repletion pilot in men, each with an oral methionine load.
          population: Male C57BL/6J mice and eight healthy men aged 20–46 years.
          result: >-
            Two hours after the load, choline-deficient mice had about twice the
            plasma homocysteine of choline-fed mice. Fasting values did not
            differ. Four hours after the load, clinically choline-depleted men
            had plasma homocysteine about 35% higher than when not depleted.
            Hepatic betaine in the mice was not significantly lower.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            About twofold higher post-load homocysteine in deficient mice. About
            35% higher post-load homocysteine in depleted men. Mouse liver
            betaine 1.3 ± 0.3 versus 1.1 ± 0.3 nmol/mg protein.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Dietary choline depletion can change post-load plasma homocysteine.
            It does not isolate BHMT flux, and the mouse betaine pool was not
            shown to fall.
          limitations: >-
            Human sample of eight men, clinical depletion rather than ordinary
            intake, and no enzyme or tracer measurement.
      - label: Huang et al. (2015)
        citation_key: tao_huang_effect_2015
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#tao_huang_effect_2015
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Vitamin B12, fish oil and their combination lowered plasma
          homocysteine without any betaine intervention, so the biomarker is not
          specific to BHMT.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Randomised trial of vitamin B12, fish oil, or both, with plasma
            homocysteine as an endpoint.
          population: Thirty-eight participants randomised to three groups.
          result: >-
            The repository abstract reports plasma homocysteine reductions of
            about 22% with vitamin B12, 19% with fish oil, and 39% with the
            combination. Betaine and BHMT were not the interventions.
          effect_magnitude: 'About 22%, 19% and 39% lower plasma homocysteine in the three arms.'
          evidence_summary: >-
            Shows that plasma homocysteine can fall through inputs that are not
            the BHMT substrate.
          limitations: >-
            The attached abstract does not report BHMT activity, betaine status
            or a clinical neurological outcome. Design detail beyond the
            abstract was not re-extracted.
  - id: PM2-F3
    finding_label: ADHD diet reviews do not test BHMT
    presentation: phenome-relationship
    primary_phenome: Focus / Attention Stability
    finding_summary: >-
      The attached attention reviews discuss dietary patterns, supplements and
      choline in neurodevelopment. They do not measure BHMT or test betaine as a
      treatment for attention.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      An attention relationship can remain a framework bridge. It should not be
      read as evidence that this remethylation route changes focus.
    finding_statement: >-
      The repository ADHD diet review and choline neurodevelopment review do not
      directly demonstrate that BHMT-dependent remethylation changes Focus /
      Attention Stability.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      One review surveys sugar restriction, additive-free diets, elimination
      diets, fatty acids, iron and zinc in ADHD. Another surveys choline status
      in autism, ADHD and dyslexia. Neither assigns an attention outcome to BHMT
      activity or to betaine supplementation. The biochemical reaction can be
      true while this phenome link stays untested.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      This is a gap in the attached reviews, not proof that no attention
      relationship exists. The sources are narrative reviews and mix many
      dietary exposures.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Millichap and Yee (2012)

  - id: PM2-F5
    finding_label: >-
      Betaine availability and choline supply can constrain remethylation
      reserve
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Controlled human choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced
      challenged remethylation reserve in participants who developed clinical
      depletion. In rats, choline deprivation lowered hepatic betaine and the
      phenotype was suppressed by choline or betaine; specific BHMT inhibition
      independently produced the expected pathway failure.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Together with the established BHMT reaction, these intervention, pool,
      rescue and specific-inhibition edges support a constraint on
      betaine-dependent remethylation capacity. They do not directly measure
      human tissue BHMT flux or show a benefit from intake above adequacy.
    finding_statement: >-
      Inadequate betaine availability, including from conditional failure of
      choline provision, can constrain BHMT-dependent homocysteine remethylation
      capacity.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Da Costa et al. fed eight healthy men a 550 mg/day choline baseline diet
      followed by 50 mg/day for up to 42 days. Plasma choline and betaine fell
      by about 30% and 47% while folate remained adequate. In the four
      participants who developed hepatic steatosis, post-load homocysteine was
      5.2 µmol/L higher and returned to the baseline response after repletion.
      In rats under low-methionine conditions, Setoue et al. found that choline
      deprivation markedly lowered hepatic betaine and raised plasma
      homocysteine, while either choline or betaine restored hepatic betaine and
      suppressed the increase. Strakova et al. independently showed that a
      specific BHMT inhibitor reduced liver BHMT activity by more than 90%,
      raised plasma homocysteine two- to five-fold and lowered liver SAM by more
      than 40%. Human BHMT biochemistry establishes betaine as the methyl donor.
      These edges form a supported constraint chain.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The human study was a pilot in eight men, with the challenged response
      confined to four clinically depleted participants. The pool-rescue and
      specific-inhibition evidence is from rat liver, and neither study measured
      isotope-resolved human BHMT flux. Choline partitioning, endogenous
      synthesis and methionine/folate state modify the provision route. The
      chain supports capacity constraint under demonstrated depletion, not
      universal limitation on ordinary diets, benefit from supplementation above
      adequacy, or a cognitive outcome.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: da Costa et al. (2005)
        citation_key: da_costa_choline_2005
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#da_costa_choline_2005
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Controlled choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced
          post-methionine-load homocysteine-handling reserve in the participants
          who developed clinical depletion; both the phenotype and challenge
          response reversed with repletion.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Controlled depletion–repletion pilot with a methionine-load
            challenge.
          population: >-
            Eight healthy men aged 20–46 years; four developed hepatic steatosis
            during depletion.
          result: >-
            Plasma choline and betaine fell about 30% and 47% in the full group.
            In the four clinically depleted men, post-load homocysteine
            increased by 5.2 µmol/L (95% CI 1.2–9.1; P = 0.025) relative to the
            550 mg/day baseline phase and returned to the baseline response
            after repletion. Folate did not fall.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Betaine fell from 66 ± 7 to 35 ± 2 nmol/mL in all eight men;
            clinically depleted participants had a 5.2 µmol/L greater post-load
            homocysteine response.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Human intervention evidence linking choline inadequacy, lower
            betaine availability and reduced remethylation reserve under
            challenge.
          limitations: >-
            Small male-only pilot, severe controlled depletion, shared
            circulating endpoint, and no direct tissue or isotope-resolved BHMT
            flux.
      - label: Evans et al. (2002)
        citation_key: evans_betaine_2002
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#evans_betaine_2002
        data_level: Cellular / Molecular
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Human BHMT structures establish the betaine-to-homocysteine methyl
          transfer that links betaine availability to the challenged
          remethylation response.
        assessment:
          study: X-ray structural analysis of human BHMT.
          population: Purified human BHMT; no participants.
          result: >-
            BHMT transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine to form
            methionine and dimethylglycine.
          effect_magnitude: No human intervention effect size.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Provides reaction-specific attribution for the donor-pool
            intervention chain.
          limitations: >-
            Purified-enzyme evidence does not itself establish dietary
            constraint.
      - label: Setoue et al. (2008)
        citation_key: setoue_choline_deprivation_2008
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#setoue_choline_deprivation_2008
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Under low-methionine conditions, choline deprivation depleted hepatic
          betaine and raised plasma homocysteine; either choline or betaine
          suppressed the phenotype.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Controlled rat feeding experiments varying choline, methionine
            context and lipotrope rescue.
          population: Male Wistar rats fed casein- or soybean-protein-based diets.
          result: >-
            On the choline-deprived soybean-protein diet, hepatic betaine fell
            from about 3.65 to 0.13 µmol/g and plasma homocysteine rose from
            about 12.5 to 33.5 µmol/L. Choline or betaine supplementation
            restored hepatic betaine to about 9.81 or 13.3 µmol/g and lowered
            plasma homocysteine to about 7.3 or 7.7 µmol/L. Ex-vivo BHMT
            activity did not decline.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            Approximately 96% lower hepatic betaine with deprivation; rescue
            restored the pool above control and suppressed
            hyperhomocysteinaemia.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Pool depletion and rescue connect conditional choline inadequacy to
            loss of substrate-supported remethylation capacity rather than loss
            of BHMT protein competence.
          limitations: >-
            Rat liver model under low-methionine conditions; homocysteine
            removal also involved transsulfuration, and no in-vivo
            isotope-resolved BHMT flux was measured.
      - label: Strakova et al. (2011)
        citation_key: strakova_bhmt_inhibition_2011
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#strakova_bhmt_inhibition_2011
        data_level: Preclinical
        exposure_context: isolated-substance
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Specific pharmacological BHMT inhibition produced the pathway
          direction expected when BHMT-dependent capacity fails.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Rat feeding study using the potent and specific BHMT inhibitor
            S-(δ-carboxybutyl)-L-homocysteine for 3 or 14 days across adequate,
            cysteine-free and methionine-deficient diets.
          population: Rats; no human participants.
          result: >-
            The inhibitor reduced liver BHMT activity by more than 90%,
            increased plasma homocysteine two- to five-fold and lowered hepatic
            SAM by more than 40% across dietary conditions.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            >90% lower BHMT activity; 2–5-fold higher plasma homocysteine; >40%
            lower liver SAM.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Specific perturbation confirms that impaired BHMT capacity can
            generate the observed remethylation and methylation-state direction.
          limitations: >-
            Pharmacological inhibition in rats does not quantify the effect of
            ordinary human betaine or choline intake.
    evidence_dependency:
      - >-
        Da Costa et al. (2005) is also used in PM2-IC1. PM2-IC1 establishes that
        plasma homocysteine alone is non-specific; PM2-F5 relies on the combined
        depletion, pool, challenge, repletion and reaction chain rather than
        treating that biomarker alone as BHMT flux.
      - >-
        Evans et al. (2002) is also primary evidence in PM2-F1. Its reuse in
        PM2-F5 supplies the same reaction-specific link and is not independent
        replication.

## BRS2-1-2 - Betaine/BHMT Remethylation

(Regenerating methionine from homocysteine with betaine)

## 1. Mission & Overview + Dietary Levers

### Mission

Provide a parallel homocysteine clearance route so methionine and SAMe supply remain resilient when folate demand is high.

**Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Dominant

### Overview

Betaine–homocysteine methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from betaine to homocysteine, forming methionine and dimethylglycine. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) A bound zinc ion activates homocysteine. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Folate and vitamin B12 are not part of that reaction. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) Betaine may come from the diet or from oxidation of choline. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) In healthy men, controlled choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and reduced homocysteine-handling reserve, and repletion reversed that change. [[6]](#pm-ref-6)

- **Benefits:** This route replenishes methionine, and with it the capacity to handle a homocysteine load, without using folate or vitamin B12. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) In the men who became clinically depleted, that reserve fell with the betaine pool and returned after repletion. [[6]](#pm-ref-6)
- **Implementation Notes:** Betaine and choline are the provision routes. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) The bound zinc ion is part of the enzyme, not a dietary zinc target. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Choline depletion lowered the betaine pool; that study does not set a dose for people whose supply is already adequate. [[6]](#pm-ref-6)
- **Biological Relevance:** [Folate- and vitamin B12-dependent remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) is a neighbouring reaction, not this methyl transfer. [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

## 2. Primary Biological Effects

↑ folate-independent remethylation of homocysteine to methionine<br />
↑ methionine available for later SAMe formation<br />
→ no direct claim that this reaction itself raises SAMe or improves symptoms

## 4. Mechanistic Basis + Scientific Findings

### Summary

Homocysteine (an amino acid left after methyl groups are used) can be turned back into methionine by a betaine-dependent reaction that does not use folate or vitamin B12. The methionine can later be used to make SAMe, but this reaction stops at methionine. A fall in plasma homocysteine after betaine is taken is a blood result, not a measurement of how fast the enzyme is working in tissue.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>Betaine/BHMT Remethylation — mechanistic detail</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

<span id="pm2-mechanism-f1" />
<span id="the-methyl-transfer" />

#### PM2-F1

BHMT moves one methyl group from betaine (trimethylglycine) onto homocysteine. The products are methionine and dimethylglycine (what remains of betaine after that methyl group leaves) [Breksa and Garrow (1999) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); Evans et al. (2002) [[1]](#pm-ref-1)]. A zinc ion held by three cysteines in the active site activates the homocysteine thiol. Changing any of those cysteines to alanine abolishes activity in the recombinant human enzyme [[2]](#pm-ref-2). Human structures capture both a zinc-free oxidised form and a zinc-bound form [[1]](#pm-ref-1).


Supporting evidence: [PM2-F1](#pm2-f1).

#### (What the reaction does not use)

Folate and vitamin B12 are required by the parallel methionine-synthase route. They are not substrates or cofactors of this transfer. Methyl flow through BHMT does not depend on them [Obeid (2013) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)]. The enzyme is especially active in liver and kidney rather than throughout the brain [[2]](#pm-ref-2), [[3]](#pm-ref-3).

<span id="pm2-mechanism-f2" />
<span id="choline-is-a-supply-route" />

#### PM2-F2

Choline can be oxidised to betaine aldehyde by choline dehydrogenase, then to betaine by betaine-aldehyde dehydrogenase. That oxidation is irreversible, so it can feed betaine into BHMT without being the BHMT reaction itself [Obeid (2013) [[3]](#pm-ref-3); Salvi and Gadda (2013) [[4]](#pm-ref-4)]. Human choline dehydrogenase sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane and is found mainly in kidney and liver [[4]](#pm-ref-4).


Supporting evidence: [PM2-F2](#pm2-f2).

<span id="pm2-mechanism-f5" />

#### PM2-F5

Inadequate betaine availability, including from conditional failure of choline provision, can constrain BHMT-dependent homocysteine remethylation capacity. Evans et al. (2002) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); da Costa et al. (2005) [[6]](#pm-ref-6); Setoue et al. (2008) [[12]](#pm-ref-12); Strakova et al. (2011) [[13]](#pm-ref-13)

Supporting evidence: [PM2-F5](#pm2-f5).

#### (Plasma homocysteine is a shared marker)

In healthy adults, 1.5–6 g/day of supplemental betaine lowered fasting plasma homocysteine over six weeks [Olthof et al. (2003) [[5]](#pm-ref-5)]. Experimental choline depletion raised homocysteine after a methionine load in mice and in a pilot of eight men, without a fall in mouse liver betaine and without an enzyme assay [da Costa et al. (2005) [[6]](#pm-ref-6)]. Vitamin B12 and fish oil also lower plasma homocysteine, so the same blood result is not specific to this enzyme [Huang et al. (2015) [[7]](#pm-ref-7)].

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

This PM is the betaine-dependent methyl transfer only.

Folate/B12-dependent remethylation belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation). Methionine-to-SAMe conversion belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM3](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis). Combined cycle throughput belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM4](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux).

SAMe-dependent phosphatidylethanolamine methylation belongs to [BRS2-FM3-PM7](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-pm7-phosphatidylcholine-formation). Acetylcholine formation from choline belongs to [BRS1-FM2-PM6](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-pm6-acetylcholine-synthesis-support).

#### (Integration within BRS2)

Within [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency), this reaction is one way to regenerate methionine when the folate-dependent route is under strain [Obeid (2013) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)]. The methionine can enter SAMe formation afterwards. Whether a shortfall in the wider methyl-donor pool limits the enzyme's activity in people has not been shown, because plasma homocysteine does not measure that activity [[5]](#pm-ref-5), [[6]](#pm-ref-6).

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Human structure and mutagenesis studies establish BHMT’s betaine-dependent reaction and catalytic zinc requirement. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Controlled human choline depletion lowered plasma betaine and worsened the homocysteine response to a methionine challenge in participants who developed hepatic steatosis; repletion restored that response. [[6]](#pm-ref-6) Animal depletion and enzyme-inhibition studies complement this supported dependency chain, but human tissue BHMT flux and cognitive outcomes were not measured. [[12]](#pm-ref-12) [[13]](#pm-ref-13)

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS1-FM2-PM6 — Acetylcholine Synthesis Support](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-pm6-acetylcholine-synthesis-support) — Choline that is oxidised becomes betaine for this methyl transfer, while choline that is not oxidised is the substrate used to make acetylcholine. Betaine is not converted back to choline, so this shared use of choline does not show that dietary betaine raises brain acetylcholine.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS2-FM1-PM1 — Folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) — This sibling regenerates methionine from homocysteine by methionine synthase, using a folate-derived methyl group and vitamin B12. BHMT uses betaine instead, so the routes are parallel and folate is not a cofactor of this reaction.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM3 — SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis) — Methionine produced here can be joined to ATP by methionine adenosyltransferase to form the later methyl donor. That conversion is a separate enzyme step and is not catalysed by BHMT.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM4 — Methionine Cycle Flux](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux) — The wider methionine cycle combines remethylation, methyl-group use and regeneration into one throughput. This PM is only the betaine-dependent remethylation step, not that combined throughput.

## 7. Phenome Connections

These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

Mission & Overview ### Mission Maintain coordinated one-carbon cycling that supports homocysteine remethylation, SAMe production, and methyl-group transfer. ### Overview Coordinates folate/B12- and betaine-dependent homocysteine remethylation with methionine-cycle flux and SAMe production. This integrated state maintains methyl-donor availability for phospholipid, neurotransmitter, and other methylation-dependent chemistry across the brain and body. * Maintains methyl-donor context for neurotransmitter-related chemistry — Supporting BRS1. * Connects homocysteine handling with transsulfuration and redox pathways — within BRS2 and Supporting BRS3. * Supplies SAMe-dependent methyl-group transfer used across cellular metabolism — Supporting BRS4. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects Methionine regeneration; SAMe production; homocysteine handling; methyl-group transfer. ## 4. Mechanistic Basis (Integrated FM Narrative) ### 4.1 Functional Rationale Remethylation, SAMe formation and regulated cycle routing maintain methyl-transfer capacity while handling homocysteine. Their coordination provides a biological basis for methylation-dependent functions without defining a universal optimum for metabolite concentrations. ### 4.2 Evidence Summary Human enzyme studies establish distinct folate/B12, betaine and MAT reaction requirements. Choline-depletion challenge evidence supports a bounded upstream dependency. Human tracer measurements found unchanged mean cycle rates during moderate vitamin B6 restriction despite altered PLP and cystathionine concentrations. [[10](#fm-ref-10), [11](#fm-ref-11), [12](#fm-ref-12), [13](#fm-ref-13), [14](#fm-ref-14)] Together, functioning provision and routing capacities would support methionine regeneration and SAMe-dependent methyl transfer. This is a synthesis of complementary pathway evidence, not proof that lowering blood homocysteine increases tissue methylation or improves cognition. ### 4.3 Suboptimal Function & Its Effects Effects depend on the affected route and nutritional context. In the choline-depletion study, the four clinically depleted men had reduced homocysteine-handling reserve after a methionine challenge; this does not establish the same impairment in adequately nourished people or measure human BHMT flux. [[13](#fm-ref-13)] The [accepted child-PM connections](#key-constraints) distinguish this conditional PM2 constraint from supported supply in PM1, PM3 and PM4. Whether donor availability limits tissue MTR capacity, MAT-dependent synthesis or integrated cycle rates remains unresolved. A change in homocysteine or SAMe concentration alone cannot establish a cascade of impaired synthesis, routing and methylation across all four PMs. [[12](#fm-ref-12), [14](#fm-ref-14)] ## 5. Connected Mechanisms - [BRS1-FM2-PM6 — Acetylcholine Synthesis Support](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-pm6-acetylcholine-synthesis-support) — Shares the choline resource with methyl-donor provision. Animal folate/methionine-cycle impairment studies report altered brain choline and acetylcholine; they do not establish donor-intake control of acetylcholine synthesis in adequately nourished humans. [[15](#fm-ref-15), [16](#fm-ref-16), [17](#fm-ref-17)] - [BRS1-FM3-PM7 — Neuronal Membrane DHA Incorporation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm3/brs1-fm3-pm7-neuronal-membrane-dha-incorporation) — Choline supports phosphatidylcholine production through the Kennedy pathway, connecting nutritional provision with DHA-carrier biology. Separately, choline can contribute methyl groups through betaine and SAMe to the PEMT route. Whether inadequate choline or methyl-donor supply limits adult brain DHA incorporation remains unresolved and context-dependent; these supported pathways do not establish benefit from additional intake. [[18](#fm-ref-18), [20](#fm-ref-20), [21](#fm-ref-21), [22](#fm-ref-22)] - [BRS2-FM2-PM5 — Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) — Uses homocysteine at the cycle's transsulfuration exit: CBS joins it with serine to form cystathionine. This shares an intermediate with remethylation, without making homocysteine concentration a measure of either branch's flux. [[19](#fm-ref-19)] - [BRS2-FM3-PM7 — Phosphatidylcholine Formation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-pm7-phosphatidylcholine-formation) — Uses SAMe as the methyl donor for PEMT-mediated conversion of phosphatidylethanolamine to phosphatidylcholine. Supply of the donor does not establish increased PEMT activity or phosphatidylcholine output. [[20](#fm-ref-20)] - [BRS2(FM3) — Methylation–Membrane Coupling](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-methylation-membrane-coupling) — Connects this FM's SAMe-producing metabolism with the SAMe-dependent phospholipid chemistry assessed in its PEMT child. This is shared reaction-resource context, not a demonstrated improvement in brain delivery or cognition. [[20](#fm-ref-20)] ## 7. scientific_findings_intro: >-
  Human-pathway evidence establishes methionine synthase’s folate-substrate and
  methylcobalamin requirements and distinguishes them from upstream
  flavin-dependent enzymes. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) In an adult observational study,
  riboflavin status modified the association between an MTHFR variant and
  circulating homocysteine. [[10]](#pm-ref-10) Together, these findings clarify
  enzyme-specific dependence and a status–genotype interaction; the circulating
  marker does not directly measure tissue remethylation flux.
scientific_findings:
  - id: PM1-F1
    finding_label: Methionine synthase remethylates homocysteine
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Methionine synthase transfers the methyl group of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate
      to homocysteine, producing methionine and tetrahydrofolate.
      Methylcobalamin carries that methyl group. Betaine remethylation, SAMe
      synthesis, transsulfuration and phospholipid methylation are different
      reactions.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      This defines the reaction and its direct participants. It does not show
      that eating more folate or vitamin B12 speeds the reaction in human
      tissues, and it does not make riboflavin a cofactor of the synthase.
    finding_statement: >-
      Cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase transfers the methyl group of
      5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, producing methionine and
      tetrahydrofolate, and uses methylcobalamin as its cofactor.
      Betaine-dependent remethylation, methionine adenosyltransferase,
      transsulfuration and phosphatidylethanolamine methylation are separate
      reactions.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      A human-pathway review states the reaction directly: methionine synthase
      (MTR) converts homocysteine plus 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to methionine
      plus tetrahydrofolate and requires the methylated form of cobalamin.
      Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase produces that folate substrate.
      Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase is a separate, mainly liver and
      kidney route. Methionine adenosyltransferase then converts methionine to
      SAMe, and cystathionine beta-synthase starts transsulfuration. The review
      also traces dietary folate, including folic acid reduced by dihydrofolate
      reductase, into 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and dietary cobalamin through
      absorption and intracellular processing onto the enzyme as
      methylcobalamin.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The primary source is a biochemical review, not a new human flux study.
      Reaction identity does not show that ordinary dietary intake controls
      tissue remethylation rate, and it does not assign clinical benefit.
      Phosphatidylethanolamine methylation is a later SAMe-consuming reaction,
      not part of this step.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Froese et al. (2019)
        citation_key: froese_vitamin_2019
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#froese_vitamin_2019
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin to remethylate homocysteine
          with 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, producing methionine and
          tetrahydrofolate. Parallel and downstream reactions are named
          separately.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Narrative review of cobalamin absorption, intracellular cofactor
            processing, folate-mediated one-carbon metabolism and
            methionine-cycle regulation.
          population: >-
            No new participants. The review synthesises human pathway
            biochemistry and inherited disorders of cobalamin and folate
            metabolism.
          result: >-
            Methionine synthase (MTR, EC 2.1.1.13) catalyses homocysteine plus
            5-methyltetrahydrofolate to methionine plus tetrahydrofolate and
            requires methylcobalamin. Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
            produces 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. Betaine-homocysteine
            methyltransferase is an alternative remethylation enzyme, mainly in
            liver and kidney. Methionine adenosyltransferase converts methionine
            and ATP to SAMe. Cystathionine beta-synthase combines homocysteine
            with serine to start transsulfuration. Dietary folic acid is reduced
            to tetrahydrofolate by dihydrofolate reductase, and dietary
            cobalamin is processed to methylcobalamin on the synthase.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            No new numeric effect size. The result is reaction identity and
            pathway separation.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct statement of the human methionine synthase reaction, its
            methylcobalamin cofactor, the folate route to its substrate, and the
            neighbouring reactions this PM does not include.
          limitations: >-
            A review does not measure tissue remethylation flux, ordinary-diet
            dose response, or a cognitive or attention outcome.
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Aragão et al. (2024)
        citation_key: aragao_revitalising_2024
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#aragao_revitalising_2024
        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: >-
          Riboflavin is often discussed beside folate-cycle enzymes, so this
          review was checked against the synthase reaction.
        why_excluded: >-
          Its abstract describes general riboflavin physiology. It does not
          state the methionine synthase reaction, methylcobalamin dependence, or
          separation from betaine remethylation.
  - id: PM1-F2
    finding_label: Riboflavin is not the synthase cofactor
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_summary: >-
      Riboflavin supplies the flavin cofactor of methylenetetrahydrofolate
      reductase, which makes 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and of methionine
      synthase reductase, which repairs inactive cobalamin. Methionine synthase
      itself uses methylcobalamin.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Riboflavin can matter upstream of the substrate and in enzyme repair. It
      is not a cofactor bound at the methionine synthase catalytic site.
    finding_statement: >-
      Flavin adenine dinucleotide derived from riboflavin is a cofactor of
      methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase and of methionine synthase reductase,
      not of the methionine synthase catalytic site, which uses methylcobalamin.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      The human-pathway review assigns methylcobalamin, not a flavin, to
      methionine synthase, and places methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase
      upstream as the source of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. An adult
      cross-sectional study states the same split: methylenetetrahydrofolate
      reductase uses FAD, methionine synthase reductase binds flavin
      mononucleotide and FAD, and methionine synthase uses methylcobalamin. In
      that study, riboflavin status modified the association of an MTHFR variant
      with blood homocysteine. That is a circulating-marker interaction at the
      upstream enzyme, not evidence that riboflavin occupies the synthase
      cofactor site.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      The flavin assignment for the two neighbouring enzymes is stated in the
      study introduction from prior enzymology, and the new data are genotype
      associations with blood homocysteine. Neither source shows that dietary
      riboflavin changes tissue methionine-synthase flux.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: García-Minguillán et al. (2014)
        citation_key: garcia_minguillan_riboflavin_2014
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#garcia_minguillan_riboflavin_2014
        data_level: Human Study
        exposure_context: dietary
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: >-
          Riboflavin status modified MTHFR-linked differences in blood
          homocysteine. The synthase cofactor named in the paper is
          methylcobalamin, while FAD is assigned to MTHFR and to MTRR.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Cross-sectional analysis of whether fasting plasma total
            homocysteine associations with MTHFR 677C>T, MTRR 66A>G and MTRR
            524C>T depend on riboflavin status, measured by the erythrocyte
            glutathione reductase activation coefficient.
          population: >-
            771 adults aged 18–75 years in Tarragona province, Spain, excluding
            B-vitamin users and pregnant or lactating women. Recruitment was in
            1998–2002, before mandatory folic acid fortification of flour in
            that setting.
          result: >-
            The paper states that FAD is a cofactor of MTHFR, that MTRR binds
            flavin mononucleotide and FAD, and that methionine synthase uses
            methylcobalamin and is reactivated by MTRR. Among MTHFR 677T
            carriers with plasma folate below 14.7 nmol/L, blood homocysteine
            was 8.2% higher than in the 677CC genotype, and that difference was
            not seen when riboflavin status was optimal (interaction p = 0.048).
          effect_magnitude: >-
            8.2% higher blood homocysteine in the specified MTHFR contrast (p <
            0.01), eliminated at optimal riboflavin status (interaction p =
            0.048). No methionine-synthase activity or tissue-flux estimate is
            reported.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Separates the riboflavin-dependent enzymes (MTHFR and MTRR) from the
            methylcobalamin cofactor of methionine synthase, and shows a
            riboflavin-status interaction with an MTHFR variant on blood
            homocysteine.
          limitations: >-
            Observational genotype analysis. The endpoint is plasma
            homocysteine, not enzyme rate. Optimal riboflavin status did not
            identify riboflavin as a prosthetic group of methionine synthase.
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Froese et al. (2019)
        citation_key: froese_vitamin_2019
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#froese_vitamin_2019
        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: >-
          States that methionine synthase requires methylcobalamin and that
          methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase produces its folate substrate.
        why_excluded: >-
          It does not itself test riboflavin status or assign FAD to MTHFR or
          MTRR, so it is not the study that adjudicates the riboflavin split.
  - id: PM1-IC1
    finding_label: Plasma homocysteine is not remethylation flux
    presentation: interpretive-constraint
    finding_summary: >-
      Folic acid lowers blood homocysteine, and vitamin B12 adds a further
      reduction. That change is in a circulating marker. It does not measure how
      fast methionine synthase runs in tissues.
    finding_interpretation: >-
      Blood homocysteine can move when folate or vitamin B12 status changes. It
      still cannot be read as tissue remethylation rate, methylation output, or
      a clinical benefit.
    finding_statement: >-
      A reduction in blood homocysteine after folic acid or vitamin B12 does not
      measure tissue methionine-synthase flux.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: >-
      Individual data from 12 randomised trials show that folic acid lowers
      blood homocysteine, with a larger effect at higher starting homocysteine
      and lower starting folate, and that vitamin B12 produces a further
      reduction while vitamin B6 does not. The measured endpoint is blood
      homocysteine concentration. A separate small trial also lowered plasma
      homocysteine with vitamin B12, fish oil, or both, which mixes this marker
      with a fatty-acid exposure that is not a synthase substrate.
    synthesis_limitations: >-
      Standardised percentage reductions describe blood concentration after
      supplements, often at doses above ordinary food intake. They do not report
      tissue methionine appearance, SAMe production, or a clinical outcome. Fish
      oil co-administration shows that the marker can move for reasons outside
      this reaction.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Collaboration (1998)
        citation_key: collaboration_lowering_1998
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#collaboration_lowering_1998
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: supplemental-formulation
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: >-
          Folic acid lowered blood homocysteine, vitamin B12 added a further
          reduction, and vitamin B6 did not. The endpoint was blood
          concentration, not tissue enzyme flux.
        assessment:
          study: >-
            Meta-analysis of randomised trials of folic-acid-based supplements,
            using individual data and multivariate regression to separate folic
            acid dose from added vitamin B12 or vitamin B6.
          population: >-
            1114 people in 12 trials. Results were standardised to pretreatment
            blood homocysteine of 12 µmol/L and blood folate of 12 nmol/L,
            described as approximate Western-population averages.
          result: >-
            After that standardisation, dietary folic acid reduced blood
            homocysteine by 25% (95% confidence interval 23% to 28%). Effects
            were similar from 0.5 to 5 mg folic acid daily. Vitamin B12 (mean
            0.5 mg daily) produced an additional 7% reduction (3% to 10%).
            Vitamin B6 (mean 16.5 mg daily) had no significant additional
            effect. Reductions were larger at higher pretreatment homocysteine
            and lower pretreatment folate.
          effect_magnitude: >-
            25% (23% to 28%) blood homocysteine reduction with folic acid;
            additional 7% (3% to 10%) with vitamin B12; no significant added
            effect of vitamin B6.
          evidence_summary: >-
            Direct human evidence that folic acid and vitamin B12 lower a
            circulating homocysteine marker, with the folate effect depending on
            starting folate and homocysteine.
          limitations: >-
            Supplement doses, blood concentration only, no tissue
            remethylation-flux measurement, and no clinical-outcome test in this
            meta-analysis.
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Tao Huang et al. (2015)
        citation_key: tao_huang_effect_2015
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#tao_huang_effect_2015
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        why_relevant: >-

### Overview

Methionine synthase transfers a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, forming methionine and tetrahydrofolate. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) Methylcobalamin, the vitamin B12 cofactor, takes part in that transfer. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) Regenerated methionine can later be used to form SAMe, in a separate reaction. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) Folic acid and vitamin B12 can lower blood homocysteine. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) That change is a circulating marker, not tissue remethylation flux. [[1]](#pm-ref-1)

- **Benefits:** Remethylating homocysteine restores methionine, which can then be converted into SAMe. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) This helps maintain the methyl-group supply used by later methylation.
- **Implementation Notes:** 5-Methyltetrahydrofolate, vitamin B9 (folate), methylcobalamin, and vitamin B12 (cobalamin) are the provision routes. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) [[1]](#pm-ref-1) Homocysteine is the substrate already in the pathway, not a dietary target. Lowering blood homocysteine does not set a dose for tissue remethylation flux. [[1]](#pm-ref-1)
- **Biological Relevance:** [Betaine-dependent remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation) and [transsulfuration](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) are neighbouring routes, not this reaction. [[9]](#pm-ref-9)

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Maintaining a usable methionine supply depends on recycling homocysteine through the folate- and B12-dependent route. That reaction feeds methionine toward later SAMe formation, but it is not itself SAMe synthesis, betaine remethylation, or homocysteine disposal.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>Folate/B12-dependent homocysteine remethylation — mechanistic detail</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Methionine synthase reaction)

Methionine synthase transfers a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (a reduced folate carrying one methyl group) to homocysteine. The products are methionine and tetrahydrofolate. The methyl group is carried by methylcobalamin, the active vitamin B12 cofactor on the enzyme [Froese et al. (2019) [[9]](#pm-ref-9)].

Dietary folate, including folic acid after reduction by dihydrofolate reductase, can be converted to that 5-methyltetrahydrofolate substrate. Dietary vitamin B12 is absorbed and processed to methylcobalamin on the enzyme. Those are provision routes, not evidence that a higher intake speeds the reaction in tissues [Froese et al. (2019) [[9]](#pm-ref-9)].

#### (Riboflavin sits beside the reaction)

Riboflavin is the precursor of flavin adenine dinucleotide. That flavin is a cofactor of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase, the enzyme that makes 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and of methionine synthase reductase, which repairs inactive cobalamin. It is not the cofactor in the synthase active site. That site uses methylcobalamin [García-Minguillán et al. (2014) [[10]](#pm-ref-10)].

In adults, riboflavin status changed how an upstream reductase variant related to blood homocysteine. That interaction does not place riboflavin on methionine synthase itself [García-Minguillán et al. (2014) [[10]](#pm-ref-10)].

#### (Blood homocysteine is not the reaction rate)

Folic acid lowers blood homocysteine, and vitamin B12 lowers it further. Vitamin B6, which serves a different disposal route, did not add a clear further reduction in the same pooled trials [Collaboration (1998) [[1]](#pm-ref-1)]. Blood homocysteine is a circulating marker. A lower value does not measure how fast this reaction runs in a tissue.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

This reaction is folate- and B12-dependent remethylation only.

The parallel betaine route, which also makes methionine but does not use 5-methyltetrahydrofolate or vitamin B12, belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM2 — Betaine/BHMT Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation). Conversion of methionine to SAMe belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM3 — SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis). Integrated cycle throughput belongs to [BRS2-FM1-PM4 — Methionine Cycle Flux](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux).

Homocysteine disposal through transsulfuration belongs to [BRS2-FM2-PM5 — Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway). SAMe-dependent phospholipid methylation belongs to [BRS2-FM3-PM7 — Phosphatidylcholine Formation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-pm7-phosphatidylcholine-formation). Later incorporation of DHA into neuronal membranes belongs to [BRS1-FM3-PM7 — Neuronal Membrane DHA Incorporation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm3/brs1-fm3-pm7-neuronal-membrane-dha-incorporation).

B-vitamin effects on cognitive decline can depend on omega-3 status, but that interaction is a later, combined outcome, not a measurement of this reaction [Oulhaj et al. (2016) [[4]](#pm-ref-4)].

#### (Integration within methylation-cycle efficiency)

Within [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency), this is the folate- and B12-dependent way to return homocysteine to methionine. The betaine route is parallel. SAMe formation uses the methionine product later. Folate supply explains where 5-methyltetrahydrofolate comes from. It does not, by itself, show that the wider set of methyl donors limits the tissue rate of this reaction.

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Human-pathway evidence establishes methionine synthase’s folate-substrate and methylcobalamin requirements and distinguishes them from upstream flavin-dependent enzymes. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) In an adult observational study, riboflavin status modified the association between an MTHFR variant and circulating homocysteine. [[10]](#pm-ref-10) Together, these findings clarify enzyme-specific dependence and a status–genotype interaction; the circulating marker does not directly measure tissue remethylation flux.

### 5.1 BRS Pathways

[BRS2-FM1-PM1 — Folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation)
↓
[BRS2-FM3-PM7 — Phosphatidylcholine Formation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm3/brs2-fm3-pm7-phosphatidylcholine-formation)
↓
[BRS1-FM3-PM7 — Neuronal Membrane DHA Incorporation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm3/brs1-fm3-pm7-neuronal-membrane-dha-incorporation)

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS1-FM2-PM6 — Acetylcholine Synthesis Support](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm2/brs1-fm2-pm6-acetylcholine-synthesis-support) — This reaction remethylates homocysteine with 5-methyltetrahydrofolate rather than betaine, so it is a parallel methyl route to the path that draws on choline. It supplies methionine, not the choline used for acetylcholine.
- [BRS1-FM3-PM7 — Neuronal Membrane DHA Incorporation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm3/brs1-fm3-pm7-neuronal-membrane-dha-incorporation) — Methionine from this reaction can later become SAMe and support phospholipid methylation. That is downstream use through other reactions, not a substrate step of methionine synthase.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS2-FM1-PM2 — Betaine/BHMT Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation) — Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase also remethylates homocysteine, using betaine in liver and kidney and not 5-methyltetrahydrofolate or vitamin B12. Parallel route to the same methionine product.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM3 — SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis) — Methionine produced here is the amino-acid substrate for the later reaction that forms SAMe from methionine and ATP. Downstream use of the product, not part of methionine synthase.
- [BRS2-FM1-PM4 — Methionine Cycle Flux](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux) — Cycle flux combines this remethylation step with SAMe use, homocysteine return and the parallel betaine route. Shared cycle context, not the synthase reaction itself.

## 7. Phenome Connections

These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

## BRS2(FM2) - Transsulfuration & Redox Coupling (Sulfur Amino Acids for Antioxidant Defence) ### Primary Mechanisms - [BRS2-FM2-PM5 — Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) - [BRS2-FM2-PM6 — Glutathione Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm6-glutathione-synthesis) ### Key Constraints - [BRS2(KC2) — Methionine–Cysteine Sulfur Amino Acid Pool](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/kc/brs2-kc2-methionine-transsulfuration-substrate-pool) - [BRS2(KC1) — Methyl Donor Pool](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/kc/brs2-kc1-one-carbon-donor-pool) The following are independently admitted child-PM connections. They do not establish a uniform constraint on the whole FM or benefit from increasing intake. | PM | Accepted connection | Evidence and boundary | |---|---|---| | [BRS2-FM2-PM5](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) | **Supported upstream supply:** Methionine enters the methionine cycle, producing homocysteine that supplies the CBS reaction and carries sulfur into cysteine formation. | Supported upstream supply, not direct CBS substrate or established sulfur-pool limitation. Cysteine is the product of this PM and is not admitted as an additional supply input. Tissue allocation, compensation and benefit from extra methionine intake are not established. [Lamers et al. (2011) [7]](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway#pm-ref-7) | | [BRS2-FM2-PM5](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) | **Conditional constraint:** Combined folate/choline deprivation reduced measured hepatic CBS catalytic activity in rats; donor-resource context can therefore constrain this step under that defined deprivation condition. SAM-responsive CBS regulation is a supported connection, not a measured mediator of the dietary effect. | Four-week combined folate/choline deprivation in male rats on a 20% casein formula with antibiotic suppression of microbial folate synthesis. Extracted liver CBS activity, not in-vivo flux or brain activity, was measured. Neither constituent alone significantly reduced CBS activity in this experiment. SAM mediation is supported mechanistically but was not isolated causally; liver lipid changes accompanied deprivation. This does not establish extra-intake benefit, betaine deficiency or uniform donor limitation. [Liu et al. (2012) [9]](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway#pm-ref-9); [McCorvie et al. (2014) [8]](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway#pm-ref-8) | | [BRS2-FM2-PM6](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm6-glutathione-synthesis) | **Conditional constraint:** Removing methionine and cysteine together slowed whole-blood glutathione synthesis, and removing cysteine alone did not when methionine stayed adequate. That is the sulfur-amino-acid provision relationship already recorded for cysteine and methionine. | Lyons used a 10-day amino-acid formula that removed both methionine and cysteine in healthy young men, and whole-blood glutathione concentration was maintained. Courtney-Martin kept methionine adequate and found that removing cysteine did not lower erythrocyte synthesis in young men. Neither study identifies a bottleneck beyond those provision relationships. This is not neuronal synthesis, ordinary mixed-diet advice, or a benefit from increasing an adequate intake. [Lyons et al. (2000) [3]](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm6-glutathione-synthesis#pm-ref-3); [Misra and Griffith (1998) [1]](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm6-glutathione-synthesis#pm-ref-1); [Courtney-Martin et al. (2008) [5]](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm6-glutathione-synthesis#pm-ref-5) | ## 1. Mission & Overview ### Mission Coordinate homocysteine routing into cysteine production with downstream glutathione synthesis and cellular redox defence. ### Overview Coordinates transsulfuration with glutathione synthesis, linking homocysteine disposal to cysteine availability and cellular antioxidant capacity. This coupling connects one-carbon metabolism with redox defence without implying that pathway activity alone determines resilience or recovery. * Routes homocysteine toward cysteine as an alternative to remethylation — within BRS2. * Supplies substrate for glutathione-dependent antioxidant defence — Supporting BRS3. * Contributes to the redox environment surrounding mitochondrial function — Supporting BRS4. ## 2. Primary Biological Effects ↑ cysteine generation; ↑ glutathione synthesis; ↓ oxidative load ## 4. Mechanistic Basis (Integrated FM Narrative) ### 4.1 Functional Rationale Cysteine generation and glutathione assembly connect sulfur-amino-acid metabolism with provision for cellular redox defence. Glutathione use and recycling are downstream capacities beyond these two PMs. ### 4.2 Evidence Summary Human enzyme studies establish PLP-dependent cysteine production and ATP-dependent glutathione assembly. Blood-cell tracer studies show reduced synthesis during combined methionine/cysteine withdrawal, no reduction during cysteine withdrawal with adequate methionine, and increased synthesis after combined precursors in older adults. [[3](#fm-ref-3), [5](#fm-ref-5), [6](#fm-ref-6), [7](#fm-ref-7), [8](#fm-ref-8), [9](#fm-ref-9)] Adequate sulfur-amino-acid supply and assembly capacity would therefore support glutathione provision under the studied conditions. They do not establish universal dietary cysteine limitation, neuronal synthesis, or successful peroxide clearance simply from producing more glutathione. ### 4.3 Suboptimal Function & Its Effects Transsulfuration and redox coupling may weaken when methionine and transsulfuration substrate pools become chronically inadequate. Low protein quality or insufficient sulfur-amino-acid intake may reduce [BRS2(KC2) — Methionine & Transsulfuration Substrate Pool](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/kc/brs2-kc2-methionine-transsulfuration-substrate-pool). Chronic methionine substrate insufficiency, increased glutathione demand, oxidative burden driving sulfur-amino-acid utilisation, and restrictive dietary patterns reducing substrate diversity may further limit cysteine supply for glutathione synthesis. These pressures may impair [BRS2-FM2-PM5 — Transsulfuration Pathway](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm5-transsulfuration-pathway) and weaken [BRS2-FM2-PM6 — Glutathione Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm2/brs2-fm2-pm6-glutathione-synthesis). At the FM level, this may shift BRS2(FM2) toward reduced transsulfuration–redox coupling capacity—with downstream relevance to antioxidant defence in BRS3 [Minich et al., 2019]. ## 5. Connected Mechanisms - [BRS2-FM1-PM1 — Folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm1-folate-b12-dependent-homocysteine-remethylation) — folate/B12-Dependent Homocysteine Remethylation - [BRS2-FM1-PM2 — Betaine/BHMT Remethylation](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm2-betaine-bhmt-remethylation) — betaine/BHMT Remethylation - [BRS2-FM1-PM3 — SAMe Synthesis](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm3-same-synthesis) — sAMe Synthesis - [BRS2-FM1-PM4 — Methionine Cycle Flux](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-pm4-methionine-cycle-flux) — methionine Cycle Flux - [BRS3-FM2-PM5 — Lipid Peroxidation Control](/docs/biological-targets/brs3/fm2/brs3-fm2-pm5-lipid-peroxidation-control) — broader redox signalling ## 7. Phenome Connections These outcomes describe translational contexts for the FM as an integrated biological capacity. They are not single-mechanism treatment claims. FM confidence uplift: FM confidence may exceed that of any individual child PM only where multiple PMs converge on the same phenome and the integrated FM biology provides additional biological rationale (biological uplift) beyond the individual mechanisms.
