  - id: PM5-F2
    finding_label: Serotonin formation depends on tryptophan hydroxylation and PLP-dependent decarboxylation
    finding_summary: 'Brain serotonin is formed from tryptophan. Tryptophan hydroxylase (the first and rate-limiting enzyme) needs iron and tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). Pyridoxal-5′-phosphate (PLP; the active form of vitamin B6) then supports decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan to serotonin. These are biological requirements, not proof that extra tryptophan, iron or B6 raises brain serotonin.'
    finding_interpretation: 'Tryptophan remains the pathway starting material. Circulating amino-acid supply and competitive brain entry are earlier steps. Iron, BH4 and PLP are candidates for dietary assessment. This finding does not admit an intake-responsive serotonin lever.'
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: 'Serotonin formation depends on tryptophan-hydroxylase conversion of tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan, requiring iron and BH4, followed by PLP-dependent decarboxylation; cofactor or substrate necessity is not evidence of intake-responsive human brain serotonin.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'Aromatic-amino-acid hydroxylase biochemistry identifies tryptophan hydroxylase as an iron- and tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent monooxygenase that forms 5-hydroxytryptophan. A second tryptophan hydroxylase isoform (TPH2) accounts for neuronal serotonin synthesis. BH4-pathway review evidence places the same cofactor on serotonin as well as dopamine synthesis. B-vitamin review evidence places PLP in neurochemical decarboxylation, and a transport study shows that B6 vitamers can enter the central nervous system. Together they establish the defining synthesis sequence and its participants. They do not show ordinary-diet control of human brain serotonin.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The synthesis is mechanistic and review-level. It does not show that ordinary dietary tryptophan, iron or vitamin B6 changes human brain serotonin, mood, sleep or ADHD when status is already adequate.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Fitzpatrick (1999)
        citation_key: fitzpatrick_aromatic_1999
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#fitzpatrick_aromatic_1999
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Tryptophan hydroxylase is a tetrahydropterin-dependent aromatic amino-acid hydroxylase that uses non-haem iron and molecular oxygen to form 5-hydroxytryptophan.
        assessment:
          study: Biochemical review of tetrahydropterin-dependent amino-acid hydroxylases.
          population: Enzyme and experimental literature; not a human dietary sample.
          result: 'Identified iron, tetrahydrobiopterin and oxygen as required participants in tryptophan hydroxylation.'
          effect_magnitude: No dietary or functional effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes the rate-limiting hydroxylation chemistry.
          limitations: Enzyme-mechanism review; not an intake-to-serotonin trial.
      - label: Walther et al. (2003)
        citation_key: walther_tph2_2003
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#walther_tph2_2003
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'A second tryptophan hydroxylase isoform (TPH2) synthesises serotonin in the brain, distinct from the peripheral TPH1 enzyme.'
        assessment:
          study: Identification of neuronal tryptophan hydroxylase 2.
          population: Experimental biochemistry and mouse genetics; not a dietary trial.
          result: Showed that brain serotonin synthesis uses TPH2 rather than treating TPH as a single peripheral enzyme.
          effect_magnitude: Not a dose-response estimate.
          evidence_summary: Places the hydroxylase step in neuronal serotonin formation.
          limitations: Isoform discovery; does not measure diet or mood.
      - label: Fanet et al. (2021)
        citation_key: fanet_tetrahydrobioterin_2021
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#fanet_tetrahydrobioterin_2021
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: Tetrahydrobiopterin is required for serotonin as well as dopamine synthesis and is made and recycled in the body.
        assessment:
          study: Review of BH4 metabolism and neuropsychiatric relevance.
          population: Mixed preclinical and clinical literature; not an ordinary-diet serotonin trial.
          result: Identified BH4 as an essential cofactor for serotonin synthesis.
          effect_magnitude: No ordinary-diet serotonin effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Supports BH4 as an endogenous hydroxylase cofactor on this path.
          limitations: Pathway and disease-context review; not a food-to-serotonin study.

### Overview

Serotonin is made in neurons when tryptophan is converted through two enzyme steps, then shaped by release, receptors, reuptake and breakdown. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) [[14]](#pm-ref-14) [[15]](#pm-ref-15) Across brain regions, the same transmitter can support different responses. [[15]](#pm-ref-15) That system supports mood stability, inhibition and behavioural regulation. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[15]](#pm-ref-15) Tryptophan, iron and vitamin B6 are part of the chemistry. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) [[10]](#pm-ref-10)

- **Benefits:** Serotonin signalling supports emotional regulation, impulse control and behavioural stability. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[15]](#pm-ref-15)
- **Implementation Notes:** Tryptophan, iron, and vitamin B6 are the substrate and cofactor relationships. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) Extra intake is not established to raise brain serotonin or improve mood or attention. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[4]](#pm-ref-4) Tetrahydrobiopterin is made in the body and is not a dietary recommendation. [[12]](#pm-ref-12)
- **Biological Relevance:** This is the signalling step after tryptophan has [entered the brain](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation); circulating supply and competitive transport come first. [[1]](#pm-ref-1)

## 2. Primary Biological Effects
↑ serotonergic signalling capacity; ↑ emotional regulation support; ↑ stress-response modulation; ↑ behavioural inhibition; ↑ sleep-compatible neurochemical signalling

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

Serotonin is a monoamine neurotransmitter synthesised from tryptophan and influenced by precursor availability, competitive amino-acid transport, micronutrient-dependent synthesis pathways, and broader metabolic context. Within [BRS1(FM1)](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-monoaminergic-function), serotonergic signalling operates alongside dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems to influence emotional regulation, behavioural control, stress responsiveness, and sleep-related neurobiology.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>Serotonergic synthesis, transport, and monoaminergic integration</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Tryptophan availability and serotonin synthesis)

Dietary tryptophan is the starting material for serotonin. Tryptophan hydroxylase converts it to 5-hydroxytryptophan using iron and tetrahydrobiopterin; aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase then uses PLP to form serotonin. Brain access of tryptophan also depends on competition with other large neutral amino acids at blood–brain barrier transport systems.

#### (LAT1 competition and transport dynamics)

Transport of tryptophan across the blood–brain barrier occurs through LAT1 transport mechanisms shared with other amino acids. Meal composition, insulin response, and amino-acid competition may influence relative brain tryptophan availability → [Fernstrom, 2013]

#### (Serotonergic regulation and emotional function)

Serotonin participates in emotional processing, behavioural inhibition, stress regulation, and impulse control. Alterations in serotonergic signalling have been associated with emotional dysregulation and impulsive behavioural phenotypes → [Shaw et al., 2014] [Banerjee and Nandagopal, 2015]

#### (Monoaminergic integration)

Serotonergic signalling does not operate independently. Functional outcomes emerge through interaction with dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems as part of broader monoaminergic regulation represented under [BRS1(FM1)](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-monoaminergic-function).

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

Amino-acid pool sufficiency belongs to [BRS1-FM1-PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation). LNAA competitive transport belongs to [BRS1-FM1-PM2](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation). Noradrenergic attention context belongs to [BRS1-FM1-PM4](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation).

</div>
</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Enzyme studies and biochemical reviews establish the neuronal tryptophan-to-serotonin synthesis sequence and its cofactor dependence. [[13]](#pm-ref-13) [[14]](#pm-ref-14) [[12]](#pm-ref-12) Broader reviews support receptor diversity and transporter-mediated handling as additional determinants of serotonergic function. [[15]](#pm-ref-15) Together, the evidence supports synthesis and signalling as related but distinct capacities; it does not directly establish that ordinary dietary changes regulate human brain serotonin or produce uniform functional benefits.

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency) — Pineal conversion of serotonin toward melatonin can use SAM from one-carbon metabolism. The attached corpus does not establish that ordinary methylation-cycle variation controls serotonergic signalling, mood or sleep.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS1-FM1-PM1 - Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) — Supplies the circulating amino-acid pool, including tryptophan used to make serotonin. Amino-acid quality and precursor-pool adequacy are assessed there. That is precursor supply, not serotonin signalling.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM2 - LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) — Governs competitive brain entry of large neutral amino acids, including tryptophan, after a meal. Transport bias is not serotonin synthesis or receptor signalling.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM3 - Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation) — Parallel catecholamine path that shares LAT1 presentation and some decarboxylase chemistry. Dopaminergic signalling is not serotonergic signalling.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM4 - Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) — Parallel monoamine path from shared precursor transport. It does not form serotonin.

## 7. Phenome Connections

These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

title: Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation
pm_id: BRS1-FM1-PM3
mission: 'Maintain appropriately regulated dopamine synthesis, storage, release, receptor signalling, reuptake and metabolism across changing functional demand.'
parent_fm: BRS1(FM1)
parent_brs: BRS1
summary: 'Dopamine signalling is set by how much is made, stored, released, sensed, taken back up and broken down. The result depends on brain region, receptor type, baseline state and the task, so more signalling is not always better. Tests of synthesis, release, receptors and transporters are not one dopamine level. This regulation supports cognitive control and willingness to spend mental effort.'

scientific_findings_intro: 'Human pharmacology and PET evidence supports context-dependent dopamine regulation: baseline synthesis capacity, receptor involvement and cognitive demand influence motivation and flexibility, so effects are not uniformly enhancing. [[15]](#pm-ref-15) [[16]](#pm-ref-16) [[17]](#pm-ref-17) Biochemical and deficiency evidence separately supports synthesis requirements, without establishing that extra precursor intake improves human signalling.     finding_summary: 'Dopamine synthesis proceeds through tyrosine hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase. Iron and tetrahydrobiopterin support the hydroxylase step, while pyridoxal-5′-phosphate supports decarboxylation{{cite:fanet_tetrahydrobioterin_2021,beard_iron_2003,kennedy_b_2016}}. These biochemical requirements do not show that extra intake increases dopamine in an adequately nourished human brain.'
    finding_interpretation: 'This finding supports tyrosine as the hydroxylase substrate, iron, PLP and vitamin B6 as dietary-requirement atoms, and BH4 as an endogenous biochemical cofactor; none is an intake-responsive dopamine lever.'
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: 'Neuronal dopamine synthesis depends on separable tyrosine-hydroxylase and aromatic L-amino-acid-decarboxylase reactions with iron, tetrahydrobiopterin and pyridoxal-5′-phosphate requirements; cofactor requirement is not evidence of intake responsiveness.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'Biochemical reviews identify tetrahydrobiopterin and iron as requirements for aromatic amino-acid hydroxylation and pyridoxal-5′-phosphate as a catecholamine-synthesis cofactor. Experimental iron deficiency alters striatal and nucleus-accumbens dopamine metabolites in rats, supporting biological sensitivity under deficiency. Together this establishes pathway dependence, not ordinary-diet control of human brain dopamine.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The most direct deficiency evidence is preclinical, and the reviewed sources do not establish common inadequacy in a defined clinical population, responsiveness when baseline status is adequate, or functional benefit mediated by dopamine.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Fanet et al. (2021)
        citation_key: fanet_tetrahydrobioterin_2021
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#fanet_tetrahydrobioterin_2021
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: BH4 is required for aromatic amino-acid hydroxylation and therefore for dopamine synthesis.
        assessment:
          study: Narrative biochemical review of tetrahydrobiopterin and monoamine synthesis pathways.
          population: Mixed mechanistic literature; not a defined dietary intervention population.
          result: Identified BH4 as necessary for aromatic amino-acid hydroxylation and monoamine synthesis.
          effect_magnitude: No pooled intake-response effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Supports reaction-level requirements and pathway boundaries.
          limitations: Does not establish that increasing dietary intake modifies human brain dopamine or improves function.
      - label: Erikson et al. (2000)
        citation_key: erikson_iron_2000
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#erikson_iron_2000
        data_level: Animal Data
        exposure_context: dietary iron deficiency
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: Increasing severity of iron deficiency altered locomotor activity and dopamine metabolites in rat striatum and nucleus accumbens.
        assessment:
          study: Controlled rat dietary iron-deficiency experiment with regional dopamine-metabolite and locomotor outcomes.
          population: Laboratory rats under graded iron deficiency.
          result: 'Iron deficiency changed regional dopamine-metabolite profiles and locomotor activity, with severity-dependent effects.'
          effect_magnitude: Directional severity-response; no human-equivalent effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Supports dopamine-system sensitivity to marked iron deficiency.
          limitations: Animal deficiency model; metabolite concentrations do not directly measure synthesis flux or predict human clinical benefit.
    connected_supportive_evidence:

        citation_key: beard_iron_2003

        data_level: Animal Data

        why_excluded: Review-level and predominantly preclinical; it does not add a human intake-to-dopamine estimate.

        citation_key: kennedy_b_2016
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#kennedy_b_2016
        data_level: Mechanistic
        why_relevant: 'Reviews B-vitamin roles in neurochemical synthesis, including vitamin B6 as a cofactor context for dopamine formation.'
        why_excluded: General B-vitamin review; it does not isolate aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase or show an intake-to-dopamine response.
      - label: Spector (1978)
        citation_key: spector_vitamin_1978
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#spector_vitamin_1978
        data_level: Animal Data

    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F2
    finding_label: Dopamine supports cognitive control nonlinearly
    finding_summary: 'Human pharmacology and patient studies show that dopamine effects on working memory and control depend on baseline state, brain region and task. Both insufficient and excessive stimulation can impair performance.'
    finding_interpretation: Dopamine is not a single directional cognitive-performance variable; “more dopamine” is not a valid general recommendation.
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: 'Dopaminergic modulation of working memory and cognitive control follows baseline-, region- and process-dependent nonlinear relationships rather than a uniformly beneficial direction.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'The reviewed human evidence supports an inverted-U framework in which prefrontal stability and striatal flexibility can respond differently to dopaminergic manipulation. Baseline dopamine, receptor context, region and cognitive demand explain why the same manipulation may improve one process or participant while impairing another.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The synthesis integrates pharmacological studies, Parkinson disease withdrawal studies and preclinical evidence. Drug effects may include non-dopaminergic actions and do not establish nutritional modifiability.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Cools & D'Esposito (2011)
        citation_key: cools_inverted-u_2011
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#cools_inverted-u_2011
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: pharmacological dopaminergic manipulation and medication withdrawal
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Dopaminergic effects on working memory and cognitive control varied with baseline dopamine, brain region and stability-versus-flexibility demand, consistent with an inverted-U relationship.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Mechanistic review of experimental animals, healthy-human pharmacology and Parkinson disease medication-withdrawal studies.'
          population: 'Healthy adults and people with Parkinson disease, with supporting animal evidence.'
          result: Both low and high dopaminergic stimulation could impair cognition; effects differed between prefrontal stability and striatal flexibility.
          effect_magnitude: No pooled effect estimate; direction depended on baseline and task.
          evidence_summary: Directly rejects a unitary more-is-better dopamine model for cognition.
          limitations: Heterogeneous paradigms and pharmacological exposures; not a dietary intervention synthesis.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F3
    finding_label: Striatal dopamine influences willingness to expend cognitive effort
    finding_summary: 'In healthy adults, higher striatal dopamine synthesis capacity predicted greater willingness to choose demanding cognitive work, while methylphenidate and sulpiride shifted benefit-versus-cost weighting most in people with lower synthesis capacity.'
    finding_interpretation: 'This supports effort allocation and motivation, not a claim that dopamine simply increases energy or that diet reproduces medication effects.'
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: Striatal dopamine synthesis capacity and controlled dopaminergic manipulation influence cognitive-effort choice by altering benefit-versus-cost weighting.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'PET-derived synthesis capacity and a placebo-controlled pharmacology design converged on a baseline-dependent role for dopamine in cognitive motivation. Higher synthesis capacity increased benefit weighting on placebo, and drug effects were larger at lower baseline capacity.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'A modest healthy-adult sample and an effort-choice task do not establish sustained performance, fatigue resistance, clinical benefit or dietary modification. Methylphenidate also affects noradrenaline.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Westbrook et al. (2020)
        citation_key: westbrook_dopamine_2020
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#westbrook_dopamine_2020
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: 'methylphenidate, sulpiride and placebo'
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Higher striatal dopamine synthesis capacity and dopaminergic drugs increased willingness to expend cognitive effort by strengthening benefit relative to cost weighting.
        assessment:
          study: Within-participant pharmacological study combined with PET measurement of striatal dopamine synthesis capacity and computational modelling of effort choices.
          population: Fifty healthy adults; complete model estimates were available for a smaller subset depending on analysis.
          result: 'Baseline synthesis capacity predicted cognitive motivation, and methylphenidate and sulpiride increased motivation most at lower baseline capacity.'
          effect_magnitude: Reported model coefficients and baseline interactions; no general clinical effect size.
          evidence_summary: Provides human mechanistic evidence linking a measured dopamine process to cognitive-effort allocation.
          limitations: 'Healthy sample, acute drugs, modest size, choice rather than endurance; methylphenidate is not dopamine-selective.'
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F4
    finding_label: D2-receptor signalling contributes to cognitive flexibility
    finding_summary: 'Human pharmacological evidence supports a role for D2-receptor signalling in set shifting, while broader evidence shows that dopamine effects vary by task, baseline state and frontostriatal locus.'
    finding_interpretation: Flexibility and stability can move in opposite directions; receptor engagement is not equivalent to a global dopamine concentration change.
    finding_statement: 'Dopamine, including D2-receptor signalling, contributes to cognitive flexibility and set shifting in a task- and baseline-dependent manner.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A human agonist-antagonist pretreatment experiment provided receptor-specific evidence that D2 signalling contributes to flexibility, while a broader review situated this within frontostriatal and clinical evidence. The combined result supports a functional role without implying uniform enhancement.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Acute pharmacology in healthy volunteers and mixed human/animal review evidence do not quantify everyday dopamine function, nutritional modification or clinical treatment effects.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: van der Schaaf et al. (2012)
        citation_key: van_der_schaaf_human_2012
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#van_der_schaaf_human_2012
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: bromocriptine with sulpiride pretreatment
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'The effect of a dopamine agonist on cognitive flexibility was abolished by D2-antagonist pretreatment, supporting D2-receptor involvement.'
        assessment:
          study: Double pharmacological challenge study of task switching in healthy young adults.
          population: Healthy young adult volunteers.
          result: Bromocriptine changed flexibility performance and sulpiride pretreatment blocked the effect.
          effect_magnitude: Task-specific drug interaction; no general cognitive enhancement estimate.
          evidence_summary: Strengthens receptor-specific attribution for human cognitive flexibility.
          limitations: 'Acute pharmacology, limited sample, and no dietary or clinical outcome.'
      - label: Klanker et al. (2013)
        citation_key: klanker_dopaminergic_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#klanker_dopaminergic_2013
        data_level: Mixed
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Human and animal evidence linked striatal dopamine to reversal learning and set shifting, with direction contingent on receptor, baseline state and task.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Narrative review of pharmacological, genetic, patient and animal studies of cognitive flexibility.'
          population: 'Healthy humans, clinical groups and experimental animals.'
          result: Supported dopamine involvement but not a single direction across flexibility paradigms.
          effect_magnitude: No pooled effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Provides scope and heterogeneity context around the receptor-specific experiment.
          limitations: Mixed models and designs; review predates newer evidence and does not establish dietary modification.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F5
    finding_label: Aging affects dopamine targets differently
    finding_summary: 'Across 95 imaging studies, healthy aging was associated with lower dopamine receptor and transporter measures, while synthesis capacity was not significantly lower.'
    finding_interpretation: Age-related change is process-specific; receptor or transporter decline must not be restated as global dopamine depletion.
    finding_statement: Healthy aging is associated with declines in dopamine receptor and transporter availability but not a significant pooled decline in dopamine synthesis capacity.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'The meta-analysis separated receptors, transporters and synthesis measures across PET and SPECT studies. Moderate-to-large negative age associations were found for receptors and transporters, with larger effects for D1-like than D2-like receptors, while synthesis capacity was spared on average.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Cross-sectional imaging cannot establish within-person decline or causal cognitive effects. Ligands and regions varied, and availability measures are not dopamine concentration.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Karrer et al. (2017)
        citation_key: karrer_reduced_2017
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#karrer_reduced_2017
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Age was negatively associated with dopamine receptors and transporters but not significantly with synthesis capacity.
        assessment:
          study: Meta-analysis of cross-sectional PET and SPECT studies of distinct dopamine targets.
          population: 'Ninety-five studies comprising 2,611 healthy adults.'
          result: Receptor and transporter measures declined by target-specific amounts with age; synthesis capacity did not show a significant pooled age effect.
          effect_magnitude: Average age reductions across assessed dopamine targets ranged from 3.7% to 14.0% per decade.
          evidence_summary: Directly establishes process-specific age variation and rejects a global decline formulation.
          limitations: 'Cross-sectional studies, heterogeneous ligands and regions, and no direct mediation test for cognitive decline.'
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F6
    finding_label: ADHD does not show one uniform dopamine abnormality
    finding_summary: 'Dopamine biology is relevant to ADHD, but imaging and mechanistic findings differ by dopamine process, brain region, developmental stage, medication exposure and study method. The evidence does not support ADHD as a uniform global dopamine-deficiency disorder.'
    finding_interpretation: Medication target engagement supports dopamine relevance but cannot identify a universal baseline lesion or establish nutritional modifiability.
    therapeutic_area_ids:
      - TA001
    finding_statement: 'ADHD-related dopamine findings are heterogeneous across synthesis, release, receptors and transporter measures and do not establish a uniform global dopamine deficit.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A recent broad evaluation found hypo-, hyper- and null findings across human and animal evidence. A transporter meta-analysis found an average group difference but large heterogeneity and a strong relationship with prior psychostimulant exposure. Together these support dopamine as one relevant regulatory domain while making medication history, region, age and measured process essential to interpretation.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Small samples, different tracers and diagnostic groups, medication confounding and cross-sectional designs limit causal interpretation. Transporter binding, synthesis capacity, receptor availability and extracellular release are not interchangeable.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: MacDonald et al. (2024)
        citation_key: macdonald_dopamine_2024
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#macdonald_dopamine_2024
        data_level: Mixed
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: 'Human and animal findings did not consistently support a generalized hypodopaminergic ADHD state; results varied by process, region, task and population.'
        assessment:
          study: Critical review of the dopamine hypothesis across human studies and animal models.
          population: 'Children and adults with ADHD, healthy comparison groups and ADHD-relevant animal models.'
          result: 'Reported lower, higher and null dopamine-related findings and concluded that a simple global deficiency model is not supported.'
          effect_magnitude: No pooled global effect estimate because dopamine processes and methods were heterogeneous.
          evidence_summary: Supports dopamine relevance while constraining the direction and universality of the ADHD interpretation.
          limitations: Broad narrative synthesis across heterogeneous methods; many studies were small or medication-confounded.
      - label: Fusar-Poli et al. (2012)
        citation_key: fusar-poli_striatal_2012
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#fusar-poli_striatal_2012
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Striatal dopamine-transporter density was 14% higher on average in ADHD, but heterogeneity was large and medication exposure materially moderated the result.'
        assessment:
          study: Meta-analysis of nine PET and SPECT studies of striatal dopamine-transporter binding.
          population: 169 participants with ADHD and 173 matched controls.
          result: 'Average transporter density was higher in ADHD, but studies were significantly heterogeneous and medication exposure explained important variation.'
          effect_magnitude: Approximately 14% higher mean striatal transporter density in the ADHD group.
          evidence_summary: Shows a process-specific group difference while demonstrating why medication history cannot be ignored.
          limitations: 'Small number of imaging studies, heterogeneous tracers and designs, and transporter binding is not dopamine concentration or release.'
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F7
    finding_label: L-tyrosine did not provide sustained ADHD benefit
    finding_summary: A small open trial in adults with attention deficit disorder reported an initial response to L-tyrosine that disappeared as tolerance developed.
    finding_interpretation: 'The study does not establish sustained clinical benefit, dopamine target engagement, or a food-based treatment claim.'
    therapeutic_area_ids:
      - TA001
    finding_statement: Open-label L-tyrosine supplementation did not produce a sustained ADHD benefit and did not demonstrate modification of brain dopamine biology.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'The trial is retained as non-supportive clinical evidence at the boundary between precursor provision and PM3 signalling. An initial symptom response was not sustained, and no dopamine process was measured.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Very small, uncontrolled, older study with no placebo group, no dopamine biomarker and limited diagnostic comparability to current ADHD definitions.'
    evidence_considered:

        citation_key: f_w_reimherr_open_1987

          effect_magnitude: Small uncontrolled sample; no robust comparative effect estimate.

    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F8
    finding_label: Meal preparation can improve non-haem iron absorption
    finding_summary: Human absorption studies show that ascorbic-acid pairing and phytate degradation can increase non-haem iron absorption from selected meals. This supports iron-delivery practices only; neither study measured brain dopamine.
    finding_interpretation: 'Preparation and pairing can improve iron absorption from a meal. Iron is required by tyrosine hydroxylase, but these studies did not test brain iron delivery, dopamine signalling or cognition.'
    finding_statement: 'Ascorbic-acid pairing and validated phytate degradation can increase meal-level non-haem iron absorption in matrix-dependent human studies, but no direct dopamine effect has been demonstrated.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A controlled meal study found that ascorbic acid countered dose-dependent phytate and polyphenol inhibition of non-haem iron absorption. A separate human radioiron study found that complete phytate degradation increased iron absorption from several water-prepared cereal porridges, with smaller or absent effects in some matrices. A later review of 42 human interventions found that most dephytinisation and phytase studies improved short-term iron or zinc bioavailability while identifying limited long-term evidence.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'These studies measured gastrointestinal mineral absorption or bioavailability, not human brain iron delivery, dopamine synthesis, dopamine release or functional benefit. Results depend on meal matrix and baseline status, and no dopamine-specific dose or preparation prescription is established.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Siegenberg et al. (1991)
        citation_key: siegenberg_ascorbic_1991
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#siegenberg_ascorbic_1991
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: ascorbic acid added to phytate- or tannin-containing test meals
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Ascorbic acid prevented dose-dependent inhibition of non-haem iron absorption by phytate and polyphenols under the tested meal conditions.
        assessment:
          study: Controlled human test-meal iron-absorption study.
          population: 199 adult participants across the meal experiments.
          result: Iron absorption fell as phytate or tannic acid increased; ascorbic acid countered this inhibition in a context- and dose-dependent manner.
          effect_magnitude: Thirty milligrams of ascorbic acid overcame inhibition from the tested maize-bran phytate exposure; higher tannic-acid exposure required more ascorbic acid under the experimental conditions.
          evidence_summary: Supports same-meal ascorbic-acid pairing as an iron-delivery practice.
          limitations: 'Test-meal absorption rather than long-term iron status; no brain, dopamine or functional endpoint.'
      - label: Hurrell et al. (2003)
        citation_key: hurrell_phytic_2003
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#hurrell_phytic_2003
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: phytase-dephytinised cereal porridges
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Complete phytate degradation increased iron absorption from several water-prepared cereal porridges, but effects varied by matrix and were reduced or absent with milk and high-tannin sorghum.'
        assessment:
          study: Controlled human radioiron-absorption experiments across nine cereal porridges.
          population: 78 adults distributed across the test-meal comparisons.
          result: 'Dephytinisation increased absorption from rice, oat, maize, wheat and wheat-soy porridges prepared with water, with matrix-specific exceptions.'
          effect_magnitude: 'For example, wheat-porridge absorption rose from 0.99% to 11.54%; effects ranged from absent to approximately twelve-fold across matrices.'
          evidence_summary: Supports validated phytate reduction as a matrix-dependent iron-delivery practice.
          limitations: 'Short-term absorption experiments in adults; infant-style test matrices, no long-term status outcome and no brain or dopamine endpoint.'
    connected_supportive_evidence:
      - label: Chondrou et al. (2024)
        citation_key: chondrou_phytic_2024
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#chondrou_phytic_2024
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        why_relevant: Narrative review of 42 human interventions found that most dephytinisation and phytase studies improved iron or zinc bioavailability.
        why_excluded: Review-level support with heterogeneous matrices and limited long-term status evidence; it adds no dopamine endpoint.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F9
    finding_label: Acute voluntary exercise releases dorsal-striatal dopamine
    finding_summary: 'In healthy adults, voluntary mild-to-moderate cycling elicited endogenous dopamine release in dorsal striatum, and the PET signal correlated with faster Go/No-Go reaction time. Peripheral muscle stimulation without voluntary central command did not reproduce the behavioural effect.'
    finding_interpretation: 'This supports an acute state-dependent exercise relationship, not a chronic exercise prescription, clinical treatment claim or global “more dopamine” model.'
    finding_statement: 'Acute voluntary cardiovascular exercise can elicit dorsal-striatal dopamine release in healthy adults, with the measured release associated with faster reaction time.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'A human PET experiment measured endogenous dopamine release during mild-to-moderate cycling and related it to Go/No-Go performance. Additional electrical-muscle-stimulation experiments suggested that voluntary central command, rather than peripheral movement alone, was important for the reaction-time effect.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The PET experiment was acute and small, and the dopamine-performance association was correlational. It does not establish mediation, chronic adaptation, optimal exercise dosing, ADHD benefit or clinical efficacy.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Ando et al. (2024)
        citation_key: ando_dopamine_exercise_2024
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ando_dopamine_exercise_2024
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: acute voluntary mild-to-moderate cardiovascular exercise
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Voluntary cycling elicited endogenous dopamine release in caudate and putamen, and greater release was associated with faster Go/No-Go reaction time.'
        assessment:
          study: Human PET exercise experiment with two additional electrical-muscle-stimulation experiments.
          population: Sixteen healthy adults in the PET experiment; 18 and 22 healthy adults in the supporting stimulation experiments.
          result: Dorsal-striatal dopamine release occurred during voluntary exercise and correlated with reaction-time improvement; peripheral stimulation alone did not produce the same behavioural effect.
          effect_magnitude: Study-specific PET and reaction-time associations; no clinical effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Provides direct acute human mechanistic evidence for an exercise–dopamine relationship.
          limitations: 'Small healthy samples, acute exposure, correlational mediation evidence and no chronic, clinical or dietary comparison.'
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F10
    finding_label: Acute sleep deprivation downregulates ventral-striatal D2/D3 availability
    finding_summary: 'In healthy adults, one night of total sleep deprivation reduced ventral-striatal D2/D3 receptor availability and was associated with lower alertness and greater sleepiness. The methylphenidate comparison supported receptor downregulation rather than increased dopamine release.'
    finding_interpretation: This identifies an acute sleep-state constraint on receptor signalling; it is not evidence that ordinary sleep extension increases dopamine or improves a clinical condition.
    finding_statement: One night of total sleep deprivation reduces ventral-striatal D2/D3 receptor availability in healthy adults and is associated with reduced alertness.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'Within-person PET scans after rested sleep and one night of total sleep deprivation showed lower ventral-striatal D2/D3 receptor availability during deprivation. Methylphenidate-induced dopamine increases did not differ by sleep state, supporting receptor downregulation rather than a deprivation-induced rise in dopamine release.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'The experiment was acute, involved a small healthy sample and used receptor availability as an imaging construct. It does not establish effects of normal sleep variation, a sleep intervention, chronic outcomes or clinical benefit.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Volkow et al. (2012)
        citation_key: volkow_sleep_deprivation_2012
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#volkow_sleep_deprivation_2012
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: one night of total sleep deprivation versus rested sleep
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: 'Sleep deprivation reduced ventral-striatal D2/D3 receptor availability, associated with lower alertness and greater sleepiness, without increasing the methylphenidate-evoked dopamine response.'
        assessment:
          study: 'Within-person [11C]raclopride PET study after rested sleep and total sleep deprivation, each under placebo and methylphenidate conditions.'
          population: Twenty healthy adults.
          result: Ventral-striatal receptor availability decreased after deprivation and tracked reduced alertness; pharmacological comparison supported receptor downregulation.
          effect_magnitude: Region-specific PET change and behavioural associations; no general clinical effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Provides direct human evidence that acute sleep state constrains a specific dopamine-receptor measure.
          limitations: 'Small healthy sample, one night of total deprivation, pharmacological probe and no chronic or clinical outcome.'
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
  - id: PM3-F11
    finding_label: Short restrictive dietary protocols alter dopamine receptor binding in obesity
    finding_summary: Two small human PET studies found lower regional D2/D3 receptor binding potential after short restrictive dietary protocols in adults with obesity. The imaging changes are compatible with altered endogenous dopamine occupancy but do not uniquely identify that mechanism.
    finding_interpretation: 'This supports two tightly bounded Dietary & Fasting Protocol relationships for adults with obesity, not general reduced-fat or very-low-calorie diet recommendations.'
    finding_statement: Short-term selective fat restriction and very-low-calorie dieting can alter regional D2/D3 receptor binding potential in adults with obesity under controlled research conditions.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'In a randomized inpatient crossover study, five days of selective isocaloric fat restriction reduced striatal D2/D3 binding potential and food-cue activity, whereas selective carbohydrate restriction did not. In a separate before-and-after study, about ten days of very-low-calorie dieting reduced substantia-nigra D2/D3 binding potential in women with obesity, with regional changes tracking leptin reduction.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Both studies were short and population-specific. D2/D3 binding potential reflects receptor availability and competition from endogenous dopamine, so the imaging result cannot by itself distinguish receptor regulation from altered dopamine occupancy.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Darcey et al. (2023)
        citation_key: darcey_dietary_fat_2023
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#darcey_dietary_fat_2023
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: five-day selective isocaloric dietary-fat or carbohydrate restriction
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Selective fat restriction reduced striatal D2/D3 receptor binding potential and food-cue activity; selective carbohydrate restriction did not.
        assessment:
          study: 'Randomized inpatient crossover study using [18F]fallypride PET and food-cue functional MRI.'
          population: Seventeen adults with obesity.
          result: 'D2/D3 binding potential decreased in bilateral striatal clusters after the reduced-fat diet, with no significant change after carbohydrate restriction.'
          effect_magnitude: Significant cluster-level reductions in left putamen and right caudate/putamen; no general clinical effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: 'Directly supports a short, controlled dietary-protocol relationship with a specified dopamine imaging measure.'
          limitations: 'Small obesity-specific sample, five-day exposure and no ability to separate receptor regulation from endogenous dopamine occupancy.'
      - label: Dunn et al. (2017)
        citation_key: dunn_caloric_restriction_2017
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#dunn_caloric_restriction_2017
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: approximately ten days of very-low-calorie dieting
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search

    applicability_proposition: Imbalance of LAT1 competitive large-neutral-amino-acid balance can constrain this mechanism’s governed dopaminergic capacity.
    disposition: unresolved
    established_links:
      - Competitive LAT1 presentation can change tyrosine arrival (Fernstrom 2013).
      - Fernstrom 2013: ordinary protein-driven LNAA changes have minimal effects on tyrosine uptake and catecholamine synthesis.
    inferred_links:
      - 'The same competitive arm, under branched-chain amino-acid mixtures or activated tyrosine hydroxylase, would constrain dopamine synthesis.'
    evidence_source:
      finding_ids:
        - PM3-F1
      citation_keys:
        - fernstrom_lnna_2013
    rationale: Assessment of ordinary protein-driven LNAA change is complete and does not support a constraint on dopamine synthesis. That exposure does not close the whole competitive arm. Branched-chain amino-acid mixtures remain a different exposure and were not used to claim non-application. Public mapping is not published.
  - kc_id: BRS2(KC1)
    ikc_id: BRS2(KC1)
    arm_id: one-carbon-methyl-donor-pool
    applicability_proposition: Inadequacy of the shared methyl-donor pool can constrain this mechanism’s governed dopaminergic capacity.
    disposition: unresolved
    established_links:
      - COMT contributes to dopamine metabolism and uses SAM (PM3 §5.2; MacDonald 2024).
      - Kennedy 2016 treats B-vitamin one-carbon chemistry as relevant to brain methyl-group transfer.
    inferred_links:
      - Methyl-donor inadequacy would therefore constrain COMT-dependent dopamine metabolism.
    evidence_source:
      citation_keys:
        - kennedy_b_2016
        - macdonald_dopamine_2024
    rationale: 'This existing KC was added after a mission-coverage scan. SAM use by COMT is enzyme chemistry, not a demonstrated constraint on synthesis, storage, release, receptor signalling or reuptake. The attached corpus does not show that ordinary one-carbon variation controls regional dopamine clearance. Not a negative finding.'

    applicability_proposition: Inadequacy of the shared glutathione antioxidant-substrate pool can constrain this mechanism’s governed dopaminergic capacity.

    established_links:

    inferred_links:
      - GSH-substrate inadequacy would therefore constrain dopamine signalling or clearance.
    evidence_source:

    rationale: 'PM3 already listed BRS3 as a constrained dependency. GSH-pool evidence is about glutathione synthesis, not dopaminergic capacity. Antioxidant exposure was not shown here to modify human dopaminergic signalling. The capacity-constraint link remains a material gap.'

## BRS1-1-3 - Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation

(Dopamine synthesis, signalling, reuptake and metabolism)

## 1. Mission & Overview

### Mission

**Intervention Dominance:** Diet-Supported

### Overview

Dopamine signalling is set by how much is made, stored, released, sensed, taken back up and broken down. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) The result depends on brain region, receptor type, baseline state and the task, so more signalling is not always better. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) Tests of synthesis, release, receptors and transporters are not one dopamine level. [[8]](#pm-ref-8) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) This regulation supports cognitive control and willingness to spend mental effort. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[5]](#pm-ref-5)

- **Benefits:** Dopamine contributes to working memory, cognitive control and the choice to spend mental effort. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) Those effects depend on baseline state and brain region. They are not a measured benefit from taking more iron, vitamin B6 or tyrosine. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) [[11]](#pm-ref-11)
- **Implementation Notes:** Tyrosine, iron, and vitamin B6 are the substrate and cofactor relationships. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[19]](#pm-ref-19) An open tyrosine trial did not show a sustained attention benefit. [[11]](#pm-ref-11) Extra iron or vitamin B6, once status is adequate, is not established to raise brain dopamine. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Tetrahydrobiopterin is made in the body and is not a dietary recommendation here. [[1]](#pm-ref-1)
- **Biological Relevance:** This signalling sits downstream of precursor supply and entry into the brain - see [PM2](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation).

## 2. Primary Biological Effects

Tyrosine hydroxylation and L-DOPA conversion → neuronal dopamine synthesis capacity → vesicular storage and activity-dependent release → receptor-mediated signalling → dopamine-transporter-mediated reuptake → MAO- and COMT-related metabolism.

## 4. Mechanistic Basis

### Summary

This PM converts arriving tyrosine and regulates the sequence of synthesis, vesicular handling, release, receptor signalling, transporter-mediated reuptake and enzymatic metabolism. Precursor-pool availability and LAT1 competition are assessed upstream. Each stage can vary independently, so no single dopamine measure represents the whole mechanism.

<div class="brs-fm-hub-item" data-brs-fm-hub>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-shell">
<button type="button" class="brs-fm-hub-summary" aria-expanded="false">
<span class="brs-fm-hub-chevron" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<strong>Dopaminergic signalling regulation — process, boundaries and integration</strong>
</button>
<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

#### (Synthesis, storage and activity-dependent release)

Fanet et al. (2021) [[1]](#pm-ref-1), Beard et al. (2003) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) and Erikson et al. (2000) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) describe the distinct substrate and cofactor steps in dopamine synthesis: tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to L-DOPA using tetrahydrobiopterin and iron, and aromatic L-amino-acid decarboxylase forms dopamine using PLP. MacDonald et al. (2024) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) describe activity-dependent tonic and phasic dopamine release. Substrate or cofactor dependence establishes reaction biology, not that additional dietary provision increases synthesis, release or function.

#### (Receptors, transporter-mediated reuptake and metabolism)

Cools and D'Esposito (2011) [[4]](#pm-ref-4), Klanker et al. (2013) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) and van der Schaaf et al. (2012) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) show that D1-like and D2-like receptor families have different distributions and circuit effects. MacDonald et al. (2024) [[9]](#pm-ref-9) and Fusar-Poli et al. (2012) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) describe how dopamine-transporter activity controls extracellular signal duration in transporter-rich regions, while COMT and monoamine oxidases contribute to metabolism with region-dependent importance. Karrer et al. (2017) [[8]](#pm-ref-8) and the ADHD studies [[9]](#pm-ref-9) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) also show why receptor availability, transporter binding, synthesis capacity, extracellular release and metabolite concentration must not be used interchangeably.

#### (Boundaries of the mechanism)

[BRS1-FM1-PM1 — Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) covers systemic amino-acid availability and prioritisation. [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) covers competitive transport into the brain. This PM begins with dopaminergic synthesis capacity and extends through signalling, reuptake and metabolism. [BRS1-FM1-PM4 — Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) covers noradrenergic signalling downstream of catecholamine synthesis.

Dietary tyrosine availability must not be equated with increased brain dopamine or improved ADHD symptoms. Pharmacological evidence may establish the relevance of dopaminergic signalling to ADHD, but it cannot establish that a dietary intervention modifies that signalling or improves outcomes.

#### (Integration and evidence boundary)

Cools and D'Esposito (2011) [[4]](#pm-ref-4), Westbrook et al. (2020) [[5]](#pm-ref-5), Klanker et al. (2013) [[6]](#pm-ref-6) and van der Schaaf et al. (2012) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) show that dopaminergic effects on cognition and behaviour are nonlinear, region-specific and state-dependent. Prefrontal stability and striatal flexibility can respond differently to the same manipulation, and Fusar-Poli et al. (2012) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) show that medication exposure can alter transporter measurements. BRS2 methyl-donor availability, BRS3 redox handling, BRS4 synaptic energy supply and BRS6 metabolic, stress and circadian context remain constrained dependencies: they may shape this PM but do not become dopamine findings or dietary levers without relationship-specific evidence.

</div>
</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

Human pharmacology and PET evidence supports context-dependent dopamine regulation: baseline synthesis capacity, receptor involvement and cognitive demand influence motivation and flexibility, so effects are not uniformly enhancing. [[4]](#pm-ref-4) [[5]](#pm-ref-5) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) Exercise, sleep deprivation and dietary restriction studies demonstrate changes in different dopaminergic endpoints—release and receptor availability must be distinguished. [[15]](#pm-ref-15) [[16]](#pm-ref-16) [[17]](#pm-ref-17) Biochemical and deficiency evidence separately supports synthesis requirements, without establishing that extra precursor intake improves human signalling. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[3]](#pm-ref-3)

### 5.2 Cross-BRS Mechanism Relationships

- [BRS-X(Circadian-FM1) — Light and Feeding Zeitgeber Entrainment](/docs/biological-targets/brs-x/circadian/fm1/brs-x-circadian-fm1-zeitgeber-entrainment) — circadian and dopamine/reward regulation may interact bidirectionally. [Glavan et al. (2026)](/docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#glavan_chronobiological_2026) synthesise human and animal evidence; end-to-end human mediation and dietary responsiveness remain unresolved. Circadian timing belongs to BRS-X.

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- **BRS2 constrained dependency:** COMT contributes to dopamine metabolism MacDonald et al. (2024) [[9]](#pm-ref-9). SAM availability is relevant to that chemistry, but this pass did not establish that ordinary one-carbon variation controls regional dopamine clearance or clinical outcomes. Magnesium as a COMT catalytic participant and FAD as a MAO cofactor were assessed as candidates and are not admitted: this page’s sources name the enzymes, not those dietary routes. COMT genotype-specific interpretation remains on the COMT Specific Mechanism.
- **BRS3 constrained dependency:** dopamine oxidation and cofactor recycling create redox interactions, but antioxidant exposure was not shown here to modify human dopaminergic signalling.
- **BRS4 constrained dependency:** synthesis, vesicular cycling and signalling require cellular energy, but no dopamine-specific energy intervention was established.
- **BRS6 constrained dependency:** insulin, stress and circadian state can influence dopamine-related circuits, but end-to-end human mediation and dietary responsiveness remain unresolved.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS1-FM1-PM1 — Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) — Addresses the precursor pool supplying tyrosine for PM3’s dopamine-synthesis step. PM1 assesses availability and prioritisation; PM3 assesses its use in synthesis.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM2 — LAT1 Competitive Transport Modulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm2-lat1-competitive-transport-modulation) — governs competitive transport of large neutral amino acids, including tyrosine, before this PM begins synthesis. Meal composition can change precursor ratios; that is transport bias, not dopamine signalling.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM4 — Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) — uses catecholamine products downstream of dopamine formation. It does not supply this PM’s substrate or cofactors.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM5 — Serotonergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm5-serotonergic-signalling-regulation) — is a parallel monoamine path from shared precursor transport. It does not feed dopaminergic synthesis.

## 7. Phenome Connections

These mappings are translational relationships, not single-mechanism outcome claims. Phenomes are emergent functional patterns supported by multiple interacting PMs across the BRAIN Framework.

scientific_findings:
  - id: PM2-F1
    finding_label: Shared LAT1 transport and precursor competition
    finding_summary: 'Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) carries competing amino acids as part of an exchanger complex. Blood ratios describe substrate presentation, not measured transport flux.'
    finding_interpretation: This establishes competitive transport biology. It does not show that eating more tyrosine or tryptophan increases brain monoamines or improves function.
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: Large neutral amino acids share competitive transport through LAT1 (SLC7A5) with the SLC3A2 heavy chain; plasma composition helps shape substrate availability but is not a direct measurement of net brain uptake.
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'Curated human SLC3A2 annotation and the deposited human LAT1 complex support transporter identity; the inherited Fernstrom review supplies the physiological competition context. Exchange, substrate affinity and cellular context qualify the simple plasma-ratio model. No numerical score is assigned merely for curated identity.'
    synthesis_limitations: Curated transporter and structural records do not quantify an ordinary meal effect in the human brain. The plasma-ratio proxy is not the sole determinant of net flux. The original Finding ID and source history are retained.
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Fernstrom (2013)
        citation_key: fernstrom_lnna_2013
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#fernstrom_lnna_2013
        data_level: Mechanistic
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: 'Dietary and plasma LNAA ratios influence LAT1-mediated brain uptake of tyrosine, tryptophan and related amino acids and can change precursor availability for neurotransmitter synthesis.'
        assessment:
          study: Narrative review of dietary LNAA effects on brain transport and neurochemistry.
          population: Mixed human and experimental literature; not a single intervention sample.
          result: Identified competitive LAT1 transport and plasma-ratio dependence as determinants of brain LNAA entry.
          effect_magnitude: No pooled meal-response effect estimate.
          evidence_summary: Establishes the shared-transporter rule that defines this PM.
          limitations: Review synthesis; does not by itself demonstrate that ordinary meals change human brain monoamines or function.
    presentation: mechanistic-basis
    sec_assessment_ref:

  - id: PM2-F2
    finding_label: Meal composition and protein source alter plasma precursor ratios
    finding_summary: Human feeding experiments demonstrate context-dependent plasma-ratio changes. A higher ratio after one meal than another is not necessarily an increase above baseline.
    finding_interpretation: 'Retain the admitted meal-composition regulatory relationship at its plasma-ratio ceiling. Protein-source experiments qualify generalisation; they do not establish a best ratio, an additional nutrient requirement or a clinical protocol.'
    fm_rollup: true
    finding_statement: 'In the studied healthy adults, meal composition and tested protein sources can alter plasma tryptophan relative to competing large neutral amino acids; the direction and tyrosine response depend on the exposure and sampling context, without establishing increased human brain transport or neurotransmitter synthesis.'
    synthesised_evidence_confidence: not-yet-scored
    synthesis: 'Breakfast contrasts and separate protein-source experiments support meal-responsive precursor ratios, but not one universal direction. The recovered Wurtman table shows lower tryptophan and tyrosine ratios after the protein-rich breakfast, not an increased tyrosine ratio. Evening-meal null results and a starch-control null constrain extrapolation. Brain uptake and downstream effects were not measured by those plasma experiments.'
    synthesis_limitations: 'Small acute healthy-adult samples; different meals, ratio denominators and sampling windows; incomplete historical methods retrieval. No population-wide optimum or direct human brain-flux estimate. Evening null results limit generalisation but are not equivalence evidence.'
    evidence_considered:
      - label: Ashley et al. (1985)
        citation_key: ashley_breakfast_1985
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#ashley_breakfast_1985
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: breakfast meal composition
        evidence_source: repository-inherited
        directional_finding: Breakfast carbohydrate-versus-protein composition changed the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio in healthy lean young men.
        assessment:
          study: Controlled breakfast-composition experiment measuring plasma tryptophan relative to competing large neutral amino acids.
          population: Healthy lean young men.
          result: Breakfast composition altered the plasma tryptophan-to-LNAA ratio.
          effect_magnitude: Directional meal contrast; no general clinical effect size.
          evidence_summary: Shows that a single ordinary breakfast can move the tryptophan competitive ratio.
          limitations: 'Plasma ratio only; no brain transport, serotonin or functional measure; young male sample.'
      - label: Wurtman et al. (2003)
        citation_key: wurtman_effects_2003
        href: /docs/papers/BRAIN-Diet-References#wurtman_effects_2003
        data_level: Human Mechanistic
        exposure_context: high-carbohydrate versus high-protein ordinary meals
        evidence_source: bounded-external-search
        directional_finding: Both plasma precursor ratios fell from baseline after the protein-rich breakfast; between-breakfast responses differed. A tyrosine increase was not demonstrated.
        assessment:
          study: 'Random-order two-breakfast crossover; sampling through four hours, chromatographic amino-acid assays and mixed-model analysis with order and multiplicity considered.'
          population: 'Nine young adults entered; eight completed both conditions (six women, two men).'
          result: Both plasma precursor ratios fell from baseline after the protein-rich breakfast; between-breakfast responses differed. A tyrosine increase was not demonstrated.
          effect_magnitude: 'Median between-breakfast contrast: 54% for tryptophan ratio and 28% for tyrosine ratio; these are not increases after protein. Carbohydrate-arm increases from baseline were not significant.'
          evidence_summary: 'Direct plasma contrast, not brain transport.'
          limitations: One incomplete participant; visible meal differences and unreported concealment/assay blinding; residual uncertainty in magnitude and generalisation.

### Overview

Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) helps control which amino acids can enter the brain. Tyrosine, tryptophan and other large neutral amino acids (LNAAs) compete for this shared route. Human feeding experiments show that meal composition and protein source can alter their relative availability in blood. The response depends on the tested meal and sampling period, rather than a universal carbohydrate-to-protein rule. This transport step connects circulating precursor supply with downstream neurotransmitter pathways. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

- **Biological role:** Relative precursor availability helps shape competition at the blood-brain barrier. It does not directly measure brain transport. [[1]](#pm-ref-1)
- **Implementation Notes:** Meal composition is the retained regulatory input. The tested breakfasts differ from an optimal everyday eating rule, and protein source also matters. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)
- **Biological Relevance:** This transport step follows [amino-acid provision in PM1](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) and precedes downstream signalling.

## 2. Primary Biological Effects
Meal-responsive plasma precursor ratios; direction depends on the tested exposure. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

## 4. Mechanistic Basis + Scientific Findings

### Summary

Large neutral amino acid transporter 1 (LAT1) provides a shared exchange route for amino acids at the blood-brain barrier. Relative blood concentrations help describe competition; they do not alone determine net transport. Meal composition changes that blood-side context, not a measured brain dose. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [Curated C1](#pm2-curated-c1) [Curated C2](#pm2-curated-c2)

<div class="brs-fm-hub-panel" hidden>

<span id="pm2-mechanism-f1" />
<span id="lat1-and-competitive-precursor-transport" />

#### PM2-F1

Tyrosine, tryptophan and other large neutral amino acids (LNAAs) share an exchanger containing LAT1 and its SLC3A2 heavy chain. The curated annotation and deposited human complex establish molecular identity; affinity, exchange conditions and blood-side supply qualify the ratio model. Neither a structural record nor a blood ratio measures an ordinary meal's net brain uptake. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [Curated C1](#pm2-curated-c1) [Curated C2](#pm2-curated-c2)

Supporting evidence: [PM2-F1](#pm2-f1).

<span id="pm2-mechanism-f2" />
<span id="insulin-mediated-partitioning-and-meal-macronutrient-bias" />

#### PM2-F2

Feeding changes circulating amino-acid supply and peripheral handling. The breakfast comparison found different plasma responses between meals, but its protein-rich arm lowered both the tryptophan and tyrosine ratios from baseline. That is not evidence that protein raised the tyrosine ratio. [[2]](#pm-ref-2) Another breakfast experiment supported a tryptophan-ratio contrast, while unfortified evening meals did not show the same change. [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[7]](#pm-ref-7)

Protein identity also matters: tested alpha-lactalbumin, gluten and zein gave different tryptophan-ratio responses, and the starch control was null. Ratios, denominators and measurement windows must remain source-specific; these results do not establish a universal meal rule or human neurotransmitter increase. [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

Supporting evidence: [PM2-F2](#pm2-f2). The existing meal-composition regulatory input remains distinct from an additional preparation or supplementation protocol.

#### Boundaries and functional interpretation

Enriched-protein studies include attention or sleep endpoints, but do not establish ordinary-meal efficacy or direct mediation by LAT1. Positive acute findings and a newer null sleep/performance trial remain separate from the plasma proposition. [[9]](#pm-ref-9) [[10]](#pm-ref-10) See [PM2-F3](#pm2-f3) and the audit. Pool provision belongs upstream in PM1; neurotransmitter synthesis and signalling remain downstream mechanisms.

</div>
</div>

### 4.1 Scientific Findings

#### Summary

LAT1 transport identity is separated from the experimental finding that meal composition changes plasma precursor ratios. Breakfast, evening-meal and protein-source results show why a between-meal difference must not be described as a universal rise above baseline. Plasma ratios do not directly measure brain transport or neurotransmitter production. [[1]](#pm-ref-1) [[2]](#pm-ref-2) [[3]](#pm-ref-3) [[7]](#pm-ref-7) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)

Primary Mechanisms in other Biological Regulatory Systems that directly interact with, constrain or support this mechanism.

- [BRS2(FM1) — Methylation Cycle Efficiency](/docs/biological-targets/brs2/fm1/brs2-fm1-methylation-cycle-efficiency) — One-carbon status can associate with amino-acid metabolism, but this page does not establish that methylation-cycle efficiency regulates LAT1 competition.

### 5.3 Local BRS Mechanism Relationships

Related Primary Mechanisms within the same Biological Regulatory System that collectively support the integrated biological function.

- [BRS1-FM1-PM1 - Amino-Acid Availability & Prioritisation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm1-amino-acid-availability-and-prioritisation) — Supplies the circulating amino-acid pool whose tyrosine and tryptophan then compete at LAT1. That is substrate supply, not transport.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM3 - Dopaminergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm3-dopaminergic-signalling-regulation) — Uses tyrosine after LAT1 presentation for dopamine synthesis. Transport bias is not dopaminergic signalling.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM4 - Noradrenergic Signalling](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm4-noradrenergic-signalling-attention-executive-modulation) — Uses tyrosine after the same transport step for noradrenaline synthesis. Downstream conversion, not a LAT1 input.
- [BRS1-FM1-PM5 - Serotonergic Signalling Regulation](/docs/biological-targets/brs1/fm1/brs1-fm1-pm5-serotonergic-signalling-regulation) — Uses tryptophan after LAT1 presentation for serotonin synthesis. Parallel conversion, not this transporter’s control.

## Scientific Lesson

A ratio can differ between two meals even when neither raises it above its own baseline. Blood precursor ratios, net brain transport and neurotransmitter production are distinct measurements. Do not turn an acute plasma contrast into a nutrient dose or clinical recommendation. [PM2-F2](#pm2-f2).

scientific_findings_intro: 'Longitudinal animal imaging supports task-related spine formation and selective retention; sleep experiments add pruning and resizing, including electron-microscopy-confirmed contacts. Local signalling, actin remodelling and developmental microglial engulfment explain distinct steps. Nutrient experiments show membrane-precursor responses and a DHA–UMP spine effect, not verified human synapse growth. Excitatory spine, inhibitory-marker, ultrastructural, protein and behavioural endpoints remain separate. A developmental DHA study adds contact-marker and cortical-function evidence; defined meal scheduling changes regional maintenance under obesogenic exposure. These contexts do not establish ordinary adult-human benefits.'

## BRS1-5-12 - Synaptic Structural Plasticity

(Formation, selective retention, remodelling and elimination)

## 1. Mission & Overview

### Mission

Maintain and adapt physical connections between neurons through synapse formation, selective stabilisation, structural remodelling and elimination.

### Overview

Neural circuits adapt partly by changing their physical connections. New connections can form, useful ones can persist, and others can be resized or removed. This supports a biological basis for learning and adaptation; increasing connection counts alone is not the goal. The clearest direct structural evidence reviewed here is from animals and neuronal slices, rather than human synapse measurements. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); Li et al. (2017) [[5]](#pm-ref-5)


- **Benefits:** Selective structural adaptation provides a biological basis for retaining learned skills and adapting circuits. The animal studies do not establish a human cognitive treatment. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Li et al. (2017) [[5]](#pm-ref-5)


- **Implementation Notes:** Skill practice, sleep and physical activity are the most directly relevant assessed behaviours. Nutrient supply and experimental combinations have separate, bounded evidence; the studies do not provide a human synapse-growth prescription. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Yang et al. (2014) [[4]](#pm-ref-4); Sakamoto et al. (2007) [[9]](#pm-ref-9); Stranahan et al. (2007) [[13]](#pm-ref-13)


- **Biological Relevance:** Physical circuit organisation supports neuronal communication alongside transmitter signalling. Membrane production and DHA incorporation provide supporting material processes, while developmental pruning and ageing require their own context. Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); Chen et al. (2012) [[7]](#pm-ref-7); Schafer et al. (2012) [[8]](#pm-ref-8); Gupta et al. (2016) [[14]](#pm-ref-14)

## 2. Primary Biological Effects

Formation and persistence of selected dendritic spines; actin and scaffold remodelling; inhibitory-contact dynamics; developmental pruning; sleep-associated synaptic resizing. These are different structural endpoints, not a single measure of better cognition. Xu et al. (2009) [[1]](#pm-ref-1); Bosch et al. (2014) [[2]](#pm-ref-2); de Vivo et al. (2017) [[6]](#pm-ref-6); Chen et al. (2012) [[7]](#pm-ref-7); Schafer et al. (2012) [[8]](#pm-ref-8)
